extraction_result.title: Culture and Aesthetic Preference: Comparing the Attention to Context of East Asians and Americans

findings.consequent: Location of the horizon in landscape paintings (percentage of frame height)
findings.mechanism: East Asian perspective allows artists to use multiple viewpoints, placing the horizon higher to include more contextual information.
findings.quote: the location of the horizon in East Asian paintings was significantly higher than that of Western paintings, t(581) = 10.39, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Ratio of the face area to the entire visual field in portraits (percentage)
findings.mechanism: East Asian painters deemphasize the face in portraits, consistent with contextual emphasis.
findings.quote: the ratio of the size of the face to the size of the entire visual field was substantially smaller in East Asian than in Western portraits, t(415) = 9.10, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Location of the horizon in paintings of people in a scene (percentage of frame height)
findings.mechanism: East Asian paintings are more likely than Western paintings to depict field information.
findings.quote: the location of the horizon was significantly higher in East Asian than in Western paintings, t(399) = 6.08, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Ratio of the largest face area to the entire visual field in paintings of people in a scene (percentage)
findings.mechanism: East Asian paintings emphasize contextual information over the figure.
findings.quote: The ratio of the size of the largest face to the size of the entire visual field was significantly smaller in East Asian than in Western paintings, t(399) = 2.88, p < .005.

findings.consequent: Average location of horizons drawn in landscape pictures (percentage of picture plane)
findings.mechanism: People maintain culturally specific ways of drawing, reflecting context-inclusive styles.
findings.quote: the average location of horizons drawn by East Asians was 19% higher in the picture plane than those drawn by Americans, t(87) = 2.98, p < .005.

findings.consequent: Number of additional contextual objects drawn in landscape pictures
findings.mechanism: East Asians drew 74% more contextual objects, indicating greater context inclusiveness.
findings.quote: East Asians drew 74% more contextual objects than did Americans, t(87) = 2.16, p < .05.

findings.consequent: Size of faces in portrait photographs taken by participants (percentage of frame)
findings.mechanism: East Asians tended to place the model in the background, whereas Americans prioritized the figure.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of culture, F(1, 76) = 6.77, p < .02.

findings.consequent: Self-reported preference for smaller models (9-point rating scale)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer smaller models, consistent with context-inclusive aesthetics.
findings.quote: the Japanese (M = 3.70) were more likely than their Americans counterparts (M = 4.89) to prefer smaller models, t(99) = 3.20, p = .002.

findings.consequent: Self-reported preference for context-inclusive pictures (9-point rating scale)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer context-inclusive images, reflecting holistic attention.
findings.quote: the Japanese (M = 3.79) were more likely than Americans (M = 4.57) to prefer context-inclusive pictures, t(99) = 1.99, p = .05.

findings.mechanism: Middle-range lenses (standard/narrow background) were generally preferred over extremely wide or extremely narrow backgrounds.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of lens, F(1, 98) = 12.05, p < .001.

findings.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Japanese) x Lens focal length (breadth of context)
findings.mechanism: Japanese rated extremely narrow backgrounds more negatively than Americans, showing cultural differences in context preference.
findings.quote: there was an interaction of culture and lenses, F(3, 98) = 7.04, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Average preference for background size (selection from sets with same model size)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely to prefer wider width backgrounds, while Americans preferred context exclusive images.
findings.quote: there was only a main effect of culture, F(1, 98) = 7.90, p < .006. In general, the Japanese were more likely than Americans to prefer wider width backgrounds.

findings.mechanism: The 1.25-in. model was generally preferred by both groups of participants.
findings.quote: there was a main effect for the size of the model, F(1, 98) = 35.82, p < .001.

findings.antecedent: Culture (American vs. Japanese) x Model size
findings.mechanism: Japanese were less likely than Americans to prefer extremely large models (1.75-in. and 2.25-in.).
findings.quote: there was an interaction of culture and model, F(3, 98) = 7.04, p < .001.

findings.consequent: Average preference for model size (selection from sets with same background size)
findings.mechanism: Japanese were more likely than Americans to prefer small models.
findings.quote: there was a main effect of culture, F(1, 98) = 6.34, p < .013 (see Table 5). In general, the Japanese were more likely than the Americans to prefer small models.

stimuli.description: Digital images of traditional East Asian (660) and Western (731) landscape, portrait, and people-in-scene paintings (15th-19th centuries) from major museums.
Blank 8.5 x 11 inch paper with a black frame for participants to draw landscapes.
Digital camera (Sony Digital Mavica 500) used by participants to photograph confederates in various laboratory and atrium settings.
Sets of four artificially composed portrait photographs manipulated for background breadth (using 28mm, 50mm, 100mm, 140mm lenses) and model size (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25 inches tall).

tables.description: Average ratio in percentage of the height of the horizon to the height of the entire frame for landscape paintings, comparing Western and East Asian.
Average ratio in percentage of the area of the face to the total area of the portraits, comparing Western and East Asian.

Average ratio in percentage of the height of the horizon to the entire frame and the average ratio of the area of the face to the area of the entire frame for paintings of people in a scene, comparing Western and East Asian.
Average ratio in percentage of the height of the horizon to the height of the entire frame and the number of additional objects drawn in landscape drawings, comparing Western and East Asian.
Average selection of the model sizes and the background sizes, comparing Westerners' and Japanese' preferences.

limitations: The study cannot isolate the exact cognitive-perceptual information processing that produced the reported results.
Identifying the causal directions among artistic traditions, perceptual habits, and preferred representations is beyond the scope of the current article.
Representational preferences might merely reflect adherence to artistic traditions rather than genuinely different ways of seeing the world, potentially lacking profound psychological meaning.

tables.description: Summary of previous reviews of office environmental factors and occupants' mental and work performances, indicating intervention items and outcome items for each review.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria for the systematic review, based on population, intervention/exposure, comparator, outcome, type of space, type of study, and type of publication.
Summary of final studies included (n = 55) by country/region, study design, sample size, and publication period.
PIEC domains achieved across the 55 studies, indicating whether objective measures, subjective measures, or no measures were used for each domain by author.
Characteristics of included studies (outcome: mental well-being, n = 31), detailing author, country, study type, population, PIEC interventions, measures (objective/subjective), and effect of PIEC.

Characteristics of included studies (outcome: cognitive performance, n = 14), detailing author, country, study type, population, PIEC interventions, measures (objective/subjective), and effect of PIEC.
Characteristics of included studies (outcome: productivity, n = 13), detailing author, country, study type, population, PIEC interventions, measures (objective/subjective), and effect of PIEC.
Characteristics of included studies (outcome: satisfaction, n = 26), detailing author, country, study type, population, PIEC interventions, measures (objective/subjective), and effect of PIEC.
Results of the methodological quality assessment of the individual studies (observational cohort and cross-sectional studies, n = 38) using 14 criteria.
Results of the methodological quality assessment of the individual studies (controlled intervention studies, n = 13) using 14 criteria.
Results of the methodological quality assessment of the individual studies (before-after studies with no control group, n = 4) using 12 criteria.

limitations: The overall quality of the included studies remains as 'fair' according to the protocol of the National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool, indicating possible biases.
The validation analysis of sample size has not been clearly reported in some studies, which might reduce the generalizability of the achieved findings.

Over half of the reviewed studies adopted cross-sectional surveys to collect subjective evaluation of perceived environmental features via self-reported questionnaires, which are less suitable for providing strong evidence for specific interventions.

Controlled intervention experiments and longitudinal studies in the included studies have mainly explored effects of conventional environmental characteristics, with less attention to other PIEC domains (e.g., decoration, naturalness, perceived privacy).
Articles published in non-English sources and grey literature were not included.
Some studies meeting the inclusion criteria may not have been retrieved due to the search syntax used in this review.
Possible biases occurred in the review process despite individual evaluation by reviewers following a strict protocol.

limitations: Need to know more about the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and the way in which the tension between them plays out at different scales in the museum visit, at different times, and with different audiences.
Need for further study of the impact of interactivity on learning.

Nonverbal studies would also help to reveal the learning impacts of a controversial and increasingly common display technique we call “gratuitous interactivity,” where the interactive features of an exhibit are unrelated to its central phenomenon.
Large-scale design issues (e.g., conceptual coherence) are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.
How can we encourage visitors to make more connections among exhibits in a collection?

More research is needed to determine whether instantiations of narrative have simply been flawed, or whether perhaps the chaotic, high-energy environment of a science museum and the nonanecdotal nature of science combine to make storytelling an ineffective strategy for learning in these settings.

findings.antecedent: Correct placement, position, and size of signs, maps, and other wayfinding aids
findings.consequent: Efficient flow of people, quick destination reach, minimum confusion and disorientation in built environments (e.g., transport hubs)
findings.quote: if people are able to find their way in a built environment in an efficient manner due to the correct placement, position and size of signs, maps and other wayfinding aides, then the flow of people during peak periods in places such as train and bus stations, airports and malls will be such that they will be able to reach their desired destination as quickly as possible, with minimum confusion and disorientation.

findings.consequent: Design of spaces for quick and efficient wayfinding
findings.quote: If the principles and elements of wayfinding are understood, then spaces can be designed to ensure that this process can be undertaken as quickly and efficiently as possible.

findings.antecedent: Lack of generic airport terminal design and varied locations/operations of critical points (e.g., check-in, security, gates)
findings.consequent: Confusion and disorientation in airport terminals
findings.quote: Airport terminals are often characterized by confusion and disorientation (Arthur & Passini, 1992; Seidel, 1982). The lack of a generic airport terminal design, combined with different locations and operations of critical points such as check-in counters, security screening points and gates can contribute to this.

findings.antecedent: Passenger characteristics (first-time users, unfamiliarity, cultural/language differences, time-constrained, nervous)
findings.quote: many passengers are first-time users, others are unfamiliar with the particular airport, some come from different cultural backgrounds, others are unfamiliar with the language used and some are often time-constrained and nervous, all of which can put them into a stressful state (Raubal, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Emergency evacuation combined with wrong directions and poor architectural design
findings.consequent: Escalated stress and confusion, potential for injury or death
findings.quote: If the evacuation of the building is required, stress and confusion levels can escalate and passengers must rely on the correct placement and accuracy of signs and maps in order to be able to evacuate the terminal as quickly as possible. This was not the case in 1996 at Dusseldorf Airport where the deaths that occurred were attributed to the communication of wrong directions and poor architectural design (Raubal, 2001).

findings.consequent: Increased efficiency and effectiveness of public building design for people with disabilities
findings.quote: A better understanding of wayfinding may increase efficiency and effectiveness of the use and design of public buildings and spaces for people with disabilities to allow them to make their way from their current location to a desired destination more easily.
The frustration felt when a person is lost or disoriented due to illegible, missing or incorrect signs is a common experience.

findings.consequent: Facilitated passenger progress and improved satisfaction in airports
findings.quote: airports can best facilitate passenger progress and improve satisfaction by focussing on key elements, one of which was the clarity of signage.

findings.consequent: Tangible business costs (lost staff time, reduced staff concentration, lost business, missed appointments, lawsuits, missed operational targets, injury/death)
findings.quote: The cost associated with being lost is tangible. Lost staff time, reduced staff concentration due to providing directions, lost business, missed appointments or delayed meetings, potential lawsuits due to a lack of accessibility, failure to meet legislative or operational targets such as inbound or outbound passenger processing times and injury or death during an emergency situation are all areas of costs for businesses (Arthur & Passini, 1992; Carpman & Grant, 2002).

findings.antecedent: Design adhering to universal design principles (equitable use, flexibility, simple/intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, appropriate size/space)
findings.consequent: Improved usability, accessibility, safety, efficiency, comfort, and wayfinding
findings.quote: Connell et al. (1997) proposed principles of universal design, outlined in Table 1, in an attempt to guide designers, engineers and architects design environments that are not only functional, but are also conducive to wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Diversity of users (e.g., in transportation hubs)
findings.quote: In a setting like a transportation hub, the diversity of users present increases the complexity of wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Formation of a suitable cognitive map of the environment
findings.quote: Successful spatial orientation occurs when a person can form a suitable cognitive map of the environment in order to establish their position (Casakin et al., 2000).

findings.consequent: Quick identification of the shortest and most efficient route
findings.quote: Once this orientation has been obtained, the shortest and most efficient route from their current position to a desired destination is quickly identified (Seneviratne & Morrall, 1985; Ueberschaer, 1971).

findings.antecedent: Implicit strategies (e.g., least angle, initial segment, fewest landmarks/turns)
findings.consequent: Route choice and minimized mental/physical effort
findings.quote: Route choice is affected by implicit strategies that minimize the mental and physical efforts involved in moving through the environment when there is no obvious correct decision (Christenfeld, 1995; Conroy Dalton, 2003; Hochmair & Karlsson, 2005; Hölscher, Meilinger, Vrachliotis, Brösamle, & Knauff, 2006; Seneviratne & Morrall, 1985; Wiener & Mallot, 2003; Wiener, Schnee, & Mallot, 2004).
Sometimes, due to people's different preferences, a strategy is chosen even if it results in selecting a relatively inefficient route (Brunyé et al., 2010).
Successfully obtaining spatial orientation depends on a person's spatial ability (Lawton, 2010).

findings.consequent: Ability to form spatial orientation and undertake successful wayfinding
findings.quote: Additionally, the language used to communicate directions impacts on a person's ability to successfully form spatial orientation, and hence undertake successful wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Impaired spatial orientation and wayfinding errors
findings.quote: Using verbal directions instead of or in addition to maps can cause the formation of spatial orientation, and hence wayfinding to go awry (Allen et al., 2004).

findings.antecedent: Culture and social situation of an individual
findings.quote: Spatial decision-making and wayfinding are impacted by the cultural and social situation of an individual.

findings.antecedent: Cultural/linguistic differences (vocabulary, terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms, conversation style)
findings.quote: Differences in vocabulary and terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms and in conversation style (Frank, 2009; Grice, 1989; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Montello, 1995) also exist.

Studies have found that differences exist in male and female spatial navigation and performance (Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Jonasson, 2005; Linn & Petersen, 1985, Tlauka, Brolse, Pomeroy, & Hobbs, 2005), with men usually performing better than women in many spatial activities in wayfinding (Chen, Chang, & Chang, 2009; Contreras, Martínez-Molina, & Santacreu, 2012; Lawton, 2010; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Malinowski & Gillespie, 2001).

Spatial anxiety is also experienced differently, with women showing greater spatial anxiety than men (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Gabriel, Hong, Chandra, Lonborg, & Barkley, 2011; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Malinowski & Gillespie, 2001).
It has been shown that the spatial performance and the effects of stress are negatively correlated (Quaiser-Pohl, Geiser, & Lehmann, 2006; Titze, Heil, & Jansen, 2008).

findings.consequent: Preference for and reliance on distal cues (e.g., hill lines) for orientation and direction
findings.quote: Men seem to prefer and rely on distal cues such as hill lines that give information on orientation and direction (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Fortenbaugh, Chaudhury, Hicks, Hao, & Turano, 2007).

findings.consequent: Dependence on exact pinpoint cues (e.g., landmarks) to identify visual scenes and form spatial orientation
findings.quote: In comparison, women depend on exact pinpoint cues such as landmarks to identify a visual scene and form spatial orientation (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Lawton, 2010).

Men have also shown to be more accurate in navigating tasks when directional information is given (Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Lawton, 2010; Levy, Astur, & Frick, 2005; Postma, Jager, Kessels, Koppeschaar, & van Honk, 2004)

findings.consequent: Better object memory and object-location memory
findings.quote: women have a better object memory and object-location memory than men (Levy et al., 2005).

findings.consequent: Significantly better scores in mental rotation, spatial perception, dynamic spatial ability, and slightly better in spatial visualization tests
findings.quote: Studies have found that males score significantly better in mental rotation, spatial perception tests and dynamic spatial ability (Cherney & Collaer, 2005; Collaer & Hill, 2006; Halpern & Tan, 2001; Jonasson, 2005; Lawton, 2010; Linn & Petersen, 1985; Silverman, Choi, & Peters, 2007; Titze et al., 2008) and only slightly better than females in spatial visualization (Linn & Petersen, 1985).
Testosterone levels, or exposure to testosterone, have been shown to increase the performance in navigational tasks (Halpern & Tan, 2001; Jonasson, 2005; Lawton, 2010).

findings.antecedent: Oestrogen levels in women during menstrual cycle phases
findings.quote: There are conflicting results on the effect of oestrogen levels in women during the different phases of their menstrual cycle and their spatial performance (Chiarello, McMahon, & Schaefer, 1989; Gabriel et al., 2011; Halpern & Tan, 2001).
The more pronounced right hemisphere on males is attributed to better performance in spatial tasks as this part of the brain is engaged during spatial processing (McGlone, 1980).

findings.consequent: Easier adaptation to changing route instructions
findings.quote: Women tend to adapt more easily to changing route instructions than men.

findings.antecedent: Instructions given in a relative frame of reference
findings.consequent: Better wayfinding performance, fewer stops and deviations
findings.quote: People perform better at wayfinding tasks when they are given their instructions in a relative frame of reference. More stops and deviations were needed to find a destination when people were given instructions in the absolute reference frame.

findings.consequent: Important role in everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation
findings.quote: These elements, particularly landmarks, play an important role in the everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation (Caduff & Timpf, 2006; O'Neill, 1991a; Richter, 2007; Tom & Denis, 2003)

findings.consequent: Vital factors for wayfinding, providing information for orientation, direction, decision-making, and connectivity visualization
findings.quote: communication mechanisms such as maps and signs are also vital factors. These elements are shown in Figure 1, with examples of these elements from airports. Maps and signs are wayfinding devices (Lynch, 1960) that provide information for orientation, direction for decision-making and visualize the connectivity between a current and desired location.

findings.antecedent: Good map design principles (organizes spaces, shows elements without overload, identifies current position, orients map, unambiguous graphics, proportional lettering, sufficient info)
findings.quote: The elements of good map design, outlined in Table 5 (Apelt, 2008; Hölscher, Büchner, Brösamle, Meilinger, & Strube, 2007; Thorndyke & Hayes-Roth, 1982), include the organization of the environment into clear spaces and ensure that the map remains uncluttered while showing enough information and all the elements of a built environment.

findings.antecedent: Correct positioning, lighting, noticeability, legibility, and orientation of directional/information signs
findings.quote: Directional and information signs must be positioned in well-lit places at critical points (such as nodes and decision points), be noticeable and unobstructed, be legible and oriented so that they relate to the actual environment (Apelt, 2008; Tzeng & Huang, 2009).

findings.consequent: User reassurance of correct direction of travel
findings.quote: Reassurance signs signal confirmation to an individual that they are headed in the right direction. These signs should be placed beyond decision points to provide the user reassurance of the correct direction of travel (Fewings, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Consistent design elements (size, colour, lettering, symbols) combined with correct lighting in signage system
findings.quote: A good signage system within an environment must use consistent design elements of size, colour, lettering and symbols. When combined with correct lighting, it is more likely to be noticed by users (Fewings, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices
findings.quote: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices are easier to comprehend (Lynch, 1960).

findings.antecedent: Placement of landmarks at decision points
findings.consequent: Affected cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitated orientation
findings.quote: The placement of landmarks at decision points affect cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitate orientation (Lynch, 1960; Richter, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Landmark salience (contrast in attributes, status, or spatial location)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of the landmark for wayfinding
findings.quote: For a landmark to be salient, it must contrast with the environment in either its attributes (colour, texture, etc.), status (e.g. a church or commercial building) or its spatial location with respect to other objects in the environment (e.g. in the middle of town) (Caduff and Timpf, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Use of landmarks as primary means of providing directions to pedestrians
findings.quote: Landmarks should be used as the primary means of providing directions to pedestrians (May, Ross, Bayer, and Tarkiainen, 2003).

findings.consequent: Calming effect, increased focus on visual/mental tasks, increased awareness, directed people to destination, increased navigability (cool-coloured walls)
findings.quote: Cool colours are calming and help people focus on visual and mental tasks. Cool colours can increase awareness and help direct people to a destination. It has been shown that cool-coloured walls are seen as more navigable (Hidayetoglu, Yildirim, and Akalin, 2012; Stone, 2003).

findings.consequent: Outward focus, increased awareness, easier space perception, effective landmarks for wayfinding
findings.quote: Warm colours focus people outwards and increase their awareness. The use of warm colours allows people to more easily perceive the space and it has been shown that warm colours can be effectively used as landmarks for wayfinding purposes (Hawes, Brunyé, Mahoney, Sullivan, and Aall, 2012; Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Stone, 2003).

findings.consequent: Affects emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation, problem-solving abilities; low brightness perceived negatively; increased brightness correlated with positive perception of space
findings.quote: Indoor lighting directly effects people's emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation and problem-solving abilities. Spaces with low brightness levels are perceived negatively compared to other brightness levels. Increases in the brightness level of a space positively correlated with positive perception of the space (Hawes et al., 2012; Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Knez and Kers, 2000).

findings.antecedent: Cool colours and high brightness levels
findings.quote: The use of cool colours and high brightness levels help people to be spatially orientated (Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Hygge and Knez, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Map learning aligned with initial orientation of the map
findings.consequent: Superior wayfinding performance (precise but inflexible representation)
findings.quote: Map learning leads to superior performance only when aligned with the initial orientation of the map. The resulting representation is precise, yet inflexible (Richardson, Montello, and Hegarty, 1999).

findings.antecedent: Access to floor maps in an unfamiliar building
findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning
findings.quote: There is mixed evidence regarding the existence of a positive relationship between access to floor maps and an improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning in an unfamiliar building (Hölscher et al., 2007).
Signage is used to compensate for complex floor plans in order to make wayfinding easier (O'Neill, 1991a).
Signs placed at decision points improve the wayfinding performance (Best, 1970).

findings.consequent: Greatest effect on wayfinding and heavy reliance for decision-making
findings.quote: Direction signage has been shown to have the greatest effect on wayfinding and is relied upon heavily in order to make decisions regarding wayfinding (Tzeng and Huang, 2009).

findings.consequent: Enhanced wayfinding, reduced confusion and stress (but can be ignored or confusing in other cases)
findings.quote: In some settings, signage enhances wayfinding and reduces confusion and stress; however, in other cases, it is ignored or found to be confusing (Seidel, 1982; O'Neill, 1991a).

findings.consequent: More effective in reducing wayfinding errors (wrong turns, backtracks)
findings.quote: Textual signage has been shown to be more effective than graphical signage in reducing wayfinding errors such as wrong turns and backtracks.

findings.consequent: Faster flow of people in a building
findings.quote: Graphic signage though has been shown to allow for a faster flow of people in a building.

findings.consequent: Increased wayfinding difficulty, decreased cognitive map accuracy, increased time to destination, increased wrong turns and backtracking incidents
findings.quote: Increases in the ICD result in an increase in wayfinding difficulty due to the decrease in the accuracy of the cognitive map formed (O'Neill, 1991b). It also increases the mean time to find a destination, the average number of wrong terms and the average number of backtracking incidents.

findings.antecedent: Building's spatial configuration (space syntax measures like integration)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance and spatial learning adaptation
findings.quote: correlations existed between the measures of a building's spatial configuration and indicators of the wayfinding performance (Peponis et al., 1990). [...] travel patterns began to correlate strongly with 'integration' and other space syntax global measures which suggests that spatial learning adapts to the larger organization characteristics of the environment (Haq and Zimring, 2003).

findings.consequent: Different route choices (novices chose more visually connected/integrated paths; experts took hidden routes)
findings.quote: novices chose travel paths that were more visually connected and 'integrated' than the expert travellers who were more likely to take hidden routes (Hölscher, Brosamle, and Vrachliotis, 2010).

findings.mechanism: Alignment effects between the orientation of an observer during learning and the imagined orientation during test.
findings.quote: human observers have an easier time retrieving from memory the spatial relations between locations as seen from this viewpoint than from other, misaligned views or headings

findings.antecedent: imagined orientation during test aligned with orientation during learning (e.g., standing at 4, looking at 3, where is 2?)
findings.consequent: correctness of answers to spatial questions
findings.mechanism: Alignment effects between the orientation of an observer during learning and the imagined orientation during test.
findings.quote: Questions like “Imagine you are standing at 4, looking at 3, where is 2?” are easier to answer correctly than “Imagine you are standing at 2, looking at 4, where is 3?”.

findings.antecedent: imagined heading aligned with the first view a person has of a spatial layout during learning
findings.consequent: speed and correctness of response when recalling object locations
findings.mechanism: A person mentally represents the first view of a configuration and integrates new information from other viewpoints into this representation, leaving the original orientation intact.
findings.quote: he will be fastest and most correct in his response when imagining himself in the same heading as the first view.

findings.antecedent: imagined heading aligned with the second view a person has of a spatial layout during learning
findings.consequent: speed and correctness of response when recalling object locations
findings.mechanism: A person mentally represents the first view of a configuration and integrates new information from other viewpoints into this representation, leaving the original orientation intact.
findings.quote: Imagined headings corresponding to the second view are no better than other, not experienced headings.

findings.antecedent: imagined alignment with a square room's two main axes parallel to the walls (vs. diagonals)
findings.consequent: ease of retrieving spatial knowledge about object configuration
findings.mechanism: People are sensitive to the spatial structure of the environment.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner, Saade, & Lüer (1998)
findings.quote: she will have a much easier time retrieving the spatial knowledge about the configuration when imagining herself aligned with the room's two main axes parallel to the walls

findings.antecedent: imagined alignment with the street grid (vs. misaligned) in a large-scale city environment
findings.consequent: ease of pointing in the direction of important landmarks
findings.mechanism: People are sensitive to the spatial structure of the large-scale environment.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner & Schmidt (1999) and Montello (1991)
findings.quote: participants have a much easier time imagining themselves aligned with the street grid than misaligned with the street grid

findings.consequent: use of slant to structure spatial memories
findings.mechanism: Environmental slant provides a salient reference for spatial organization.
findings.source: text, p. 5, citing Werner (2001) and Werner, Schmidt, & Jainek (in prep.)
findings.quote: observers use environmental slant not only to communicate spatial relations verbally, but also to structure their spatial memories

findings.antecedent: imagining oneself facing uphill or downhill (aligned with steepest gradient) in a sloped environment
findings.consequent: speed and accuracy of accessing spatial knowledge about the sloped environment
findings.mechanism: Alignment with the steepest gradient of the space facilitates spatial knowledge access.
findings.quote: Accessing spatial knowledge about this sloped environment was fastest and most accurate when imagining oneself facing uphill or downhill, thus aligning oneself with the steepest gradient of the space.

findings.antecedent: floor plans with identical Inter-Connection Density (ICD) index but varying symmetry, orientation, or regularity (from left to right in Figure 3)
findings.consequent: perceived complexity of the floor plans
findings.mechanism: Figural properties beyond path options influence perceived complexity.
findings.quote: Their perceived complexity, however, rises from left to right, by making the figures less symmetric, changing the orientation, or making the figure less regular.

findings.antecedent: Göttingen town hall floor plan (with conflicting spatial reference systems, e.g., elevator area rotated 45 degrees relative to main building)
findings.consequent: difficulty to understand and navigate the building, low architectural legibility
findings.mechanism: Conflicting spatial reference systems make integration of spatial knowledge difficult.
findings.quote: Informal interviews with people working in or visiting this building revealed that it is difficult to understand and navigate. The architectural legibility is very low.

findings.antecedent: map arrangement where depicted information (street grid) was aligned with the visual vertical and horizontal
findings.consequent: ease of interpreting and using spatial information gathered from a map
findings.mechanism: Alignment with visual axes facilitates spatial information processing.
findings.quote: observers had an easier time interpreting and using spatial information gathered from a map in which the depicted information was aligned with the visual vertical and horizontal

findings.antecedent: map arrangement where depicted information (street grid) was misaligned with the visual vertical and horizontal
findings.consequent: errors in judgements about spatial relations made from memory
findings.mechanism: Misalignment with visual axes hinders spatial information processing.
findings.quote: a misalignment with these axes led to more errors in judgements about spatial relations made from memory

findings.antecedent: consistent alignment of reference axes throughout a building
findings.consequent: cognitive load for wayfinding and keeping track of position
findings.mechanism: Reduces difficulty in integrating spatial information across multiple places.
findings.quote: the consistent alignment of reference axes throughout the building, all other things being equal, will greatly reduce the cognitive load while keeping track of once position.

Schematic floor plans with varying ICD index (Figure 2)
Schematic floor plans with identical ICD but different perceived complexity (Figure 3)
Similar floor plans with different perceived complexity and views from within (Figure 5, top)
Geometric figures illustrating intrinsic and extrinsic reference systems (Figure 5, bottom)
Schematic floor plan of the city hall of Göttingen, Germany (Figure 6)
Schematic display of spatial situation in the town hall (Figure 7)
Maps of downtown Minneapolis (Warehouse district map, Downtown Hotels map) with different alignments

limitations: The paper primarily synthesizes and applies findings from other studies (including the authors' prior work) rather than presenting new, detailed empirical data with specific participant numbers, p-values, or effect sizes within this publication.
The concept of 'complexity' is vaguely defined and comprises different components, making its quantification challenging.
Figural complexity of a 2D floor plan may not accurately represent the navigational complexity of the 3D spatial environment.
The 'small experiment' and 'informal interviews' mentioned lack detailed methodological information (e.g., sample size, specific measures, statistical results) within this paper.

findings.antecedent: Visual features (contrast, grouping, symmetry) in architecture
findings.quote: The visual system is sensitive to features like contrast, grouping, and symmetry (Ramachandran & Hirstein, 1999). ... These visual mechanisms may mediate the pleasure response associated with viewing ordered patterns of form and color in architecture (Alexander, 2002). ... Balance, of which symmetry is the most straightforward example, also contributes to fluency and aesthetic preference (Wilson & Chatterjee, 2005).

findings.antecedent: Fractal dimensions (ranging from 1.3 to 1.5) in natural scenes, visual art, and computer-generated patterns
findings.quote: Aesthetic preferences for natural scenes, visual art, and computer-generated patterns seem to correlate moderately with fractal dimensions ranging from about 1.3 to 1.5 (Taylor et al., 2005; Spehar, Clifford, Newell, & Taylor, 2003)

findings.antecedent: Moderate level of visual complexity (in art and architectural interiors)
findings.quote: Empirical findings tentatively support this view, suggesting that people generally prefer at least a moderate level of visual complexity when viewing both art and architectural interiors (Dosen & Ostwald, 2016; Leder et al., 2004; Frith & Nias, 1974). As Berlyne postulated many years ago, preferences tend to follow an inverted U-shaped curve in relation to complexity (Güçlütürk et al., 2016; Imamoglu, 2000; Berlyne, 1970, 1971).
Excess architectural complexity may also overwhelm the visual system, particularly if the information is experienced as disorganized (Kotabe et al., 2016; Salingaros, 2003, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Landscapes with visual features and spatial configurations that favor survival (e.g., savannah-like environments with prospect and refuge)
findings.quote: Appleton's habitat theory offers an evolutionary framework to explain psychological responses to architectural spaces. According to habitat theory, humans evolved to prefer landscapes containing visual features and spatial configurations that favor survival (Appleton, 1975). People may have an innate visual preference for moderately complex, savannah-like environments (Joye, 2007; Balling & Falk, 1982), because these areas signal both safety and nourishment.

findings.antecedent: Open architectural interiors and urban spaces (compared to enclosed environments)
findings.consequent: Visual preference, judged more beautiful, activation in temporal lobes (associated with perceived visual motion)
findings.quote: People often prefer architectural interiors and urban spaces that are more open and visually connected to their surroundings compared with enclosed environments (Dosen & Ostwald, 2016). In an fMRI study of architectural interiors, we found that participants judged open rooms as more beautiful than enclosed rooms (Vartanian et al., 2015). Open interiors activated structures in the temporal lobes associated with perceived visual motion, including the left middle temporal gyrus and the right superior temporal gyrus (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.consequent: Preference, activation in visuo-spatial attention and exploration areas (left precuneus, left middle frontal gyrus)
findings.quote: Participants in this study also preferred rooms with higher ceilings over those with lower ceilings, which could be interpreted as a preference for greater visual prospect. Supporting this interpretation, high ceilings activated structures associated with visuo-spatial attention and exploration, including the left precuneus and the left middle frontal gyrus (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.antecedent: Living and life-like stimuli of the natural world (e.g., vegetation, wildlife, motion of leaves)
findings.consequent: Heightened sensory sensitivity, capture of attention ('soft fascinations')
findings.quote: E.O. Wilson's biophilia hypothesis proposes that our sensory systems developed heightened sensitivity to living and life-like stimuli of the natural world (Wilson, 1984). Kaplan and colleagues proposed that inherently fascinating visual stimuli in natural landscapes, like vegetation, wildlife, and “the motion of leaves in the breeze" (Kaplan, 1995, p. 174), capture the attention of our visual system in a bottom-up fashion (Berman et al., 2014; Berman, Jonides, & Kaplan, 2008; Ulrich & Parsons, 1992). This body of work suggests that within nature humans are more likely to orient and attend to these "soft fascinations" (Kaplan, 1995, p. 174) associated with living objects.

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear architectural interiors (compared to rectilinear interiors)
findings.consequent: Judged more beautiful and pleasing, activation in visual cortex (lingual and calcarine gyrus), activation in ACC (correlated with beauty ratings)
findings.quote: We, for instance, found that images of curvilinear architectural interiors activated the lingual and the calcarine gyrus in the visual cortex more than images of rectilinear interiors when participants made approach-avoidance choices (Vartanian et al., 2013). ... Our study revealed that curvilinear building interiors are judged as more beautiful and pleasing than rectilinear spaces and that beauty ratings of curved rooms correlated with increased activation of ACC (Vartanian et al., 2013).

findings.consequent: Occupant's emotional response, revival of memories (e.g., childhood home)
findings.quote: Odor affects an occupant's emotional response to a building (Barbara & Perliss, 2006), perhaps because of the direct link between the olfactory and limbic system (Ward, 2015). Olfaction can revive memories of past experiences in a place, like a childhood home, by activating neural structures governing memory, affect, and meaning (Lehrer, 2008).

findings.consequent: Perceived fullness and complexity of sound, whether a place is designed for contemplation or excitement
findings.quote: Acoustic parameters like reverberation time affect the fullness and complexity of the sound perceived and probably contributes to whether a place is designed for contemplation as in a monastery or for excitement as in a stadium.

findings.consequent: Occupant's comfort, emotional state, perception of beauty
findings.quote: A building's temperature, for instance, influences an occupant's comfort, emotional state, and perception of beauty (Thorsson, Honjo, Lindberg, Eliasson, & Lim, 2007; Nicol & Humphreys, 2002; Fanger, 1973).

findings.consequent: Neural activity in the global pallidus
findings.quote: Beauty evaluations of architecture can vary with neural activity in the global pallidus (Vartanian et al., 2013), perhaps suggestive of motor responses (Nambu, Tokuno, & Takada, 2002).

findings.consequent: Decisions to approach or avoid a space, activation in reward and emotion processing areas (nucleus accumbens, anterior insula, basolateral amygdala)
findings.quote: Aesthetic parameters like enclosure has an impact on decisions to approach or avoid a space (Vartanian et al., 2015), which may be governed by reward and emotion processing areas like the nucleus accumbens, the anterior insula, and the basolateral amygdala (Vartanian et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Exposure to images of tall buildings
findings.consequent: Heightened feelings of awe, greater immobility, slower response on manual clicking task
findings.quote: Intriguingly, Joye and Dewitte found that exposure to images of tall buildings—which were associated with heightened feelings of awe—caused participants to experience greater immobility and to respond more slowly on a manual clicking task than exposure to images of low buildings (Joye & Dewitte, 2016).

findings.consequent: Different cortical areas activated when viewing buildings, increased activation of reward circuitry (medial OFC, subcallosal cingulate gyrus) for aesthetic judgments, greater activation of hippocampus and precuneus (memory retrieval)
findings.quote: In one fMRI study, architecture students recruited different cortical areas when viewing buildings than students from other disciplines (Wiesmann & Ishai, 2011). Another experiment showed that architects, compared with nonarchitects, had increased activation of reward circuitry, including the bilateral medial OFC and the subcallosal cingulate gyrus, when making aesthetic judgments about buildings (Kirk, Skov, Christensen, & Nygaard, 2009). Architects also exhibited greater activation of the hippocampus and precuneus compared with control participants when viewing buildings but not faces, suggesting that memories rendered by education and professional experience contributed to their affective responses.

findings.antecedent: Past experiences in a built environment
findings.consequent: Generation of cognitive maps (place and grid cells in hippocampus), efficient navigation, influence on aesthetic experience (familiarity, liking)
findings.quote: A person's past experiences in a built environment can modulate their present interactions with that space. Exposure to an environment generates a cognitive map using place and grid cells of the hippocampus (McNaughton et al., 2006; O'keefe & Nadel, 1978), which in turn facilitates more efficient navigation in future encounters (Astur et al., 2002; Maguire et al., 2000). ... Because familiarity influences liking (Montoya et al., 2017), we suspect that familiarity and ease of navigation would influence the aesthetic experience of spaces.

findings.antecedent: Perceived environmental control (e.g., operable windows, fans, thermostats)
findings.consequent: Tolerance for a wider range of indoor temperatures, thermal comfort
findings.quote: Occupants who control environmental parameters affecting building temperature, such as operable windows, fans, and thermostats, tolerate a wider range of indoor temperatures than inhabitants with restricted control over their indoor climate (Nicol & Humphreys, 2002). findings.antecedent: Context and cultural meaning (e.g., labeling visual art as 'gallery pieces' vs. 'computer-generated images')
findings.consequent: Aesthetic experience, emotional responses, activation in prefrontal, orbitofrontal, and entorhinal cortices
findings.quote: Context and cultural meaning also have an impact on aesthetic experience (Leder et al., 2004). Art randomly assigned the "gallery" label generated increased activity in prefrontal, orbitofrontal, and entorhinal cortices than those assigned the “computer” label, indicating that participants' expectations about the aesthetic value of the artworks influenced their emotional responses.

findings.antecedent: Building's advertised cultural significance and intended function (e.g., prison vs. Buddhist temple)
findings.quote: Similar to the gallery condition for art, a building's advertised cultural significance could shape an occupant's expectations and alter his or her experience of the space. ... findings.consequent: Activation in OFC, BG, ACC, and anterior insula (core neural circuit for aesthetic emotions)
findings.quote: In a meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies investigating positive-valence aesthetic appraisal, Brown and colleagues proposed that the processing of aesthetic emotions occurs through a core neural circuit involving the OFC, the BG, the ACC, and the anterior insula (Brown et al., 2011).

findings.consequent: Greater reactivity to stress test, heightened and prolonged spikes in salivary cortisol, fear, negative emotions
findings.quote: Another group of researchers found that study participants immersed in a virtual simulation of an enclosed room without windows exhibited greater reactivity to a stress test than participants who undertook the test in a virtual room with windows (Fich et al., 2014). Those who took the test in the enclosed virtual space experienced both heightened and prolonged spikes in salivary cortisol compared with participants immersed in the more open environment. In these two studies, the same design parameter, enclosure, produced both fear and elevated levels of stress hormones, presumably because emotion-regulating limbic structures like the amygdala modulate downstream activity of the neuroendocrine and autonomic nervous systems (Ulrich-Lai & Herman, 2009).

findings.antecedent: Visual and limbic systems working in concert
findings.consequent: Rapid identification and evaluation of visual information, quick emotional response (positive/negative)
findings.quote: The idea that the visual and limbic systems work in concert to rapidly identify and evaluate incoming visual information is consistent with Ulrich's framework, which proposes that initial affective responses toward environments are primarily influenced by automatic, unconscious processing (Ulrich, 1983). Some studies suggest that positive and negative emotional responses to environmental scenes occur rapidly and automatically (Joye & Dewitte, 2016; Valtchanov & Ellard, 2015; Hietanen & Korpela, 2004; Korpela, Klemettilä, & Hietanen, 2002).

For example, Do Dio and colleagues found that aesthetic judgment tasks actually diminish emotional responses to visual art. Participants who were asked to rate the beauty of Renaissance sculptures showed decreased activation in the right insula compared with those who were merely instructed to passively observe the sculptures (Di Dio, Macaluso, & Rizzolatti, 2007).
For instance, chronic exposure to unwanted noise can increase blood pressure (Payne, Potter, & Cain, 2014) and hinder adolescent neural development (Gilbert & Galea, 2014).
Insufficient daylight may affect circadian rhythms and impair sleep quality (Dutton, 2014).
For example, immersion in red environments may improve performance on detail-oriented cognitive tasks whereas blue spaces might be associated with enhanced creative thinking (Mehta & Zhu, 2009).
whereas blue spaces might be associated with enhanced creative thinking (Mehta & Zhu, 2009).

Some reviewed studies (e.g., Katabaro and Yan [10]) did not clearly distinguish between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements.
Further research is required on the impact of lighting glare and colour rendering on human behaviour, which has not been studied deeply in most research, affecting visual performance and comfort.
Gaps in participant diversity, evaluation methods, and data analysis persist across the reviewed literature.
Ethical considerations and experimental design issues also need addressing in future research.

The scope of this systematic review was limited to peer-reviewed articles from a single database (Scopus), potentially excluding other academic work (e.g., dissertations, research reports) and more extensive results from specialized databases (e.g., Web of Science, PsycINFO, PubMed).

findings.quote: Where construction is more permanent, a lack of fit is repeatedly introduced into the dwelling by changes due to the developmental cycle (161, 178, 274).

findings.consequent: Larger houses, larger domestic groups, and expression of social organization changes in built form
findings.quote: Household wealth, however, determines whether changes in social organization find expression in built form (205). In these and many societies, the houses of the wealthy are larger, not only because they consume more space per person but also because the domestic groups are larger (205, 264).

findings.consequent: Architecture becomes a vehicle for representation of status differences
findings.quote: With increased wealth and social inequality, architecture becomes a vehicle for the representation of status differences.

findings.consequent: Constant rebuilding of houses, adapting to developmental cycle changes, and moving houses to reaffirm patrilocal residence/strengthen land claims
findings.quote: Because of the impermanence of housing materials in tropical climates, the people of Vanuatu must constantly rebuild their houses, adapting them to changes brought about by the developmental cycle of the household. In rebuilding, however, they often move the houses to a new site. Rodman argues that this action reaffirms patrilocal residence in a matrilineal society and helps to strengthen claims and access of offspring to land held by the father's matriline.

findings.consequent: Conditioning of household choices and abilities in altering dwelling forms to familial needs
findings.quote: Schwertdfeger concludes that larger socioeconomic forces beyond the domestic group condition the choices and abilities of households in altering dwelling forms to conform to familial needs.

findings.consequent: Spatial segregation, accommodation of privacy, and enhanced separation in built forms
findings.quote: The most extreme example of spatial segregation is found in Near Eastern Muslim societies observing purdah. A number of studies concentrate on how built forms accommodate privacy and enhance the separation required by purdah (74, 285, 341, 389).

findings.antecedent: Increasing integration into the capitalist system (Bedouins)
findings.consequent: Construction of houses with traditional tent plans but more specialized spaces
findings.quote: Layne (227) examines Bedouins who become sedentary as a result of their increasing integration into the capitalist system. While they construct houses using organizational principles found in traditional tent plans, they create more spaces and use them in a more specialized manner.

findings.antecedent: Modernization of urban Japanese apartment plans
findings.quote: Increasing participation in the capitalist system has also affected Greek housing (279), and the modernization of urban Japanese apartment plans has distanced neighborhood social relations (252).

findings.consequent: More specialized interior spaces, men staying home, reduced neighborhood interaction
findings.quote: In rural Portugal, increased affluence has added more specialized interior spaces, employment outside the local community has encouraged men to stay home, and suburban-style houses have reduced neighborhood interaction (216).

findings.consequent: Symbolize dimensions of political and social structure
findings.quote: The clearest exposition of this approach is Hilda Kuper's seminal argument that specific locations symbolize dimensions of Swazi political and social structure (210).

findings.antecedent: Different domestic forms and their landscapes (US, India)
findings.consequent: Express institutionalized strategies for presenting the self as a member of a particular social group
findings.quote: The most developed thesis on housing and identity relations is Duncan's (83), who argues from studies in the United States and India that different domestic forms and their landscapes express institutionalized strategies for presenting the self as a member of a particular social group (81, 82).

findings.consequent: Shift from collectivistic social relations/values (closed groups, segregated sexual division of labor, women as containers) to individualistic forms (open groups, high mobility, status symbols) in house styles
findings.quote: As developing countries modernize or become more westernized, collectivistic social relations and values that are represented in house styles shift to individualistic forms (83).

findings.consequent: Patterned cultural behaviors, including built forms (e.g., Trobriand settlement plans, kinship relations, food categories)
findings.quote: Jakobson, Lévi-Strauss postulates the existence of (a) a structured collective unconscious capable of generating patterned cultural behaviors, including built forms; and (b) unconscious mental structures comprised of binary oppositions that represent universal characteristics of human thought (231).

findings.antecedent: Objectification of symbolic oppositions inside the house (Kabyle)
findings.consequent: Inculcation of habitus (generative/structuring principle of collective strategies/social practices)
findings.quote: Bourdieu locates a principal mechanism for inculcating habitus in the objectification of symbolic oppositions found inside the house.

findings.antecedent: Physical activities and movement through space (Marakwet)
findings.consequent: Revelation of meaning and reinforcement of gender ideologies
findings.quote: Moore's exegesis of the spatial text of Kenya's Marakwet reveals how physical activities in and movement through space reveal its meaning and reinforce gender ideologies.

findings.antecedent: Formal geometries (rather than environmental or behavioral needs)
findings.consequent: Guidance of design and development of folk housing styles
findings.quote: His inferences from particular household architectural configurations lead him to conclude that formal geometries rather than environmental or behavioral needs guided design and development of folk housing styles.

findings.consequent: Expression, direction, and shaping of social processes (sociability, host-guest, insider-outsider relations)
findings.quote: Built forms not only express but direct and shape social processes concerned with sociability and controlling behavior in host-guest or insider-outsider relations.

findings.consequent: Primary cultural expression, means to construct identities, transform abstract to concrete, predicate/project qualities onto space, ordering experience
findings.quote: Fernandez has developed his version of metaphor theory to decode and understand the meaning expressed by the built and natural environment. His well-known work Fang Architectonics (107) begins with a study of the Fang and how their culture is represented in space. His monograph is an elaborate and detailed exegesis that links cosmology, myth, social structure, and village architecture through cultural meaning systems. In his work, he develops his notion of quality space composed of axes of continuum between bipolar oppositions of meaning and demonstrates how metaphor is both interpretive and strategic.

findings.consequent: Acts as critical symbolic elements during ritual performances, providing setting and markers for collective transcendence into communitas
findings.quote: Both temporary and permanent features of the built environment act as critical symbolic elements during ritual performances by providing setting and markers for the participants' collective transcendence of ordinary reality and passage into communitas, a temporary collective state of total unity (363, 364).

findings.consequent: Imbuing elements of the built environment with social and symbolic significance, transforming neutral spaces into meaningful places
findings.quote: A number of studies emphasize how performative aspects of ritual and social drama imbue elements of the built environment with social and symbolic significance, some becoming metaphors embodying complex meanings. Artists' performances in a New York park transform neutral spaces into meaningful places by creating 'territories' that last long after the performance is over (158).

findings.consequent: Experience of being-in-the-world (existential/phenomenological reality of place: smell, feel, color, etc.), communicating basic dynamics of culture
findings.quote: In Richardson's perspective, space is the experience of being-in-the-world—that is, the existential or phenomenological reality of the place: its smell, feel, color, etc. He uses ethnographic description to conclude that the experience of being-in-the-plaza is about the Costa Rican concept of 'cultura,' the appropriate and right behavior, which contrasts with 'vivo,' the experience of being-in-the-market, which denotes smart, quick, and clever behavior (317). For Richardson, the essential way spatial realities are experienced communicates the basic dynamics of culture (318).

findings.consequent: Disguised representation of latent thoughts, reflection of inner psyche, models of sacred space representing cosmological center
findings.quote: According to Freud (122), symbols are inherently sexual and are used for the disguised representation of latent thoughts. Many symbols are habitually or almost habitually employed to express the same thing, though symbols may also derive their meaning from private memories and employ idiosyncratic referents. Some early work in this area focuses on cross-cultural differences in how sexual tensions and anxieties have influence on, or find expression in, the built environment (198, 379).

findings.consequent: Integral to the psychological concept of the self
findings.quote: In The Non-Human Environment, Harold Searles (346) offers a psychoanalytic theory of human development that includes the spatial environment as integral to the psychological concept of the self.

findings.consequent: Structuring of space in relation to their genital modes, expressing biological, cultural, and psychological aspects of development
findings.quote: In Childhood and Society (101), he presents case histories of how children playing with blocks structure the space in relation to their genital modes.

findings.consequent: Conditioning of learning, leading to spatial perception (e.g., susceptibility to optical illusions)
findings.quote: The researchers argued that the perception of space stems from learning conditioned by different ecological and cultural environments. The finding that Westerners, more often than non-Westerners, were susceptible to certain optical illusions was explained as a result of their living in a more rectangularly shaped, 'carpentered' world (348).

findings.consequent: Modification of innate distancing mechanism, regulating contact in social situations (proxemics)
findings.quote: Hall postulates that humans may have an innate distancing mechanism, modified by culture, that helps to regulate contact in social situations.

findings.consequent: Human societies survive through culture-developed elaborate rules and practices that reduce density-related stresses
findings.quote: Reacting to inferences about a human 'behavioral sink' from early crowding experiments with laboratory rats, Anderson (17) and Draper (78), among others (9, 152, 307), argued that culture enables human societies to survive high densities.

findings.consequent: Tensions about public exposure, leading people to periodically escape through institutionalized seclusion
findings.quote: Focusing on the lack of privacy among the Mehinacu, Gregor (145) observes that flimsy house construction, typical of many nonliterate societies, creates tensions about public exposure from which people must periodically escape (324); one way is through institutionalized periodic seclusion (144).

findings.antecedent: Territoriality expressed in the environment (hierarchy of recognized spaces/symbolic markers)
findings.consequent: Regulation of behavior and enhanced control
findings.quote: When territoriality is expressed in the environment through a hierarchy of recognized spaces or symbolic markers, behavior may be regulated and control enhanced (266). An exploration of housing in Upper Volta (37) suggests that surveillance within compounds is enhanced and behavior automatically regulated by the careful configuration of dwelling forms.

findings.antecedent: Territoriality in spaces, situations, and the self
findings.consequent: Combination in actors' presentations and representations aimed at convincing others of who they are
findings.quote: Goffman identifies qualities of territoriality in spaces, situations, and in the self (138), and forcefully demonstrates how all three combine in actors' presentations and representations aimed at convincing others of who they are.

findings.consequent: People become masters of information control and stagecraft
findings.quote: For example, Gregor demonstrates in his Mehinacu study how, lacking privacy, people become masters of information control and stagecraft (146).

findings.antecedent: Linkage of psychological and physical features (home environments)
findings.consequent: Serving expressive ends and aiding in regulation of behavior through dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness
findings.quote: A cross-cultural comparison of the home reveals how the linkage of psychological and physical features serves expressive ends and aids in the regulation of behavior through the dialectical oppositions of identity/community and openness/closedness (11).

findings.consequent: Actualization of self and identity in taking control of a particular place
findings.quote: This Marx-inspired term emphasizes the actualization of self and identity in the taking of control of a particular place (202).
In describing Ojibwa knowledge of the environment, both cosmic and physical, Hallowell claims that cultural and environmental processes condition the socialization process.

findings.consequent: Expression of existing underclass created by structural inequalities in Brazilian society
findings.quote: Epstein's analysis of squatter settlements in Brasilia as an expression of the existing underclass created by structural inequalities in Brazilian society challenges the individual-agency arguments of previous squatter housing studies.

findings.consequent: New buildings emerge and others become obsolete; society produces buildings that maintain and/or reinforce its social forms
findings.quote: King (192) goes on to note that as society changes new buildings emerge and others become obsolete. Society produces buildings that maintain and/or reinforce its social forms.

findings.consequent: Creation of a 'docile body' that may be subjected, used, transformed, and improved; control of space through enclosure and organization of individuals
findings.quote: The aim of such technologies is to create a 'docile body that may be subjected, used, transformed and improved' (117:198). The control of space through enclosure and the organization of individuals in space are ways that this occurs.

findings.consequent: Architectural mechanism of control (hierarchical spatial ordering, surveillance, individual self-guarding)
findings.quote: In Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison, Foucault uses the model of Jeremy Bentham's 1787 plan for the panopticon to represent an architectural mechanism of control in its ideal form.

findings.consequent: Contribution to maintenance of power of one group over another AND functioning as a mechanism for coding reciprocal relationships (including body movement/surveillance)
findings.quote: He thus successfully illustrates how architecture as an institution contributes to the maintenance of power of one group over another and functions as a mechanism for coding their reciprocal relationships at a level that includes the movement of the body in space as well as its surveillance.

findings.consequent: Insights into developmental processes of the modern world system; functions as both product and producer (defines new spaces, creates work, represents social structures, maintains practices)
findings.quote: According to King (196) the architecture of colonialism provides insights into the developmental processes of the modern world system. Much of the contemporary global urban system is contained in, symbolized by, and integrated with a variety of building and urban forms introduced as part of Spanish, Portuguese, British, French, Dutch, and American colonialism. In this sense, the built environment of colonialism functions as both a product and a producer; it helps to define new spaces, create work, represent changing social structures, and maintain new economic, social, political, and cultural practices.

findings.antecedent: Modern French colonial planning (Lyautey in Morocco)
findings.consequent: Creation of new society, maintenance of social hierarchy, provision of social/moral stage, representation of modern French norms, reorganization of power relations
findings.quote: Lyautey's solution was to create a new society by finding French agents who could direct the modernization of the Moroccan nobility. The form of this program was to build villes nouvelles, modern French settlements, next to but separate from Morocco's existing cities. In this way urban planning and design would produce an environment that maintained the social hierarchy and provided 'a constant social and moral stage to the French' (301:286).

findings.consequent: Expression of class relations and distribution of power; reproduction of class relations through space allocation
findings.quote: Harvey emphasizes the physical form of the city as an expression of this distribution of power. His analyses focus on the reproduction of class relations in space allocation through urban planning (159, 160).

findings.consequent: Serving unacknowledged ideological ends in reproducing sociopolitical organization
findings.quote: Manuel Castells (52) argues that architecture and planning serve unacknowledged ideological ends in reproducing a structure of sociopolitical organization that itself lies at the root of urban problems.

findings.consequent: Determining allocation, quality, and control of neighborhood space (resisting dominant classes/planning elite)
findings.quote: But Castells (53) adds the critical dimension of social resistance and conflict in determining urban organization and form. Rather than perceiving an urban form as given, and planning as the sole agent of social control, Castells' historical and contemporary studies document the role of social movements and local people in determining the allocation, quality, and control of neighborhood space.

findings.consequent: Elaboration of symbolic significance in everyday discourse about property
findings.quote: The classic study Everything in its Place: Social Order and Land Use in America (287) not only presents the social structure of land use, specifically the different perceptions of home owners and apartment renters in America, but also elaborates the symbolic significance of this system in the everyday discourse about renting and buying property in Houston and Philadelphia.

findings.consequent: Signifying system with symbolic meaning, absorbed and acted upon by city dwellers and rural visitors
findings.quote: The City in Cultural Context (2) deals with 'city form as a signifying system that has symbolic meaning which is conveyed to city dwellers and rural visitors, and is absorbed by and acted upon by them' (2:284).

findings.consequent: Symbolic markers of class and social status in public and private buildings
findings.quote: Murray Edelman (94) is concerned with the legitimizing function of specific architectural features as symbolic markers of class and social status in public and private buildings.

limitations: The interpretation of clients' needs/wants is complex and requires preparation to prevent gross assumptions.

The experience of joining communities and universities is still at its initial stages, it is possible to list a number of challenges, risks and limitations that need to be addressed and resolved in similar experiences.
Risk to raise expectations in participants: goals and realistic scenarios of what can be achieved must be clearly stated immediately.
Students project very rarely can deliver concrete and finite outcomes.

Academic priorities must be clear; clients must be aware that what they can obtain from this experience is - for the moment - simply a repertoire of ideas. Further developments are expected to be produced, but this will require time and experience.
Not everyone will be willing - or capable - to contribute to the process with equal skills.
It is important to define roles, competencies and levels of commitment within the team.

The community group identified should have an organisation structure. During the process, new relationships and groups can - and almost surely will - be formed, but an initial central core helps and prevents from spending vast amount of time in identifying potential community leaders, locating target groups etc. On the other side, starting from scratch can also have benefits; leaders must in this case do a lot of networking and research in advance.
Often users' requirements and goals won't coincide with academic requirements and goals.
When working with large communities do not assume that those willing to be directly involved will accept to overcome social, racial, cultural, political barriers and get along well together.

Students show increased confidence in developing their ideas and design proposals (feeling that these are backed up by a more complete and realistic understanding of conditions). Still, they often find it hard to adjust to this new condition.

limitations: Accessing and working directly with persons who had experienced homelessness was a challenge.

Participants may have believed that the facility administration was aware of their participation, potentially affecting their responses (e.g., prompting more complimentary answers about facilities' designs and policies).
A number of resident participants spoke in dry, institutionalized language of personal responsibility and asserted gratitude for being in the facility.

The questionnaire sample size presents a limitation for generalizing the findings derived from its data alone; the study's overall goal was to explore a phenomenon, not to produce empirically verifiable results generalizable to a broader population.

The study did not address any background characteristics of the respondents, such as personal histories, relationships, health, or where they were in the process of exiting homelessness with regard to residents.
The study did not address the hierarchy of organization, experience with working with homeless persons, or position (i.e., case worker or management) with regard to staff.

extraction_result.title: The psychological benefits of indoor plants: A critical review of the experimental literature

findings.consequent: General psychological benefits (e.g., stress-reduction, pain tolerance)
findings.quote: The reviewed studies suggest that indoor plants can provide psychological benefits such as stress-reduction and increased pain tolerance. However, they also showed substantial heterogeneity in methods and results. We therefore have strong reservations about general claims that indoor plants cause beneficial psychological changes.
Some findings recur, notably enhanced pain management with plants... All four of the studies found that those with plants present had better tolerance for pain than those without plants present.

findings.consequent: Stress reduction, pain tolerance, perceived room attractiveness
findings.quote: several of the studies suggest that flowering plants have a greater effect compared to foliage plants, as seen in stress-reduction (Kim & Mattson, 2002), pain tolerance (Park et al., 2004), and perceived attractiveness of the room (Adachi, Rohde, & Kendle, 2000).

Shibata and Suzuki (2001) considered circumstances under which plants would affect task-performance through effects on attention. Their results were in line with the hypothesis that plants would more effectively reduce attentional fatigue during a break from work than while performing a task because people could allow their attention to go to the plants during a break.

findings.consequent: Creative task performance (increase) vs. attentionally demanding task performance (decrease)
findings.quote: In a later study, Shibata and Suzuki (2002) hypothesized that plants would facilitate performance on a creative task because they are a source of information, but that they would distract a person working on a more attentionally demanding task. Their participants performed better on an association task compared to a more attentionally demanding task when they had a plant placed in front of them, compared to a no-plant condition. However, this held only for their male subjects.

Similarly, Larsen et al. (1998) found that perfor- mance on a letter identification task decreased with a larger number of plants, which agrees with the notion that fascinating properties of plants may interfere with some kinds of tasks.

Several of the studies did not find effects on emotions after the participants were exposed to plants... The results were also variable among the subset of studies that used Zuckerman's (1977) Inventory of Personal Reac- tions (ZIPERS). The studies either found significant differences only on an item-level... or they reported different results across gender.

The psychophysiological results are also mixed. Some findings are consistent with the theory (e.g., Lohr et al., 1996), and others are not (Lohr & Pearson-Mims, 2000). Kim and Mattson (2002) found decreased electrodermal activity and EEG beta activity (taken as indicators of stress recovery) with exposure to red-flowering geraniums versus geraniums without flowers and no plants.

findings.consequent: Perceived room attractiveness, cheerfulness, pleasantness, invitingness
findings.quote: The room with plants was also perceived as more cheerful, pleasant, and inviting than the room with the other aesthetic amenities.
