findings.quote: The most common experience of (over) exposure to UV radiation is sunburn (erythema). As shown by the CIE action spectrum for erythema [43] in Fig. 5, the UVB wavelengths are most effective at damaging the skin in this way, but UVA wavelengths also have some effect... Erythema and cumulative exposure to UV radiation are linked with skin cancers, including the life threatening malignant melanoma [44]. Other undesirable effects of UV radiation include photoaging of the skin, DNA damage and eye damage, e.g. cataracts (cumulative exposure) and snow blindness (acute exposure) [45].
The major benefit is the cutaneous synthesis of Vitamin D, initiated by exposure to UVB radiation (Fig. 5) [46].
Vitamin D has long been recognised as necessary for calcium metabolism and hence a healthy skeleton [47].

findings.consequent: UV dose (Vitamin D production, sunburn, skin cancers)
findings.quote: In fact, common indoor lighting, used as intended, provides a UV dose that is neither useful (in terms of Vitamin D production) nor harmful (with respect to sunburn and skin cancers) to the normal person.

Common window glass is highly transmissive in the visible but the transmission decreases rapidly across the UV... daylight penetrating further into the room contains little UV and being indoors is usually considered a safe UV environment.

Boosting Vitamin D status by artificial UVB radiation is possible both for the housebound and for those at high latitudes where for several months of the year there is insufficient UVB in sunlight to enable Vitamin D synthesis [58,59]. However, any such treatments should be given in a carefully controlled situation to maximize the benefits and minimize the risks of UV exposure.

stimuli.description: Eleven different material samples (6 original building materials: blue stone, brickwork, concrete, white plaster, steel, wood; and 5 colored plaster samples equivalent in color to original materials) presented vertically at eye-height.

Pearson correlation coefficients between evaluated material warmth and physical measures in the three experimental conditions (General, Visual, Tactile).

limitations: The variety of materials allowed for a broad perspective on the concept of material warmth, but did not allow to formulate detailed findings concerning the exact relationships between material warmth and the technical material parameters.

In order to generalize these findings, the material set would have to be expanded to a larger number of different samples and the researched variables (thermal properties, surface roughness, gloss) should be controlled.
The sample set was not chosen to cover a wide variety of colors, requiring more detailed investigation utilizing a more complete color set.

The study focused on indoor wall materials; warmth perception is likely to be context-dependent, so results should be considered within the boundary conditions set for the test. Applications for other building elements (floors, ceilings, outdoor applications) require further research.

Participants were asked to imagine the materials at full scale but their ability to do so might be limited, suggesting that studies in full-scale settings might provide insights into differences in perception caused by issues of scale.

limitations: Participants were young healthy adults, potentially leading to selection bias and limited generalizability.
Study included only two environmental conditions (low BIDI=3, moderate BIDI=27), potentially underestimating impacts compared to environments with more biophilic components.

Study conducted in a building with good air quality and thermal comfort, preventing parsing of effects to single natural elements or interactions with other indoor environmental quality factors (e.g., noise, odors, lighting).

Observed differences in baseline physiological measures between visits, despite randomization and control for between-visit variables, potentially affecting physiological and cognitive changes during the experiment.
Participants were not blinded to the test environments, potentially leading to biased estimates of effects on performance.

extraction_result.title: Editorial

findings.consequent: Sustains walkable, energy-efficient environments and resilient, mixed-use economies
findings.quote: For its advocates the historic city is a source of inspiration: a high-density model that sustains a walkable, energy efficient environ- ment and resilient, mixed-use economy.

findings.antecedent: Historic city image (as a vision for the future)
findings.consequent: Offers no vision of the future, stands contrary to actual history of many contemporary cities, affected by social/economic blight and physical deterioration, indicates irreversible decline
findings.quote: For the sceptics, such an image offers no vision of the future because it stands contrary to the actual history of many contemporary cities where old centres have been affected by social and eco- nomic blight usually accompanied by acute physical deterioration.

findings.consequent: Requires radical thinking of conventional urban models
findings.quote: Instead, they propose, a radical thinking of conventional urban models is required to understand what will be needed in the twenty- first century.

findings.consequent: Humans would opt to live there
findings.quote: Edward Glaeser's argument that – all things being equal – humans would opt to live in dense, information-rich settlements, belongs (broadly speaking) in the Jane Jacobs tradition (Glaeser, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Dispersed agglomerations of built form and highly mobile populations in contemporary urban regions
findings.consequent: Necessitates new ways of conceiving 'the urban' for better understanding and design
findings.quote: However, other voices such as Thomas Sieverts assert that new ways of conceiving of 'the urban' are nece- ssary in order to fully understand and better design for the dispersed agglomerations of built form that are the characteristic milieu of highly mobile populations living in contemporary urban regions in the developed world (Sieverts, 2003).

findings.consequent: Considered a 'problem' requiring a 'solution' involving large open spaces within an extended urban fabric
findings.quote: With some license, we might put Sieverts in the tradition of Ebenezer Howard or Lewis Mumford for whom the dense industrial city was a 'problem' requiring a 'solution' in which the accommodation of large open spaces within an extended urban fabric would play an important part.

findings.antecedent: Internet and widespread availability of portable telecommunication devices
findings.consequent: Created a new 'digital layer' whose relationship with corporeal rhythms of urban space is unclear
findings.quote: The revolution in social and working practices associated with the internet and the widespread availability of portable telecommunication devices has created a new ‘digital layer'. The relationship of this aspatial (or 'transpatial') network with the corporeal rhythms of urban space is as yet far from clear.

findings.consequent: Cities are more popular than ever before
findings.quote: The traditional urbanists undoubtedly have a point in claiming that globally speaking cities are more popular than ever before.

findings.consequent: World's urban population percentage expected to rise from 10% to 75%
findings.quote: In 1900, approximately 10 per cent of the world's popu- lation inhabited cities; by 2050 this number is expected to rise to 75 per cent (Burdett and Sudjic, 2007).

findings.consequent: City form and social life are fundamentally changed
findings.quote: However, this argument should not be taken to imply that the form and social life of the city are fundamentally unchanged over time and in different historical-geographical contexts.

findings.antecedent: Idealizing the historical city as a universally applicable model OR imposing inappropriate contemporary schemes onto complex urban tissues
findings.consequent: Stunts innovation OR creates danger to urban tissues
findings.quote: From a design perspective, there is as much danger in stunting innovation by idealizing the historical city as a universally applicable model as there is in imposing inappropriate contemporary schemes onto complex urban tissues that have evolved over many centuries.

findings.antecedent: Grand modernist narratives of architecture and urban design
findings.consequent: Associated with the destruction of highly valued historical urban forms, leading to suspicion in postmodern social theory
findings.quote: Part of the 'postmodern condition' in western social theory is manifested in a suspicion of the grand modernist narratives of architecture and urban design, which have become associated with the destruction of those historical urban forms that are (now) highly valued.

findings.consequent: Requires a 'vision thing' as a necessary part of the design process
findings.quote: Nevertheless, in planning for the future, it is hard to do without the 'vision thing' entirely – as a necessary part of the design process.

findings.antecedent: Views of those who 'leave things alone' versus those who see opportunities from top-down interventions
findings.quote: It is probably inevitable therefore, that the views of those who would rather 'leave things alone' are often incommen- surate with those who see greater opportunities arising from top-down interventions.

findings.antecedent: Huge Olympic developments in East London
findings.consequent: Caused displacement or disadvantaging of many existing local amenities and small businesses
findings.quote: Much of the row over the huge Olympic developments in East London and their much-trumpeted 'legacy' for the local community has taken place on these terms – the cost being the displacement or disadvantaging of many existing local amenities and small businesses.

findings.consequent: Some are more privileged than others, not necessarily serving those most in need by local populations
findings.quote: Certainly, some historical areas seem to be more privileged than others and not necessarily the ones that matter most to the local populations who have the greatest need of them.

findings.antecedent: Highly mobile existence (especially if unable to easily separate from or maintain offline relationships via digital networks)
findings.quote: Although a highly mobile existence can liberate individuals from the weight of history, it can also be an alienating experience – especially if you are whether the two can ever be easily separated (or indeed, whether they should be) as such networks are often used to maintain relationships made offline.

findings.consequent: Offer great economic opportunity but at potential cost to the sense of 'being at home'
findings.quote: 'Edge city' developments no doubt offer great economic opportunity, but at what potential cost to that sense of being 'at home'?

findings.consequent: Preference for it can be justified in highly pragmatic terms, not just nostalgia
findings.quote: All this may sound like so much advocacy of the historic city model, but the point is rather to highlight: first, that a preference for the milieu of the historic city does not have to be justified on grounds of chocolate-box nostalgia, indeed it can be expressed in highly pragmatic terms;

findings.antecedent: Complexity and formative role of the historic city in modern, mobile, and digitally networked lives
findings.consequent: Should not be casually reduced to a one-dimensional tourist destination
findings.quote: and second, to illustrate why the whole com- plexity of the historic city should not be casually reduced to that of a one-dimensional tourist destination when it is able to play such a for- mative role in 'modern lives' that are both highly mobile and digitally networked, as personally and professionally speaking is certainly the case with my hosts in Canterbury.

findings.consequent: Makes everyday living relatively light, freeing up time for other things
findings.quote: a still-functioning his- toric city makes relatively light the everyday work of living – such that one has simply more time for other things. Surely few qualities can be more important?

findings.antecedent: Indoor 'public' spaces of Mass Transit Railway Stations (Hong Kong)
findings.consequent: Comprise increasingly important aspects of life in large cities, raising questions about what constitutes 'public' space
findings.quote: On the basis of a number of case studies, Xue argues that such spaces comprise increasingly important aspects of life in large cities – though, as he acknowledges, this raises serious questions about what exactly is recog- nized as 'public' space.

findings.antecedent: Urban morphology and vernacular urban forms
findings.consequent: Can usefully inform urban design to better understand adaptation to local climatic conditions for energy efficiency
findings.quote: His short article suggests that urban design could be usefully informed by urban morphology in order to better understand how vernacular urban forms adapt to local climatic conditions, as large-scale archi- tectural projects have not traditionally prioritized such issues.

findings.antecedent: Increased neighbourhood density and pedestrian accessibility
findings.consequent: Tend to create economic value, supporting walkability from an economic standpoint
findings.quote: On the basis of research that includes a statistical analysis of property prices across a range of land uses, their study suggests that increased neighbourhood density and pedestrian accessibility tend to create economic value.

findings.consequent: Can help address design difficulties for creating 'liveable streets' on major intra-settlement routes
findings.quote: The authors draw on research from a case study of Perth, Australia, to test how their multi-scale classification model (FUS-ion) can help address this issue. Their work is a useful contribution to the growing literature concerned with how major network infrastructure can be made more effective for users across urban scales – and particularly at the human scale.

findings.quote: Paterson's work draws on a wide range of academic, professional and community-based authorities to enquire into exactly what the new NPPF needs to do in order to function as successful urban design guidance, while at the same time negotiating the self-evident difficulties in creating a centralized regulatory regime for localized planning and design governance.

findings.antecedent: Simplified images of the urban past or visions of futurity that do not acknowledge historical dialogue between 'new' and 'old'
findings.consequent: Urban designers and societies cannot afford to be held hostage to them
findings.quote: urban designers (and urban societies) cannot afford to be hostage either to simplified images of the urban past or visions of futurity that do not acknowledge that in historical time the 'new' is always a dialogue with the 'old'.

findings.antecedent: The right to the social space of the city (when one needs recourse to it)
findings.consequent: Is still something to be valued, even in a world of global capital transfer, accelerated transit, and virtual spaces
findings.quote: the right to the social space of the city – that is, when one needs recourse to it is still something to be valued.

findings.consequent: Are not mutually exclusive, and the emergence of one does not have to imply the annihilation of the other
findings.quote: After all, none of these spaces is mutually exclusive and the emergence of one does not have to imply the annihilation of the other.

findings.mechanism: The Tate Gallery's complex layout results in a lower overall compactness compared to simpler geometries like the T-shape and Manhattan grid, but higher clustering than the Manhattan grid.
findings.quote: although the compactness index for the whole system is lower than in the first two examples, the cluster index is a lot higher than for the Manhattan grid

findings.antecedent: average distance and area of isovist fields (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: A very high correlation indicates that in Regent Street, the average distance one can see is strongly linked to the total visible area, reflecting smooth spatial variation.
findings.quote: The maps of average distance and area are highly correlated at 0.942 and fairly smooth in their spatial variation.

findings.mechanism: The curve obstructs long vistas, reducing the maximum distance one can see.
findings.quote: the effect of the massive curve in Regent Street is evident in the way this interferes with vistas.

findings.antecedent: maximum distance of isovist field (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: A strong correlation suggests that the extent of the farthest view is related to the visible perimeter, indicating consistent visual field properties.
findings.quote: quite highly correlated with perimeter at 0.784

findings.antecedent: area and perimeter of isovist fields (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Area and perimeter are highly correlated, similar to average distance and area, reflecting consistent visual field characteristics.
findings.quote: the area and perimeter maps are highly correlated with each other in the same manner as average distance and area.

findings.mechanism: Golden Square's central vantage point is the most compact, while tiny street indentations are more compact than long, narrow streets, reflecting varied spatial experiences.
findings.quote: The compactness index is dominated by Golden Square, whose central vantage point is the most compact of anywhere in the area; the tiny squares... are more compact than the long narrow streets

findings.mechanism: Long streets have low convexity, while squares (like Golden Square and Piccadilly Circus) have much greater convexity, indicating distinct visual fans and spatial experiences.
findings.quote: The index of clustering shows up these patterns quite clearly, with the long streets having low convexity values in contrast to squares which have much greater convexity in shape.

findings.consequent: frequency distributions of average distance, area, and perimeter
findings.mechanism: These distributions are clearly bimodal with mild positive skews, reflecting the distinct types of spaces (long streets vs. squares) in the morphology.
findings.quote: The distributions of average distance, area, and perimeter are clearly bimodal with mild positive skews

findings.mechanism: The farthest distance field is very positively skewed with a long right-hand tail, indicating a few very long streets that significantly extend visual reach.
findings.quote: The farthest distance field is very positively skewed with a long right-hand tail associated with the few very long streets within the morphology.

findings.mechanism: The compactness index is positively skewed, indicating a small number of very compact objects (squares) in the scene.
findings.quote: the compactness index is again positively skewed, reflecting the fact that there are only a small number of very compact objects in the scene.

findings.mechanism: The convexity index is much more normally distributed, suggesting a more uniform distribution of convex shapes.
findings.quote: The convexity index, however, is much more normally distributed.

findings.mechanism: The dominance of long streets in Regent Street's morphology leads to the lowest average compactness among all examples studied.
findings.quote: the compactness index is the lowest in all our examples to date, reflecting the domination of long streets.

findings.mechanism: Average distance is higher at street junctions and interstices due to more open space, reflecting the street-dominated morphology.
findings.quote: The average distance from each vantage point simply mirrors the fact that there is more space at junctions of streets and in the occasional interstices

findings.mechanism: The average distance field is the smoothest, being composed of averages, in contrast to the maximum distance field which is dominated by a few long streets.
findings.quote: this field is the smoothest of all, being composed of averages in contrast to the maximum distance which is dominated by four or five long streets.

findings.mechanism: Area and perimeter fields show largest values where streets enter squares, indicating clearer interaction between these spatial elements.
findings.quote: areas and perimeters where streets enter squares have the largest values.

findings.antecedent: average distance, area, and perimeter of isovist fields (Wolverhampton town center)
findings.mechanism: High correlations (greater than 0.75) indicate a strong relationship between these basic visibility measures, consistent with other examples.
findings.quote: The average distance, area, and perimeter fields are highly correlated with one another with correlations greater than 0.75 in every case

findings.mechanism: Inner parts of squares and some junctions exhibit highest compactness, while middle portions of long streets have the least, reflecting varied visual enclosure.
findings.quote: The inner parts of squares and some junctions have the highest compactness with the middle portions of long streets having the least.

findings.mechanism: Areas on the edges of streets show higher convexity than center lines, attributed to the relative irregularity of the town plan.
findings.quote: The convexity field shows that areas on the edges of streets have higher convexity than the center lines, this being a result of the relative irregularity of the town plan.

findings.mechanism: Unlike previous examples, the visual fields of Wolverhampton town center do not show distinct elements or clear groupings, appearing relatively uniform.
findings.quote: it is not possible to detect distinct elements in the visual fields of Wolverhampton town center. The street scenes appear to be relatively uniform.

findings.mechanism: All six plots are positively skewed but mildly so, with the convexity index being almost normally distributed, showing no bimodality or major deviations from normality.
findings.quote: there is no evidence whatsoever of any bimodality or other major deviations from normality. All six plots are positively skewed but only mildly so, with the exception of the convexity index which is almost normally distributed.

findings.mechanism: The morphology, dominated by long streets, results in the lowest average compactness among all examples studied.
findings.quote: Wolverhampton has the lowest average compactness of any of the examples we have dealt with, a fact that simply confirms a morphology dominated by long streets.

findings.antecedent: polygon with P vertices or edges and H holes
findings.consequent: minimum number of guards/isovists to cover the space
findings.mechanism: The Art Gallery Theorem states that at most P/3 guards (or (P+2H)/3 with holes) are sufficient to cover the space.
findings.quote: at most, P/3 guards or isovists are sufficient and sometimes necessary to cover the space; if the space has H holes, then (P+2H)/3 guards are required (O'Rourke, 1987).

findings.antecedent: Tate Gallery morphology (P=820 edges, H=33 holes)
findings.consequent: number of isovists required to cover the space using the algorithm
findings.mechanism: While the theoretical maximum is 296 isovists, the implemented algorithm covers the gallery with 84 isovists.
findings.quote: By using our algorithm, the gallery can in fact be covered by 84 isovists

findings.antecedent: total area seen along a path (Regent Street)
findings.consequent: average distance seen along the path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Strong correlation indicates that changes in visible area are closely linked to changes in average visible distance, reflecting the spatial experience of moving through streets and squares.
findings.quote: Total area seen from this path is correlated very strongly with the average distance seen and these profiles... illustrate clearly the changes in space encountered

findings.mechanism: Narrow streets allow for long views, except where curves (like Regent Street from Piccadilly Circus) or edge effects obstruct vision.
findings.quote: the walk is dominated by narrow streets where the walker can see a long way, except when entering Regent Street from Piccadilly Circus where the curve obstructs vision

findings.antecedent: isovist fields in Piccadilly Circus (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: Positions where long distances and large areas are visible provide a measure of spaciousness, contributing to a 'true' sensation of what a walker might feel.
findings.quote: where the walker can see long distances and large areas, thus providing a measure of spaciousness, a 'true' sensation of what a real walker might feel in this area.

findings.antecedent: major junctions along a path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: The perimeter measure dramatically increases at major junctions, reflecting the sudden expansion of the visual field.
findings.quote: This feature of the walk is also picked up from the perimeter measure which increases quite dramatically at major junctions.

findings.antecedent: changes in direction and area seen along a path (Regent Street)
findings.mechanism: The compactness index, which reflects how enclosed a walker feels, is highly sensitive to variations in both viewing direction and the visible area.
findings.quote: The index of compactness, however, which captures how enclosed the walker feels, is very sensitive to changes in both direction and the area seen

findings.mechanism: The clustering/convexity measure shows a more uniform trend but is 'noisy' due to local detail from pixelation, indicating less sensitivity to overall changes but high sensitivity to fine-grained features.
findings.quote: the clustering or convexity of spaces defining the walk is more uniform as a trend, yet much more 'noisy' as a profile in that this measure picks up all the local detail associated with the pixelation of the street map.

limitations: The computational resolution (200x200 pixels) might be too coarse to pick up fine detail in city centers, potentially affecting substantive interpretations.
The analysis of the T-shape geometry introduced edge effects from the bounding box, which can distort results.
There is no formal demonstration that the index of shape {Ψi} and the index of clustering {γi} are similar, leaving this as a conjecture for future work.
A much wider range of morphological types is needed for a comprehensive classification and development of a robust theory of morphology.
Better measures of shape consistent with new ideas concerning convexity and isovist geometry are still needed.
A specific statistical theory needs to be developed to fully understand the interplay of geometry and the local dynamics of visual movement.
The measures are not scale invariant, and visual experiences will vary across scale; local detail at very fine levels cannot yet be simulated.
Larger systems are required to minimize boundary effects, as seen in the Regent Street example where lines of sight outside the system likely produced significant distortions.
There is a need for further research into partition problems to simplify space into distinct subspaces or covers.

stimuli.description: Four office test environments: wood and plants, wood and no plants, no wood and plants, and no wood and no plants. Wood furniture had birch veneer with a clear finish. Non-wood furniture had white painted and melamine foil surfaces. Plants included Chlorophytum comosum (spider plant), Dracaena marginata (variegated red), and Schefflera actinophylla (Amate). Non-plant items were a blue glass vase, plastic inbox/outbox filer, and a stand fan. The view to the outside was blocked by closed blinds. The PASAT test was an auditory stressor.

limitations: No treatment or stressor effects found for HRV, possibly due to no real differences or undetected differences by chosen methodologies.
Baseline stress level was sufficiently high that it did not allow for parasympathetic dominance in any period.
Time spent habituating to the environment was not enough to engage the parasympathetic system.
Sitting position of subjects may have prevented HRV from being present or detectable.
2.5-minute epochs may not have been sufficient to capture HRV (5-minute epochs suggested).
Quality issues with some ECG records due to data collection from wrists instead of torso, potentially introducing more noise.
PASAT test was an acute stressor, which may not accurately characterize chronic stress in office environments.
PASAT caused subjects to stop looking at their surroundings, counteracting the study's goals.
Limited plant surface area in the study precludes conclusions on the effect of plants on stress.
Uncertainty whether observed effects are a positive effect of wood or a negative effect of man-made/artificial surfaces (e.g., melamine).
Melamine may have negative connotations, though unlikely to be a factor given its common use and lack of consumer awareness of the term.
PASAT is not a conventional measure of attention for environmental psychology, and mathematical ability was a confounding factor.
Single-blind experiment: experimenter awareness of study goals could lead to unintentional non-verbal cues influencing subjects.
Visible outside light entered the room from between the blinds, and differences in ultraviolet light were not controlled for.
Potential for a history confound as all non-wood rooms were run first, though no evidence for serial or history effects was found.
Wood/non-wood effect could be a response to color, as wood inherently has yellow-red hues not formally controlled against white furniture.

limitations: Subjects were undergraduates and postgraduates aged between 18 and 27, limiting generalizability to the broader public.
The sample size was relatively small (40 participants).

Photoshop software was used for image processing and color recognition, which may be less accurate than MATLAB or Python.

Future research should investigate the effects of plant color on non-human animals, given their different visual perception abilities and needs.

limitations: Lack of recommendations applicable to extreme cold climates for biophilic design.
Lack of adaptation to local photoperiods in biophilic design guidelines.
Absence of a systemic framework for biophilic design integrated into the design process.
Usability, adjustability, and productivity of biophilic design guidelines for extreme climates have not been assessed.
Existing lighting standards mainly fulfill image-forming demands and neglect non-image-forming effects of light.
Designers still lack an effective and practical model to actively consider and evaluate the circadian effects of light in a space.

Biophilic design qualities have not yet been defined as an index, indicator, or rating system, leading to a lack of valid and reliable assessment tools.
No investigation has been conducted regarding the efficiency of adaptive envelopes in extreme cold climates and their improvement of human NIF responses.

Biophilia: Does Visual Contact with Nature Impact on Health and Well-Being?

findings.consequent: Negative effect ('discord') on health or quality of life
findings.quote: It is concluded that an environment devoid of Nature may act as a “discord", i.e., have a negative effect.

findings.antecedent: Adding elements of Nature (parks, window views, potted plants)
findings.consequent: Amelioration of negative effects (improved health/quality of life)
findings.quote: The problem is partly due to the visual absence of plants, and may be ameliorated by adding elements of Nature, e.g., by creating parks, by offering a view through windows, and by potted plants.

findings.antecedent: Adding elements of Nature to living spaces
findings.consequent: Positively valued changes in cognition, emotion, stress level, health, and well-being
findings.quote: Adding elements of Nature to living spaces can presumably induce positively valued changes in cognition and emotion, which again may impact on stress level, health and well-being.
Thus, to the extent that a lack of natural elements is a discord, one would expect that a closer association with nature should improve psychological health.
One theory suggests that the visual environment is important for stress recovery and that stress reduction is faster in Nature compared to urban environments
A visual presence of plants may be one such stress-reducing factor as affective responses to visual stimuli deemed aesthetic may release tension.

findings.antecedent: Surroundings dominated by elements of Nature
findings.quote: Surroundings dominated by elements of Nature are thought to be restorative.
The absence of plants may suggest an “unnatural”, and thus potentially unsafe, environment.

findings.consequent: Psychological benefits (reduced stress, improved attention, mental restoration, coping with attention deficits)
findings.quote: More specifically, contact with Nature has been reported to have psychological benefits by reducing stress [12,22], improving attention [16], by having a positive effect on mental restoration [23-25], and by coping with attention deficits [26,27].

findings.consequent: Direct physical health benefits (increased longevity, improved self-reported health)
findings.quote: In addition to mental advantages, there appear to be direct physical health benefits [28], such as increased longevity [29], and self-reported health [30,31].
As might be expected, the availability of Nature correlates positively with health [32].
It is noteworthy that beneficial effects of Nature can occur even upon relatively brief exposure.
It has been reported that viewing natural landscapes provides psychological and health benefits, including a reduction in stress [12,13,45].

findings.antecedent: Hospital window with a view (of nature)
findings.consequent: Improved healing (reduced pain medication, faster recovery after surgery)
findings.quote: Having a hospital window with a view has been shown to improve healing, reflected in both the level of pain medication and the speed of recovery after surgery [48,49].
Velarde et al. [50] found that natural landscapes have a consistent positive health effect, while urban landscapes can have a negative effect

findings.consequent: Introduction of indoor plants or pictures of Nature (compensation behavior)
findings.quote: It has been shown that office employees seem to compensate for lack of window view by introducing indoor plants or pictures of Nature [52].

findings.antecedent: View to plants from work station
findings.quote: In the same study population it was found that having a view to plants from the work station decreased the amount of self-reported sick leave [53].
Several studies indicated that indoor plants improve the attractiveness of a room [55-58].
Dijkstra et al. [58], for example, found that by showing photos of hospital rooms with or without plants, those with plants reduced self-reported stress.

findings.antecedent: Adding plants to windowless work environment
findings.quote: Other studies also indicate lower stress level when adding plants to a windowless work environment [22,59].

The biophilia hypothesis might suggest an impact of plants on emotional states; however, several studies have failed to find any consistent impact [56,60-62]. Some studies, using mood scales including several items, found significant differences, but only on particular items [57,59,63].
Adachi et al. [57] even reported possible negative effects of plants on annoyance and temper.

findings.antecedent: Indoor plants (for women with preinduced stress)
findings.quote: A couple of reports suggested gender differences in that women, particularly those with a relatively high level of preinduced stress, had the most benefit [17,44].
All the studies concluded that the subjects had better tolerance for pain with than without plants present.
One report [64] suggested that flowering plants have more positive effects on pain tolerance and distress than non-flowering plants.

Positive effects of plants were reported, although the results are somewhat ambiguous. One report found that performance on a letter identification task decreased with the presence of a larger number of plants, which was taken to suggest that fascination with plants may interfere with the focus on the task at hand [56].

A decrease in health complaints, such as tiredness and coughing, has been reported in office and hospital workers when plants were added to the work environment [67,68]. Similar findings on conceived health and level of discomfort were observed in school children [68].

findings.consequent: Attention holding power and pain relief
findings.quote: They found that plants had greater attention holding power and gave greater relief from pain compared to other aesthetic objects such as a designer lamp or an abstract picture.

extraction_result.title: Can light make us bright? Effects of light on cognition sleep

findings.consequent: Human sleep-wake cycle and cognitive performance
findings.quote: Light elicits robust nonvisual effects on numerous physiological and behavioral variables, such as the human sleep-wake cycle and cognitive performance.

findings.consequent: Expression of c-fos and Per1 in SCN, phase shifts of behavioral circadian rhythms
findings.quote: Light pulses presented during the subjective day rapidly induce expression of the immediate early gene c-fos (Rusak et al., 1990) and the clock gene Per1 within the SCN (Albrecht et al., 2001; Edelstein et al., 2003), resulting in phase shifts of behavioral circadian rhythms.
exposure to light late in the biological day (dusk) leads to a delay in human sleep onset
exposure to light early in the biological day (dawn) advances activity onset

findings.antecedent: Attenuated Zeitgeber strength (low light, inappropriate wavelength/timing)
findings.quote: attenuated Zeitgeber strength (i.e., not enough light, or light of an inappropriate wavelength, i.e., light at longer wavelengths, >600 nm) and light at inappropriate times (i.e., during the biological night) can lead to improper entrainment between internal (i.e., circadian) and external (i.e., 24-h earth rotation) time
timed light exposure is a successful countermeasure of circadian misalignment in shift work (Burgess et al., 2002).

findings.consequent: Sleep-wake rhythms (stabilization) and decline in mental capabilities (attenuation) in demented older people
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light did not only stabilize sleep-wake rhythms in demented older people, but significantly attenuated the decline in mental capabilities over the investigated time span of 4.5 years (Riemersma-van der Lek et al., 2008).

findings.consequent: Circadian alignment (promotion) and detrimental effects of night work on sustained attention (prevention)
findings.quote: Similarly, bright light promoted circadian alignment and prevented the detrimental effects of night work on sustained attention, as measured in an increased response speed on the psychomotor vigilance test (Santhi et al., 2008).

findings.antecedent: Sleep/wakefulness out of phase with internal biological time
findings.quote: Strong evidence for this stems from the fact that, if sleep and wakefulness occur out of phase with internal biological time, this impairs several cognitive functions such as learning in humans (Wright et al., 2006).
Further, fragmentation of the rest-activity rhythm correlates with age-related cognitive deficits (Oosterman et al., 2009).

In nocturnal animals, there is recent evidence that the acute light-induction of sleep is mediated by melanopsin-based photoreception (Lupi et al., 2008; Tsai et al., 2009), potentially reflecting an additional clock-independent photic input to sleep.

Bright light in the morning has been shown to shorten sleep duration (Dijk et al., 1989) and advance circadian rhythms (i.e., melatonin profile), without effects on nonrapid eye movement (NREM) sleep homeostasis (Carrier and Dumont 1995; Dijk et al., 1989).

findings.antecedent: Artificial dawn (morning, last 30 min of sleep)
findings.consequent: Sleep depth (more superficial), skin temperatures (faster decline), sleepiness after waking up (less)
findings.quote: An artificial dawn in the morning during the last 30 min of sleep caused more superficial sleep along with a faster decline in skin temperatures and less sleepiness after waking up (Werken et al., 2010).

findings.consequent: Sleep latency to NREM stage 2, EEG SWA (first cycle), EEG SWA (fourth cycle)
findings.quote: Bright light in the evening may lead to an increase in sleep latency to NREM sleep stage 2 (Cajochen et al., 1992; Carrier and Dumont 1995) and changes in the temporal dynamics of electroencephalographic (EEG) slow-wave activity (SWA), such that SWA is lower during the first and higher during the fourth NREM-REM sleep cycle as compared to dim light condition (Cajochen et al., 1992).

Exposure to bright polychromatic light (2500 lux) in the morning (06:00 h–09:00 h) or in the evening (18:00 h-21:00 h) for 3 consecutive days can result in earlier sleep termination following morning light than after evening light (Gordijn et al., 1999).

Interestingly, the duration of the first REM sleep episode was longer after morning light than after evening light, most likely due to a phase advance of the circadian influence on REM sleep production.
diurnal fluctuations of alertness follow similar dynamics of core body temperature (CBT), with its maximum in the evening and nadir in the early morning (Kleitman, 1987).

findings.consequent: Subjective alertness and objective markers of sleepiness (slow eye movements)
findings.quote: even during the biological night in extended wakefulness (when sleep pressure is rising), light can dramatically enhance subjective alertness and reduce objective markers of sleepiness (e.g., slow eye movements).

been hypothesized that melatonin attenuates SCN-dependent mechanisms responsible for promoting and maintaining cortical and behavioral arousal at particular times in the circadian cycle (Cajochen et al., 1999a,b; Dijk and Czeisler 1995; Sack et al., 1997; Wright, 1997).
Light exposure at night on the nasal part of the retina does induce suppression of melatonin, without effects on alertness (Ruger et al., 2006).
bright-light exposure at night, but not in daytime, increased heart rate and increased CBT.

However, the effects of bright light on the psychological variables was time independent, since both nighttime and daytime bright light reduced sleepiness and fatigue significantly and similarly (Fig. 1a and b; Ruger et al., 2006).

findings.antecedent: White light (daytime, short duration, high intensity)
findings.consequent: Cortical activity (during oddball task) and subjective alertness
findings.quote: daytime exposure to short (21 min) white light at >7000 lux; cortical activity was enhanced during an oddball task and subjective alertness improved in a dynamic manner (Vandewalle et al., 2006).
exposure to evening bright light (5000 lux) delayed the diurnal fluctuation of sleep propensity
exposure to lower illuminances still elicits a strong effect (Boivin et al., 1996).

findings.consequent: Maximal resetting response (50% of that from 9100 lux bright light)
findings.quote: 50% of the maximal resetting response to bright light at 9100 lux can be obtained with dim room light (100 lux; Cajochen et al., 2000; Zeitzer et al., 2000; Fig. 2).
humans have the capacity to keep stable entrainment to a 24-h cycle even when ambient light levels are around 1.5 lux

findings.consequent: Alerting effect (lower sleepiness, less slow eye movements, less theta/alpha EEG)
findings.quote: nighttime exposure to typical room light can exert an alerting effect in humans, as indexed by lower subjective ratings of sleepiness, less slow eye movements, and less theta and alpha waking EEG activity.

findings.consequent: Amplitude and shape of the PRC
findings.quote: light pulse duration affects both amplitude and shape of the PRC (Comas et al., 2006).

findings.antecedent: Light pulse duration (first hour vs. subsequent hours)
findings.quote: phase-shifting effects are largest in the first hour of the light pulse, and reduce to a factor 0.22 during all hours after the first hour.
Exposure to intermittent light also seems to be highly effective at resetting the human circadian system.

findings.antecedent: Prior exposure to high levels of light
findings.consequent: Suppression of melatonin concentration at night (in response to subsequent light)
findings.quote: Prior exposure to high levels of light during periods varying from 3 days to 1 week attenuated suppression of the melatonin concentration at night in response to 200-500 lux of light, as compared to prior exposure to 3 days to 1 week of low levels or dim light (Smith et al., 2004).

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength (blue, 460 nm) monochromatic light (nighttime) vs. green (555 nm)
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness, cognitive performance (sustained attention), waking EEG power density (delta-theta range)
findings.quote: Exposure to 460-nm (blue) monochromatic light for 6.5 h during the biological night (maximum levels of melatonin secretion) can substantially decrease both subjective sleepiness, improve cognitive performance in tasks of sustained attention (i.e., psychomotor vigilance task), and decrease waking EEG power density in the delta-theta frequency range (Fig. 3), when compared to light of equal photon density of 555-nm (green) monochromatic light (Lockley et al., 2006).

findings.antecedent: Short-wavelength (blue, 460 nm) monochromatic light (evening, low intensity) vs. 550 nm
findings.quote: Similarly, a 2-h evening exposure to monochromatic light of two different wavelengths (460 and 550 nm) at very low intensities resulted in more alertness during exposure at 460 nm, which further suggests a blue-shift response to light (Revell et al., 2006).

findings.consequent: Melatonin suppression, circadian phase shifting, nocturnal decline in EEG SWA, circadian gene expression (PER2)
findings.quote: blue light... have been observed on a wide array of physiological variables, such as melatonin suppression (Lewy et al., 1980; Zeitzer et al., 2000), circadian phase shifting (Cajochen et al., 1992), nocturnal decline in EEG SWA (Münch et al., 2006; Fig. 4), and circadian gene expression (PER2) in oral mucosa (Cajochen et al., 2006).

findings.antecedent: Blue light irradiance (below melatonin suppression threshold)
findings.consequent: Light effects mediated by homeostatic mechanisms
findings.quote: Thus, one might speculate that if the irradiance of the blue-light (460 nm) stimulus is below the threshold of irradiance required for melatonin suppression, other systems may, in turn, undergo light effects, such as the homeostatic rather than circadian mechanisms (Lockley and Gooley 2006).

findings.consequent: Cortical activity, subcortical structures (brainstem, hypothalamus, thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala)
findings.quote: Light modulations on cortical activity during auditory cognitive tasks affect alertness-related subcortical structures, such as the brainstem (LC-compatible region; Vandewalle et al., 2007a,b); the hypothalamus, in a location encompassing the SCN (Perrin et al., 2004), and dorsal and posterior parts of thalamus (Vandewalle et al., 2006, 2007), in long-term memory and emotion-related areas, such as the hippocampus (Vandewalle et al., 2006) and amygdala (Vandewalle et al., 2007a,b).
blue light enhances modulations in the brainstem (in an LC-compatible location), in the thalamus and insula, in relation to green (550 nm) and violet exposures (430 nm).

findings.consequent: Onset and duration of brain modulation effects
findings.quote: effects of blue light occur 1 min after the start of the exposure... and lasted for ~20 min

findings.consequent: Long-lasting and widespread task-related brain responses
findings.quote: long-lasting and widespread task-related responses occur only when light exposure has a longer duration and at a higher intensity (Perrin et al., 2004).

exposure to 20 min of bright white light has been shown to induce thalamic and cortical modulations that steadily declined after light exposure despite the lasting effects (responses were observed after several minutes of the end of the light exposure; Vandewalle et al., 2006).

findings.antecedent: Light exposure (duration less than a minute)
findings.consequent: Effects elicited in subcortical structures (dorso-posterior thalamus, brainstem)
findings.quote: when light exposure duration was less than a minute, the majority of effects were elicited for subcortical structures, such as the dorso-posterior thalamus and the brainstem (LC-compatible area; Vandewalle et al., 2007a,b).

findings.antecedent: Presence of dark shelters in an arena
findings.consequent: Cockroaches' efficiency in reaching and time spent in the shelter
findings.quote: A closer analysis of the paths indicated that the cockroaches did take less time to reach the shelter than to reach the same area without a dark shelter present, indicating efficient goal-directed navigation. They also stayed in the darkened shelter for a longer period of time than they did in any comparable region of the arena, suggesting that the seemingly random path was in fact targeting the shelter.

findings.antecedent: Electrolytic lesions in the cockroach Central Complex (CX)
findings.consequent: Number of 'wrong' turns made while walking on a track
findings.quote: First, electrolytic lesions in the cockroach CX increased the number of "wrong" turns made while walking on a track (Harley and Ritzmann, 2010).
Second, recordings in the CX clearly demonstrated antennal responses that encoded the direction and velocity and antennal deflections (Ritzmann et al., 2008).

Finally, CX activity recorded in tethered cockroaches demonstrated increases in firing rate that preceded changes in walking speed, while stimulation through the same electrodes evoked speed changes (Bender et al., 2010).

findings.antecedent: Lesions in specific regions of the CX
findings.quote: Lesions in specific regions of the CX compromise either climbing or turning behaviors indicating that the CX plays a role in utilizing mechanosensory information during navigation (Harley and Ritzmann, 2010).

findings.antecedent: Visual cues (polarized light, non-polarized light, grating patterns)
findings.consequent: CX neuron responses (phasic, tonic excitation/inhibition, directional selectivity)
findings.quote: Neurons in the CX of several insects have been shown to respond to visual cues... These stimuli produced a wide range of CX responses including phasic and tonic excitation as well as inhibition (Figure 1). Phasic responses occurred either at the onset of stimulus presentation or at the termination of the visual stimulus. Tonic responses often were directional (Figure 2).

findings.antecedent: Procaine injection into the CX of tethered cockroaches
findings.quote: When procaine was injected into the CX of tethered cockroaches, the optomotor responses decreased significantly then returned following the same time course as that found in silencing CX neurons (Figure 3).

findings.consequent: Feature detection responses of some EB neurons (Drosophila)
findings.direction: diminished in flight, not during walking
findings.quote: For instance, feature detection responses of some EB neurons were diminished in flight, but not during walking (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2013), while a group of FB neurons were shown to be unresponsive while the fly was quiescent but responded to translational optic flow during flight (Weir et al., 2014).

findings.antecedent: Animal's current location and behavioral context
findings.quote: This is achieved by hippocampal place cells, that each encode a particular location in the environment and also information about behavioral context in one signal (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; McNaughton et al., 2006; Yartsev and Ulanovsky, 2013; Figures 4B,C).
Each head direction cell is tuned to a single preferred head orientation, thus together the network covers the entire 360° environment like a compass.

Changes in head direction cell preferred angles due to manipulations to the cue card's position suggest that head direction cells establish their preferred orientations primarily based on visual information.

findings.antecedent: Passive rotation in complete darkness (no visual landmarks)
findings.quote: The directional signal can also be maintained even when the animal is passively rotated around in an arena, indicating that vestibular cues are more critical to the head direction signal than proprioceptive feedback or motor efference copy. The head direction signal is also retained when passive rotations take place in complete darkness, supporting that the head direction system can rely on vestibular inputs when visual landmarks are not available.

findings.antecedent: Animal crosses specific locations within an environment
findings.quote: Grid cells are principal cells in the medial entorhinal cortex that, similarly to place cells, fire when the animal crosses specific locations within an environment (Figures 4B,C). While place cells only have a single place field where they fire, grid cell firing fields are hexagonally arranged and repeat at regular intervals over the entire environment creating a grid-like structure of place fields.

findings.antecedent: Inactivation of the head direction system (anterior thalamic nuclei)
findings.quote: On the other hand, an elegant study from Winter et al. showed that grid cells rely upon head direction cells to encode orientation (Winter et al., 2015). They lesioned the head direction system located in the anterior thalamic nuclei with a reversible lidocaine injection and found that the inactivation of this orientation signal source disrupts grid cell firing.
Speed cells encode the running speed of the animal at any given moment during locomotion and their firing rates proportionally increase as the animal increases walking/running speed.

findings.consequent: Selective spatial deficits (especially during learning tasks)
findings.quote: Lesion studies showed that impairment of the striatum leads to selective spatial deficits, especially during tasks that require learning (Mizumori et al., 2009).

findings.antecedent: Directional motor components (angular velocity, forward walking speed) and navigational context cues (reward location)
findings.quote: Extracellular recordings in freely behaving animals confirmed that some striatal neurons are sensitive to directional motor components of navigation, such as angular velocity, forward walking speed and navigational context cues, such as a reward's location (Lavoie and Mizumori, 1994; Figure 4).

findings.consequent: Striatal place cell and head direction cell responses (rats)
findings.quote: Because both place cell and head direction cell responses significantly change in rearranged or novel environments, the spatial code in the striatum is thought to be highly context-dependent.

findings.antecedent: Silenced R3 and/or R4d ring neurons in the Ellipsoid Body (EB) of fruit flies
findings.consequent: Performance in a detour paradigm (remembering pre-distractor heading)
findings.quote: Flies with silenced EB ring neurons perform poorly in a detour paradigm (Neuser et al., 2008)... Contrary to this, flies with silenced EB ring neurons (R3 and/or R4d) cannot remember their pre-distractor heading, suggesting that these neurons are important components of a spatial working memory circuit (Neuser et al., 2008).

findings.antecedent: Silenced R1 neurons in the EB of fruit flies
findings.consequent: Spatial learning task (Morris water maze equivalent)
findings.quote: However, individuals with silenced R1 neurons in the EB fail this spatial learning task, even though they can perform normal locomotor and optomotor behaviors, visual pattern discrimination and olfactory learning paradigms. These results indicate that R1 neurons are specifically responsible for some aspect of visually-guided place learning that is independent of basic sensory and locomotor functions (Ofstad et al., 2011).
The recorded cells' firing rates strongly correlated with the animal's stepping frequency (Bender et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2015).

findings.antecedent: Fly changes heading and visual scenery
findings.quote: At certain headings relative to the displayed pattern's position, active cells formed a so-called "activity bump," wherein projections going to approximately 5-6 wedges would show increased activity. Whenever the fly changed its heading, the activity bump in the EB rotated as well... This indicates that the neurons were not encoding the visual information itself, but rather the animal's orientation relative to the visual landmark(s).

findings.antecedent: Passive rotation in a dark arena with a single visual cue
findings.consequent: Single neurons in the Fan-shaped Body (FB) and EB (cockroaches)
findings.direction: encoded head direction (some anchored to visual landmark, some independent, some bimodal)
findings.quote: We found that single neurons in both the FB and EB encoded head direction and among all neurons, the entire 360° environment was represented equally... Through manipulating the visual cue's position in the arena, we established that, similarly to rat head direction cells, some CX neurons are anchored to the visual landmark's position and encode the animal's relative orientation compared to this cue (Figure 5A)... However, we also recorded from neurons that did not shift their peak firing rates when we shifted the position of the visual landmark (Figure 5B), and neurons that encoded two preferred angles after the landmark shift (Figure 5C).

findings.direction: encode rotation direction history by increasing or decreasing firing rates
findings.quote: We found that in addition to the compass cells, both the FB and EB contain neurons that encode the rotation direction history of the animal, by increasing or decreasing their firing rates after the rotations (Figure 6).

As with the oiled plate experiments, stimulation through the recording electrodes generated turns that were consistent with the recording biases. That is stimulation in the left FB consistently generated left turns while stimulation in the right FB generated right turns.

findings.antecedent: CX stimulation during femoral chordotonal organ (FCo) stretch and release (cockroaches)
findings.consequent: Slow depressor of the coxa (Ds) reflex
findings.quote: When FCo stretch and release was repeated in conjunction with CX stimulation, the Ds reflex reversed to follow a pattern very similar to that seen during turning.

findings.consequent: CX population code for horizontal walking
findings.quote: This observation suggests that the population code seen in Figure 11 for horizontal walking is dynamic in that it can be greatly modified when the cockroach starts to climb. Other behaviors would be expected to generate further alterations in this population code.

extraction_result.title: From objects to landmarks: the function of visual location information in spatial navigation

findings.antecedent: Object uniqueness and informative features within an environment
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being used as a landmark
findings.quote: the more unique an object is within an environment, and the more informative its features are, the more likely it is that it will be used as a landmark

findings.antecedent: Presence of stable objects in the environment
findings.quote: the presence of stable objects in the environment can significantly improve navigational performance.

findings.antecedent: Animal observes that the spatial location of an object has moved over time
findings.consequent: Object's influence on hippocampal place cell activity
findings.quote: an object's influence on hippocampal place cell activity is lost when the animal observes that the spatial location of the object has moved over time

findings.antecedent: Objects rated by participants as larger and less 'portable' (more stable)
findings.quote: Objects that were rated by participants as larger and less 'portable' elicited an increase in activity within the parahippocampal gyrus.

findings.antecedent: Spatial judgments made with reference to stable environmental objects (compared to unstable objects)
findings.consequent: Activity in navigationally relevant medial parietal and temporal brain regions (including hippocampus)
findings.quote: making spatial judgments with reference to stable environmental objects... elicit greater activity in navigationally relevant medial parietal and temporal brain regions, including the hippocampus

findings.antecedent: Objects located at navigational decision points (e.g., a T-intersection)
findings.quote: objects that occupy locations at which a navigational decision has to be made... are more important for verbal route descriptions
objects at decision points are better remembered than those at non-decision points

findings.consequent: Activity in the left and right parahippocampal gyri
findings.quote: Functional MRI data showed increased activity in the left and right parahippocampal gyri for objects at decision points relative to those at non-decision points.

findings.antecedent: Objects at decision points (remembered or forgotten)
findings.consequent: Automatic coding of navigational relevance (reflected in parahippocampal activity)
findings.quote: decision point related increases in parahippocampal activity were observed for remembered as well as for forgotten objects, suggesting that the coding of navigational relevance is an automatic process that does not require explicit memory.

findings.antecedent: Buildings at decision points (in a real-world setting, especially in less familiar campus parts)
findings.quote: buildings at decision points were more readily recognized than buildings at non-decision points. Subsequent fMRI revealed increased parahippocampal activity for pictures of buildings that had appeared at decision points than for those at non-decision points, but only for buildings that occupied less familiar parts of the campus.

findings.consequent: Landmark agnosia, impaired recognition of salient environmental landmarks, and significant way-finding deficits
findings.quote: Damage to the parahippocampal gyrus has been found to cause a form of topographical disorientation termed 'landmark agnosia' in which the patient is selectively impaired in recognizing salient environmental landmarks, and thus exhibits significant way-finding deficits

findings.antecedent: Objects with stronger perceptual features (when in conflict with spatial positioning)
findings.quote: when these two cues are placed in conflict, objects with stronger perceptual features were later recognized faster irrespective of their spatial positioning.

findings.consequent: Determination of whether objects are included in direction giving and map drawing
findings.quote: it was spatial positioning that determined whether objects were included in direction giving and map drawing.

findings.antecedent: Objects serving as beacons (compared to associative cues)
findings.quote: When objects served as beacons, route learning was more efficient than when they acted as associative cues.

findings.consequent: Enduring representation of route information and directional information
findings.quote: beacon-based route learning led to a less enduring representation of route information and a poorer representation of directional information.

findings.antecedent: Availability of beacon-like cues during learning
findings.quote: the availability of beacon-like cues during learning is enough to block or overshadow the learning of other spatial information

findings.antecedent: Damage to the dorsal striatum (in rats)
findings.consequent: Ability to use beacon cues in spatial navigation tasks
findings.quote: rats with damage to the dorsal striatum are unable to use beacon cues in spatial navigation tasks

findings.consequent: Metabolic activity in the caudate nucleus
findings.quote: metabolic activity associated with beacon-based navigation is associated with increased activity in the caudate nucleus

findings.antecedent: Goal location indicated by a beacon cue (in humans)
findings.quote: observed striatal activity during navigation tasks where the goal location was indicated by a beacon cue

findings.antecedent: Heading disorientation (due to lesions in posterior-medial brain regions like retrosplenial cortex)
findings.consequent: Difficulty using visual environmental information for heading and significant navigational impairments
findings.quote: Patients with a condition known as 'heading disorientation' have difficulty using visual environmental information to determine their current heading
Head-direction cells exhibit firing activity that is tied to an animal's heading during navigation

findings.antecedent: Rotation of salient objects around an arena
findings.consequent: Similar rotations in the preferred firing direction of head-direction cells
findings.quote: Rotation of salient objects around an arena causes similar rotations in the preferred firing direction of head-direction cells

findings.antecedent: Environmental visual cues (when in artificial conflict with idiothetic information)
findings.quote: head-direction cells fire more consistently in response to environmental visual cues when visual and idiothetic information is artificially placed in conflict

findings.antecedent: Discrete visual cues (compared to geometric cues)
findings.consequent: Influence on head direction cells and computation of heading vectors
findings.quote: head-direction cells are strongly influenced by discrete visual cues, whereas geometric cues only provide a weak influence for the computation of heading vectors

findings.antecedent: Objects corresponding to the same heading direction (relative to objects corresponding to different directions)
findings.consequent: Neural activity in the medial parietal cortex
findings.quote: Neural activity in the medial parietal cortex was significantly reduced for objects that corresponded to the same heading direction relative to objects that corresponded to different directions, indicating neural adaptation as a function of heading within this brain area.

findings.antecedent: Routes containing salient objects as landmarks (compared to routes without such objects)
findings.consequent: Ability to learn a novel route
findings.quote: our ability to learn a novel route between two locations is significantly better for routes that contain salient objects that act as landmarks

findings.antecedent: New combination of buildings at an intersection associated with the same directional movement during training
findings.quote: participants' performance was as good as in the trained condition if the new combination of buildings at an intersection was associated with the same directional movement during training

findings.antecedent: New combination of buildings at an intersection associated with a direction that conflicted with that established during training
findings.quote: Conversely, performance was poorer if the new combination of buildings at an intersection contained buildings associated with a direction that conflicted with that established during training.

findings.antecedent: Objects at decision points along a path
findings.quote: objects at decision points along a path elicit increased parahippocampal activity relative to objects at non-decision points

findings.antecedent: Number of contextual associations elicited by a visual scene
findings.quote: activity in the parahippocampal cortex can be modulated by the number of contextual associations that are elicited by a visual scene

findings.antecedent: Increased angular disparity between the presented view and the studied view of object-arrays
findings.consequent: Spatial recognition performance for remembered object-arrays
findings.quote: spatial recognition performance for remembered object-arrays decreased in a linear fashion as the angular disparity between the presented view and the studied view increased
the representation of spatial information can also be organized around environmental reference frames when these are explicitly available

findings.antecedent: Imagined orientation aligned with a salient frame of reference (compared to misaligned orientations)
findings.consequent: Spatial judgments for a learned object-array
findings.quote: spatial judgments for a learned object-array is significantly better when made from an imagined orientation that is aligned with a salient frame of reference than when made from orientations that are misaligned
rats preferentially use geometric cues over featural cues for reorientation.

findings.antecedent: Disorientation in a rectangular room (even with available featural cues)
findings.consequent: Rotational errors (in young children, indicating preferential use of geometry)
findings.quote: Young children... display similar rotational errors after disorientation when searching for a toy within a rectangular room, even when featural cues are available to distinguish the two corners

findings.antecedent: Spatial learning based on boundary information (compared to discrete proximal landmarks)
findings.consequent: Distinct sets of behavioral and neural processes
findings.quote: spatial learning based upon boundary information and discrete proximal landmarks involve two distinct sets of behavioral and neural processes
Learning trials for boundary-related target objects were associated with increased hippocampal activation
trials concerning discrete proximal objects were associated with increased striatal activity

findings.antecedent: Imagining empty visual scenes with a 'wall-like' object (compared to without the object)
findings.quote: imagining empty visual scenes with a discrete, 'wall-like' object... resulted in an increase in hippocampal activity compared with imagining a scene without the object

findings.antecedent: Increased number of 'wall-like' objects in an imagined scene
findings.quote: Increasing the number of wall-like objects in the imagined scene resulted in an increase in the amount of hippocampal activity, again supporting the notion that hippocampal activity reflects, at least to some extent, the amount of boundary information present in an environment.

findings.antecedent: Changes to the geometric properties of an environment (e.g., expansion of rectangular environments)
findings.consequent: Place cell firing (parametric stretching and reforming of place fields)
findings.quote: changes to the geometric properties of an environment might result in relative changes in place cell firing. Expansion of rectangular environments resulted in parametric stretching and reforming of place fields.

findings.consequent: Neuronal firing patterns in brain regions (subiculum and medial entorhinal cortex)
findings.quote: the shape of environmental boundaries modulates the neuronal firing patterns in these brain regions

Axial maps and black-on-white space maps representing urban grids.
