Mean spatial values, encounter rates, and correlation coefficients for ten subareas of King's Cross.
City of London-movement rates for each of the 5 time periods for the two central routes (route 1 and route 2).

limitations: It is not possible to ascertain how far the observed patterns are a result of grid properties and how it is a result of attractors, as it is not yet possible to excise areas from the larger system and compute their mean integration values read within the large system in order to compare them with mean encounter rates.
It is not possible to take the ten routes as representative of their well-defined areas.

Differences between local subareas in the City of London study may be the result of differential distribution of built forms or the distinctively regional character of the City grid, requiring further research.
Much remains to be understood about the ceteris paribus clause in the theory of natural movement.

extraction_result.title: HUMAN TERRITORIALITY

findings.consequent: Social status, population control, resource distribution
findings.quote: Territoriality is a link between social behavior (competition and dominance) and population control in many animals. Communities regulate their own numbers by the use of 'conventionalized' competition, usually among males, for territory and the accompanying rights to food and (sometimes) mates. The winners are dominant animals and acquire social status, but since they are a fraction of the population, only a few community members get access to space, scarce resources, and females, thus limiting the size of the next generation.

findings.consequent: Spatial dispersion of individuals, ensured nutrition sources, territoriality
findings.quote: He posited that intraspecific aggression is a crucial aspect of animal life and that it has important survival value for a community because it acts as a source of mutual repulsion among individuals of the same species (in opposition to the 'herd instinct'), causing members of a group to space out over their biotope. This ensures that its sources of nutrition are not exhausted. Territoriality is, in essence, the spatial expression of this intraspecific repulsion.

Territory provides three basic elements necessary to healthy life: security (strongest at the center of a territory), stimulation (strongest at the borders, where defense against outsiders is most likely to occur), and identity.

findings.antecedent: Social status in a local community
findings.quote: It is clear that man, with many vertebrates, often displays a positive correlation between social status in a local community and the size of his territory there.

A confusing point is that large territories are not always associated with high status; members of the elite may trade a large country estate for a small city penthouse with no drop in status; clearly the desirability of the physical location of the territory is a mediating factor.

findings.consequent: Substitution of pecking order for territorial order
findings.quote: animals will sometimes substitute a pecking order (hierarchy) for a relatively democratic territorial order if crowded to the point that there is no room for individual territories (e.g., Davis', 1959, work with starlings).

findings.consequent: Social equalization, individual rights and liberties
findings.quote: Relative hierarchy is the important idea that the psychological phenomenon of dominance has geographic components: An individual dominates all others so long as he is on home ground; territory is thus a social equalizer for lower ranking organisms.

findings.consequent: Individual dispersion and group cohesion (balance of repulsive and attractive forces)
findings.quote: territoriality not only disperses individuals in space but also holds them together. Individuals are rarely dispersed as widely as possible, but to distances that reflect a balance between repulsive and attractive forces.

findings.consequent: Definition and organization of social role relationships
findings.quote: territoriality is instrumental in the definition and organization of various role relationships [Proshansky et al., 1970a, p. 180] in a community.

findings.consequent: Identity, personal idiosyncrasy, freedom of action, privacy, personal autonomy, self-realization, emotional release, self-evaluation, psychological protection, sense of control
findings.quote: A clear benefit provided by many, but not all, territories is privacy (the right of the individual to decide what information about himself should be communicated to others).

findings.antecedent: Control over defined areas of space (territoriality)
findings.consequent: Increased range of options, maximized freedom of choice, reduced crowding
findings.quote: Freedom of choice becomes a key concept in understanding privacy, territoriality and crowding [p. 182].

findings.consequent: Defense of space (jurisdiction/territory) by crew members
findings.quote: Roos (1968) described territoriality aboard a warship, where he observed crew members defending work spaces against one another.

findings.antecedent: Social structure (friendship patterns, power structures) within a group
findings.consequent: Spatial arrangement of beds in a boys' camp
findings.quote: the members of a group (cabin) arranged their beds spatially to reflect the social structure of the group.

findings.antecedent: Specific chairs in an old people's home (over time)
findings.consequent: Attachment, psychic and emotional significance (territoriality) for inmates
findings.quote: individual inmates became almost exclusively attached to specific chairs; they would keep to their personal seats despite considerable psychological costs and physical inconvenience in doing so.

findings.antecedent: Dominance hierarchy in a mental hospital ward
findings.quote: the investigators attempted to relate these patterns to territorial behavior. Dominance was defined by a combination of factors: the number of personal contacts a patient made, whether he initiated these, and their duration. By dividing the ward space off into squares, and using time-sampled observations, observers noted the mobility of the patients.

The authors claimed that territoriality was related to aggression, citing the fact that of all the territory-owning patients, only three did not show aggressive behavior. A close look at the data shows that this claim is unfounded since an equal proportion of nonholders show no aggression.

findings.antecedent: Dominance (social contact, staff reports) in hospitalized children
findings.quote: A relationship between dominance (defined by social contact and by staff reports) and territoriality was discovered, which weakly resembles the previous finding.

findings.antecedent: Home territory in a mental hospital ward
findings.quote: these individuals won 85% of all attempted physical acts of dominance on home territory, and 55% of those off home ground. Off home ground, simple status in the ward-dominance hierarchy was a fair predictor of winning acts of dominance, whereas on home ground, status position did not predict outcome.

findings.consequent: Reduced psychological complexity, enhanced personal control, persistent aggressive defense
findings.quote: Territories were interpreted by the investigators as basic and necessary reducers of psychological complexity in the boys' lives and enhancers of personal control for them, hence the difficulty in changing behavior linked to them.
All immediately reclaimed or tried to reclaim their old territories; this was interpreted as 'rigidity of spatial behavior' (it may simply have reflected fondness for the familiar).

findings.consequent: Higher rank inside the building, lower general adjustment outside the building
findings.quote: territory holders generally held higher rank than nonholders. Interestingly, territorial fighting among the boys was associated with position in the pecking order, but was negatively associated with boys' standings on 'general adjustment' (a measure that included behavior outside the building). It appeared that 'territorial adaptation' was effective for raising status inside the building, but not for functioning on the outside.

Results showed a variable relationship between dominance and territory: A positive association appeared during the first of three unequal time periods and a (nonsignificant) negative association for the final period.

findings.consequent: Demeanor and behavior (defensive/agitated vs. at ease/accommodating)
findings.quote: Colman (1968) described striking changes in demeanor and behavior of a medical patient that occurred when the patient moved from a hospital setting to his own home. In the hospital he was typically defensive and agitated; at home he was at ease, in control and accommodating.

findings.consequent: Space preference (filled vs. open), aggression levels
findings.quote: retardates prefer filled territorial spaces (spaces with physical objects in), while normals prefer open spaces; normals were also less aggressive.

findings.antecedent: Group size, time, group sex composition (beach users)
findings.consequent: Territory size, space per person, marker deployment
findings.quote: Group territories were found not to expand regularly with number of people in the group; instead, space per person tended to decrease as group size increased. ... Territory size increased with time in same-sex groups, but mixed groups tended to deploy markers as time passed.

findings.antecedent: Territorial defense (no trespassing signs, fences) on suburban homes
findings.consequent: Residence duration, anticipated future residence, defensive vigilance
findings.quote: Results showed that families living in defended homes had lived significantly longer on the property, but also anticipated a longer residence there in the future. ... An additional finding was that occupants of property with 'no trespassing' signs answered the door significantly faster than controls (interpreted as heightened defensive vigilance).

findings.antecedent: Dominance and leadership shifts in a college seminar group
findings.quote: individuals' dominance ratings ... correlated nonlinearly with their positions around the seminar table ... the correlations also changed with leadership shifts in the group.

findings.antecedent: Goal (avoid others vs. actively defend claims) in library/cafeteria settings
findings.quote: if students are asked to show where they would situate themselves to avoid others in the setting, they prefer territories in libraries that (a) face away from the main entrance, (b) are close to a wall, and (c) are toward the rear of the room. However, instructed to defend actively their claims, subjects locate their territories (a) facing the entrance and (b) more often in the middle of a table, or on an aisle.

findings.antecedent: Population pressure, marker type, neighbor interaction, claimant absence duration in a library
findings.consequent: Marker effectiveness, neighbor support for marked claims
findings.quote: At moderate density, most objects (including library journals, books) were found to protect a single space claim totally, and to delay occupation of the rest of the table. limitations: Participants' 3-back performance was poor, adding noise to the model and potentially obscuring overall interaction effects on the dual n-back task.
Post-environment cognitive testing was conducted on cell phones in distracting lobby/entry areas, which may have negatively impacted performance.
Participants were required to complete multiple surveys on cell phones during their walk, potentially diminishing attention restoration effects.
The study failed to replicate a previously found association between trait impulsivity and increased positive affect in natural environments, possibly due to differences in study design.
The study had less statistical power to observe relationships for individual differences due to these being between-subject analyses.
Participants may have fully explored the study spaces by the end of the one-hour walk, potentially attenuating some observed differences later in the survey.
The duration of the observed differences in affect and thought content after leaving each environment remains unknown.
Technical difficulties prevented participants from taking pictures of visual features during surveys, limiting the ability to compare individualized visual features with thought content.
Participants visited locations without companions, limiting generalizability to social interactions in public spaces.
The study was limited to one natural and one commercial space in a single North American city, potentially limiting the generalizability of findings to other designs, amenities, or cultural contexts.
The chosen locations (conservatory and mall) differ on multiple dimensions beyond naturalness, such as visitor demographics and primary purpose, which could also influence results.

findings.quote: light helps to give meaning to the environment and drive the process of interpretation of reality (but also adaptation to that), performed by a subject in a state of cognitive uncertainty

findings.consequent: Attraction, involvement, stimulation, fascination (due to mystery/complexity)
findings.mechanism: Light's shades and gradations attract, involve, stimulate, and fascinate due to perceived mystery and complexity.
findings.quote: light, with its many shades and gradations, leads the individual through the process of exploration towards the unknown: paradoxically, light seems to hide, rather than reveal the mystery, but just for this it attracts, involves, stimulates and fascinates us so much.

findings.consequent: Specific emotions, behaviors, mood, bodily/mental health, aesthetic appreciation
findings.mechanism: Light stimuli induce specific emotions, behaviors, mood, influence bodily/mental health, and aesthetic appreciation.
findings.quote: light stimuli (i.e. sensory input) will be able to induce specific emotions, behaviours and mood (Fusco, 2005b, 2012; Fusco et al., 2011; Tomassoni, 2014), as well as influence bodily and mental health, but also the level of aesthetic appreciation

findings.antecedent: Light (natural or artificial, colored or fluorescent, evanescent or material)
findings.consequent: Perceptive alterations within human sensory sphere, effectiveness of lit environment
findings.mechanism: Light's capacity to induce perceptive alterations is key to the effectiveness of any lit environment.
findings.quote: Due to the capacity of light—whether natural or artificial, colored or fluorescent, evanescent or material—to induce specific perceptive alterations within the sensory sphere of the human, the holistic, all-encompassing, and immersive dimension of individual involvement is, therefore, the key to the effectiveness of any lit environment.

findings.antecedent: Object location + light sources (angle of incidence) + object capacity (absorbing/reflecting light)
findings.mechanism: Object location and light interaction (absorption/reflection) drive human perception, emotions, and wellness.
findings.quote: the location of an object within the environment, according to the angle of incidence of one or more light sources, as well as the capacity of the object in absorbing and reflecting the light (luminous radiance or reflectance), are capable of driving human perception and emotions, as well as influencing the bodily and mental wellness

findings.antecedent: Light Design (cumulative effect of object + light + environment)
findings.consequent: Specific emotions, behaviors, psychophysical feedbacks, health, wellness
findings.mechanism: Light Design induces specific emotions, behaviors, and psychophysical feedbacks, influencing health and wellness.
findings.quote: Light Design takes advantage of that cumulative effect, related to the sum of all the above factors (object + light + environment) to induce specific emotions, behaviours and psychophysical feedbacks by the perceiver, influencing his/her health and wellness.

findings.antecedent: Light Art (various light sources, mixed with items, exhibition strategy)
findings.mechanism: Light Art excites different emotions and behaviors during aesthetic appreciation.
findings.quote: The so-called Light Art, for example, uses various types light sources... to produce an overall perceptual effect in the perceiver, exciting different emotions and behaviours during the individual experience of aesthetic appreciation.

findings.antecedent: Dark (absence of light), different light intensities (overlaps, intersections)
findings.consequent: Environmental organization, shadows, depth, modulated feelings and emotions
findings.mechanism: Dark and light intensity variations contribute to environmental organization, creating shadows/depth and modulating feelings/emotions.
findings.quote: Even the dark, namely absence of light, contributes to organize and set out the surrounding environment... overlaps and intersections generated by different light intensities, are able to create shadows and depth, modulating feelings and emotions

findings.mechanism: Light determines color perception, influencing mood and behavior.
findings.quote: light determines the colour perception of the objects inside a lit environment, influencing the mood and behaviour of people exposed

findings.mechanism: Sensory deprivation, especially light deprivation, has negative neuropsychiatric effects.
findings.quote: The "Sendep" (i.e. sensory deprivation) or perceptual isolation, especially about light, has negative effects on the human being from a neuropsychiatric perspective

findings.antecedent: Constant and uniform light stimulus (Ganzfeld Effect)
findings.consequent: Sensory deprivation-like effects, disorientation, 'fullness of emptiness', horizon's absence, altered perception of real space
findings.mechanism: The Ganzfeld Effect (constant, uniform light) leads to sensory deprivation-like effects, disorientation, and altered perception.
findings.quote: A related phenomenon is the so-called Ganzfeld Effect (or perceptual deprivation), that occurs when a constant and uniform light stimulus is used... this leads to effects similar to sensory deprivation

findings.consequent: Biochemical/hormonal processes, body temperature, mood, psychological well-being, electrical brain activity, neurotransmitters
findings.mechanism: Light influences biochemical/hormonal processes, body temperature, mood, psychological well-being, electrical brain activity, and neurotransmitters.
findings.quote: light influences biochemical and hormonal processes, body temperature, mood, psychological well-being and electrical brain activity, influencing the neurotransmitters

findings.antecedent: Low lighting + warm colours / pastel shades (in public spaces)
findings.mechanism: Low lighting with warm colors/pastel shades induces relaxation, protection, and hospitality in public spaces.
findings.quote: low lighting is used, accompanied by warm colours or pastel shades, in order to induce relaxation and evoke a sense of protection and hospitality

findings.antecedent: High lighting + colder chromatic temperatures (in production/competitive environments)
findings.mechanism: High lighting with colder chromatic temperatures stimulates work efficiency, productivity, aggressiveness, and competition.
findings.quote: high lighting accompanied by colder chromatic temperatures is able to stimulate a greater work efficiency and productivity, but also aggressiveness and competition

findings.antecedent: Bioelectric signals transmitted to the brain by photoreceptors (scanning light photons)
findings.consequent: Aesthetic quality of reality, correlation between perceptual processes and visual brain
findings.mechanism: Bioelectric signals from photoreceptors determine aesthetic quality and correlate with perceptual processes and the visual brain.
findings.quote: the functional specialization of cerebral cortex has showed that the bioelectric signals transmitted to the brain by the photoreceptors, namely neurons specialized in scanning the light photons, determine the aesthetic quality of the reality perceived by humans, demonstrating the correlation between perceptual processes and vis-ual brain

findings.antecedent: Light intercepted and reflected by an object
findings.mechanism: Viewers perceive spatial relationships only when light is intercepted and reflected by an object.
findings.quote: viewers perceive spatial relationships only when light is intercepted and reflected by an object settled in a space-light context

findings.consequent: Higher level of concentration/attention, greater emotional response
findings.mechanism: Higher intensity of light stimulation increases concentration/attention and emotional response.
findings.quote: generally, a higher intensity of light sti-mulation corresponds to a higher level of concentration/attention, associated with a greater emotional response by the subject.

findings.antecedent: Flashing or pulsating light (vs. steady light)
findings.consequent: Faster emotional responses, innate state of alert, influenced judgment abilities, problem solving, decision making skills
findings.mechanism: Flashing/pulsating light induces faster emotional responses, activates an alert state, and influences cognitive skills.
findings.quote: flashing or pulsating light (rather than a steady light) induces faster emotional responses by the perceiver: in fact, flashing light is associated with the danger, activating an innate state of alert in the human, enabling him/her to react quickly and in a most extreme way, influencing judgment abilities, problem solving and decision making skills.

findings.mechanism: Lighting modulation and color spectrum stimulate different emotions.
findings.quote: Through the lighting modulation (and its colour spectrum), it is possible to stimulate different emotions in human being, such as physical attraction or aggres-siveness

findings.consequent: Activation of specific neurotransmitters, production of specific hormones, psychobiological bases of light perception (changing according to sex/age)
findings.mechanism: Colored light activates neurotransmitters and produces hormones, influencing light perception based on sex/age.
findings.quote: the activation of specific neurotransmitters and the production, at biochemical level, of specific hor-mones in the presence of determined colour light source, shows the psychobiological bases of light perception by human, that may change according to the subject's sex or age

findings.antecedent: Lighting conditions, intensity, colour of light source
findings.consequent: Human biological cycles, circadian rhythm, level of hormonal secretions (melatonin)
findings.mechanism: Lighting conditions, intensity, and color influence biological cycles and circadian rhythm by affecting melatonin levels.
findings.quote: Lighting conditions, as well as the intensity and colour of the light source, influence indeed the human bio-logical cycles and, by a chronopsychological point of view, the circadian rhythm, by increasing or decreasing the level of specific hormonal secretions (such as melatonin, namely the marker-hormone of circadian rhythms, produced by the pineal gland), that are responsible for certain neurophysiological states.

findings.mechanism: Higher/lower lighting levels inhibit melatonin production, inducing higher concentration.
findings.quote: throughthe use of higher or lower lighting levels, it is possible to inhibit the production of melatonin, inducing a higher concentration

findings.mechanism: Low light increases melatonin levels and stimulates sleep onset.
findings.quote: melatonin levels increase during the night, when light is low, stimulating the sleep onset

findings.consequent: Dazzle, reduced visibility, reduced visual performance, discomfort, stress, sense of danger, disorientation, neuropsychiatric disorders (if sustained)
findings.mechanism: Over-lighting/flashes cause dazzle, reduced visibility/performance, discomfort, stress, danger, disorientation, and potential neuropsychiatric disorders.
findings.quote: over-lighting or close light flashes provoke dazzle, that by reducing the perceiver's visi-bility and visual performance, bring out discomfort, stress, sense of danger, and disorientation in the individual, that if sustained over time may lead to neuropsychiatric disorders

limitations: The findings represent only a small fraction of the relations between spatial and microclimate perceptions.

stimuli.description: Actual commercial office buildings, either LEED certified (65 buildings) or non-LEED rated (79 buildings), with comparable age and size.

tables.description: Categories included in the CBE Occupant Indoor Environmental Quality Survey, listing IEQ parameters and general building/workspace satisfaction.
Description of the dataset used for the analysis, including number of buildings and occupant responses for LEED and non-LEED groups.
Summary statistics for year of construction/renovation and building size for LEED and non-LEED groups.
Distribution of occupants' responses in the dataset and comparison with all LEED certified commercial offices by LEED Rating and Version.

Distribution of occupants' responses in LEED and non-LEED buildings based on 'non-environmental' factors (spatial layout, distance from window, building size, gender, age, type of work, time at workspace, weekly working hours).

Mean and standard deviation values for LEED and non-LEED buildings, difference in means (ΔM), statistical significance (p-value), and effect size (Spearman Rho) for occupant satisfaction with building, workspace, and 15 IEQ parameters.

limitations: The collection of users' responses is not linked with direct appraisal and/or measurement of physical characteristics and IEQ parameters of the building and the workspace.
No systematic randomized approach has been enforced for building selection, so the dataset cannot be considered a representative sample of the building stock.

Other parameters not included in the CBE survey (e.g., the availability of a view out and the layers included in such view, location of the building) may have a significant influence on occupant satisfaction.
The greatest majority of the responses were obtained from buildings situated in the US (83%), so results mainly refer to the North American context.
The sample of buildings included in our analysis is only partially representative of the total amount of buildings rated by LEED to date, due to the continuous evolution of the LEED program.
The study did not consider the potential influence of the variation of 'non-environmental' factors on occupant satisfaction in LEED and non-LEED certified buildings.

Future studies need to investigate the possible correlation existing between satisfaction of occupants, LEED certification level (platinum, gold, silver, certified), LEED product, and their different versions.

An investigation of the individual scorecards of the buildings featured in the chosen dataset of the CBE survey database is necessary to ascertain the credit distribution under the IEQ category that each building has achieved, and correlate this with the votes of satisfaction.

stimuli.description: 25 color photographs of natural scenes (lakes, rivers, sea, hills) rated high in restorativeness.
25 color photographs of urban scenes (city streets, industrial zones, housing) rated low in restorativeness.
25 color photographs of geometrical patterns.

tables.description: Mean d-primes, reaction times, numbers of correct and incorrect responses in Sessions 1 and 2 for restorative and nonrestorative groups (Experiment 1).
Mean d-primes, reaction times, and numbers of correct and incorrect responses in Sessions 1 and 2 for geometric patterns group (Experiment 2).
Mean d-primes, reaction times, and numbers of correct and incorrect responses in Sessions 1 and 2 for self-paced restorative and nonrestorative groups (Experiment 3).

limitations: Participants in this research did not have time enough to pass through all phases of restoration (clearing the head, recovering attention, facing accumulated matters, reflecting on priorities, prospects, actions, goals).
The study did not identify where participants were in the total restorative process.

tables.description: Acoustic parameters (Lp,A,S,4m, D2,s, rD, RT30, D50) from field measurements and computer simulations for different sound conditions (Low, Middle, High).
Visual characteristics of different OPO layouts (Office A, B, C, D) including Window area ratio, W/L, Floor area, Capacity, and Floor area per person.
Spearman correlation coefficients (rs) between physical parameters (acoustic and visual) and perceived affective quality attributes (Loud, Variable, Reverberant, Bright, Orderly, Wide).

Spearman correlation coefficients (rs) between physical parameters (acoustic and visual) and overall quality indicators (Acoustic satisfaction, Visual satisfaction, Speech privacy, Visual privacy, Work satisfaction, Task performance).

Spearman correlation coefficients (rs) between perceived affective quality attributes (Loud, Variable, Reverberant, Bright, Orderly, Wide) and overall quality indicators (Acoustic satisfaction, Visual satisfaction, Speech privacy, Visual privacy, Work satisfaction, Task performance).

limitations: Only subjects in their 20s participated, limiting generalizability.
Normality was not achieved for survey results.
Only visual and audio stimuli in a limited office space were used, limiting cognitive model clarity.
Lack of gender balance in recruited subjects.
Task performance quantified only with digit span test, not various cognitive skills.
Short-term stimuli used, not considering long-term effects (fatigue, stress).
Audio-visual attributes selected through a small focus group interview, not representing general OPO soundscape.
Evaluation scale for indoor soundscape needs further study.
Limited to visual and auditory senses, not considering other indoor environmental quality factors (air, thermal).
Only male sound sources used, not considering female voices with different fundamental frequencies.
Further research needed for individual worker characteristics (sensitivity, work satisfaction, career, gender, education, economic level).

stimuli.description: Five public city parks in Xiamen, China (Bailuzhou (west), Huli, Haiwan, Nanhu and Zhongshan)
Actual sounds perceived during soundwalks in city parks, categorized into human, traffic, mechanical, biological, and geophysical sounds.

Panoramic landscape photos shot horizontally at 1.2m height, made up of 8-10 photos per site, used to calculate percentages of landscape elements (vegetation, water, buildings, pavement, furniture, sky).

Digitalized land cover maps (buildings, roads, water areas) from IKONOS satellite images and Google Earth data, and vegetation density (NDVI) from SPOT satellite images, used to calculate landscape spatial pattern indices within 175m radius buffer areas.

tables.description: Recognised soundscape categories and corresponding sounds in the city parks.

Relationships between perception parameters of individual sound categories (PLS, POS), as well as between perception parameters of individual sound categories and the overall soundscapes (SDI), showing Pearson correlation coefficients.
Effects of landscape elements on soundscape perception in each sampled period, showing beta coefficients, t-values, adjusted R², and F-values from stepwise multiple regressions.
Effects of landscape spatial pattern on soundscape perception parameters in each sampled period, showing beta coefficients, t-values, adjusted R², and F-values from stepwise multiple regressions.
Correlations between each of the landscape indices.
Preference for different sound categories of the general public, showing N, Mean, and Std. Deviation.

limitations: The adjusted R² values for regression models using on-site landscape composition were rather low, suggesting other variables might be more effective.

Limitations of photographic techniques for measuring landscape composition, including conical projection, fixed lens zoom, camera vertical angle, and inability to capture the whole surrounding landscape completely.
Distortion of perspective while making panorama photos was not considered when measuring landscape composition.
Collinearity between many landscape indices may have limited the number of indices introduced into regression models.
The study scale was limited to a 175m radius, meaning sounds beyond this scale might not be well related to the local landscape.
The need to consider scaling effects in future studies.
More landscape indices should be tested as suitable soundscape indicators.

limitations: The spectral variation of sounds in similar acoustic environments may be inadequate to detect the effects of spectral variation on visitors' perceptions such as pleasantness and satisfaction.
More soundscape evaluations should be conducted at different urban parks with different soundscape elements to strengthen and clarify findings.
The study did not include other acoustic metrics in temporal and spatial aspects, nor other psychoacoustic metrics such as annoyance, roughness, and pleasantness beyond loudness.
The maximum noise level of the outdoor environment is hard to be predicted due to random noise sources.
The study focused only on subjective responses of soundscape perceptions and preferences, excluding effects of noise on health quality (physiological and psychological responses).

More complicated designs are needed for integrated analyses of relationships between subjective responses of sound quality and other variables such as health quality, age, education levels, gender, and nationality.

stimuli.description: Black and white film depicting work accidents with simulated blood and mutilation ('It Didn't Have to Happen') as a stressor.
Color/sound videotapes of six different everyday outdoor settings: two natural (vegetation, water) and four urban (heavy traffic, light traffic, many pedestrians, few pedestrians).

tables.description: Describes the visual content and sound levels (dB) for the six recovery environments (Nature Vegetation, Nature Water, Urban Heavy traffic, Urban Light traffic, Urban Many pedestrians, Urban Few pedestrians).

Mean changes in ZIPERS factor scores (Fear, Anger/Aggression, Positive Affects, Sadness, Attentiveness/Interest) from pre-stressor baseline to post-recovery for Nature, Pedestrian mall, and Traffic environments, along with F-values and p-values for environmental differences.

limitations: Results cannot be generalized directly to longer term nature exposures involving active participation (e.g., wilderness back-packing).
Further studies needed to investigate psychophysiological influences across varied situations (e.g., unstressed, bored, or chronically understimulated individuals).
Research should examine person-based variables (e.g., perceived control) influencing recovery in natural/urban settings.
Heart monitoring methods used did not allow precise disentanglement of parasympathetic and sympathetic influences.
No objective procedures available for measuring information rate over time for non-static, audiovisual environmental displays.

limitations: Few studies have taken a fully robust, empirical approach, often being purely descriptive or conducted in lab settings outside actual buildings.
Statistics are often descriptive (e.g., reporting means) rather than comparing groups, making cross-study comparisons difficult.
Few studies have approached research in biophilic architecture with an embodied cognition framework.
Few studies measure physiological responses (e.g., skin conductivity, brain region activation) in addition to subjective occupant responses.
Many studies observe human responses to naturalness (e.g., fractalness) in natural landscapes or solely organic natural forms, or use images instead of actual experiences.

Many inferences must be made, such as applying findings on natural or computer-generated fractals to architectural fractals, or using greenspace data on natural forms to infer effects of imitations of natural forms.
There is a need for ecologically valid experiments that place participants within the built environment to most accurately assess biophilic architecture's effects.

VR simulations are artificially created and do not include additional sensory information (e.g., temperature).
Participants were not cognitively fatigued, which may have diminished any potential restorative effect on attentional function.
A longer exposure duration could have increased effects of the environment on attentional functions.
The amount of nature offered in the current experiment was not enough to elicit 'fascination' or 'widening of attention' to trigger enhanced cognitive flexibility.

stimuli.description: Custom-built learning environment featuring a 3D model of a human heart with 21 floating labels. Interaction via a regular computer mouse or a tangible user interface (TUI) consisting of a motion-tracked plastic heart model (200g) with a stylus pen. Label display modes were permanent (all labels visible) or selective pointing (labels appear on click/touch).

limitations: Position of the virtual heart could not be changed in mouse conditions due to technical reasons, which was overwhelming for most participants.
The transfer test may have been too difficult for participants without prior medical training.
The TUI did not affect performance in a cognitively challenging task such as labeling cross-sections.
Too many factors (spatial ability, learning strategies, short learning time) might exert higher influence on cognitively challenging tasks.
Longer learning times or repeated presentations are needed to assess whether deeper processing is facilitated by embodied interaction design featuring haptic perception.
Future research should assess the influence of different learning styles when learning with multimodal user interfaces.
Design recommendations for TUIs are limited to similar learning tasks and relatively complex objects small enough to be held with one hand.
Less complex or unhandy objects may be equally well or better learned using a traditional mouse interface.
The two-handed use of TUIs had a detrimental effect on learning in the selective pointing condition.
Learning tests should have made use of the motor representations acquired while pointing at the model with the stylus pen to potentially show advantage for TUI selective pointing.
Future studies should investigate whether single-handed 3D pointing devices offer comparably positive effects as the mouse pointing condition.
More factors influence the usefulness of the selective pointing feature, such as learning time frame and the amount of elements to be learned.
More research is needed to disentangle the roles of visual load, motor load, and processing load when using self-cueing techniques such as selective pointing.
More research is required to validate and formalize the cost-benefit model of Embodied Cognition.
The role of motor information in learning tasks should be systematically investigated further.
Additional research on Embodied Cognitive Load Theory is required to confirm results and to further clarify the role of multisensory perception, interactivity, and meta-cognition.

extraction_result.title: Material properties of wooden surfaces used in interiors and sensory stimulation

findings.antecedent: Number of knots exposed in wooden surfaces
findings.consequent: Eye fatigue, eye strain, headaches, stress, anxiety
findings.quote: A study by Nakamura and Kondo (2007) shows a positive linear relationship between the number of knots exposed in wooden surfaces in interiors and eye fatigue, which can be accompanied by eye strain and headaches (Aries et al. 2015). Eye strain occurs due to the tightness of the ciliary muscles, which changes the shape of the lens in the eye (Aries et al. 2015) and can cause difficulties in learning and information processing (Edwards and Torcellini 2002). Furthermore, eye fatigue can lead to higher levels of stress and anxiety (Edwards and Torcellini 2002).

findings.antecedent: Long-wave colors (yellow-to-red hue) of interior wooden surfaces
findings.quote: Light falling in the eyes reflected from interior wooden surfaces can trigger the visual cortex in the brain and thereby affect cognition performance, including analysing, memorising and reasoning processes (Dzulkifli and Mustafar 2013, Aries et al. 2015). Dzulkifli and Mustafar (2013) have claimed that long-wave colours with a yellow-to-red hue can improve cognitive performance.

findings.consequent: Ultraviolet light absorption, comfortable environment for the eye, retina degradation
findings.quote: Furthermore, the aromatic lignin component in wood can absorb a high amount of ultraviolet light (Kutz 2005), creating a comfortable environment for the eye. According to Van Kuijk (1991), ultraviolet exposure can cause degradation of the retina (the innermost layer of the eye).

findings.antecedent: Anatomical level relief structure of wood surfaces (scattering light)
findings.consequent: Perceived glare, luminance value, eye fatigue, eye strain, headaches, perceived stress
findings.quote: On the structure of wood, Hirata et al. (2012) say that 'the anatomical level relief structure of wood surfaces induces light to scatter and diminish surface glare'. Scattering the light can decrease perceived glare and increase luminance value (Watchman et al. 2016). In general, reduced glare and an adequate luminance value can decrease the incidence of eye fatigue, eye strain and headaches (Aries et al. 2015), thereby reducing perceived stress (Edwards and Torcellini 2002).

findings.antecedent: Wood surface treatments (providing uniform light distribution)
findings.quote: In a similar way, wood surface treatments can provide uniform light distribution and thereby decrease perceived glare (Watchman et al. 2016).

findings.antecedent: Visual stimulation from interior wooden surfaces (general)
findings.consequent: Physiological responses (blood pressure, heart rate, rCBF), perceived stress
findings.quote: Generally, visual stimulation associated with wooden surfaces in interiors was found to have positive effects on physiological responses, which resulted in a reduction in respondents' perceived stress.

findings.antecedent: Wood's acoustic performance (composition, surface treatment, type of mounting, geometry, density)
findings.quote: The auditory stimulation from interior wooden surfaces depends mainly on the wood's acoustic performance. The acoustic performance of wood can be determined by its com-position, surface treatment, type of mounting, geometry (Bucur 2006) and density (Wegst 2006).

findings.consequent: Acoustic properties, microstructure of cell walls, elastic properties
findings.quote: A higher moisture content can deteriorate the acoustic properties of wood, since it changes the microstructure of the cell walls (Wegst 2006, Rowell 2012).

findings.consequent: Physiological responses (blood pressure, peripheral blood flow, heart rate, skin conductance, respiratory rate), perceived stress
findings.quote: The results presented indicate that physiological responses to sound are indeed dependent on individual sensitivity more than on the sounds or their pressure levels.

findings.antecedent: Chemical composition of wood (volatile extractives, monoterpenes)
findings.consequent: Physiological responses (oxy-Hb, HRV, natural killer cell activity, stress hormones, CNV)
findings.quote: The effects of olfactory stimulation from wood on physiologi-cal responses depend strongly on the chemical composition of the wood, including volatile extractives (Navi and Sandberg 2012) and the subjects' individual differences in sensitivity towards olfactory stimulation (Brand and Millot 2001, Lund-ström et al. 2003).

findings.antecedent: Lower thermal conductivity of wood (compared to other materials)
findings.consequent: Heat flux, skin temperature, perceived stress, physiological responses
findings.quote: According to Wang et al. (2000), the effects of tactile stimu-lation on physiological responses, which includes skin temp-erature, depend on the heat flux of materials. In general, the thermal conductivity of wood and wood-based materials is lower than other materials commonly used to cover interiors, such as tile, marble, and concrete (Wang et al. 2000, Yaşar and Erdoğan 2008). The results from the studies mentioned above show that touching wooden surfaces has mainly positive effects on physiological responses, and can reduce perceived stress.

Adaptive thermal comfort and sustainable thermal standards for buildings

findings.antecedent: rational thermal comfort indices (e.g., ISO 7730, ASHRAE 55)
findings.consequent: prediction of comfort vote in field surveys
findings.mechanism: Rational indices fail to capture the adaptive processes observed in real-world field studies.
findings.quote: When rational indices are used to predict the thermal comfort of subjects measured in field surveys they are found to be no better at predicting the comfort vote [6] than simpler indices such as temperature alone.

findings.consequent: range of conditions subjects find comfortable
findings.mechanism: Adaptive actions by occupants allow for a wider range of comfortable conditions than predicted by rational indices.
findings.quote: In addition the range of conditions which subjects find comfortable in field surveys is much wider than the rational indices predict.

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (comparison across surveys vs. within a single survey)
findings.consequent: rate of change of mean comfort vote
findings.mechanism: People adapt to different climates, making their comfort vote less sensitive to temperature changes when comparing across diverse contexts than within a single, more stable context.
findings.quote: The rate of change of comfort vote with temperature is characteristically much lower from one survey to another than it is within any particular survey (Fig. 1).

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (in field surveys over a wide range of indoor climates)
findings.mechanism: Occupants adapt their comfort expectations and behaviors to the prevailing indoor temperature.
findings.quote: The corollary of this finding is that in field surveys the comfort temperature is closely correlated with the mean temperature measured. This was found to be the case in surveys conducted over a wide range of indoor climates (Fig. 2a).

findings.antecedent: mean indoor temperature (measured at monthly intervals throughout the year in Pakistan and Europe)
findings.mechanism: People continuously adapt their comfort expectations and behaviors to seasonal changes in indoor temperature.
findings.quote: The strong relationship with comfort temperature is clear.

findings.antecedent: indoor temperature (20-30 °C) with fans (in Pakistani offices)
findings.mechanism: Adaptive actions, such as using fans, allow occupants to maintain comfort over a wider range of indoor temperatures.
findings.quote: Pakistani buildings were found comfortable at temperatures ranging between 20 and 30 °C with no cooling apart from fans (from [12]).

findings.antecedent: outdoor monthly mean temperature (in free-running buildings)
findings.mechanism: In free-running buildings, the indoor climate is directly coupled to outdoor conditions, and occupants adapt their comfort expectations accordingly.
findings.quote: The relationship for the free-running buildings was closely linear.

findings.antecedent: outdoor monthly mean temperature (in heated or cooled buildings)
findings.mechanism: In heated or cooled buildings, the indoor climate is decoupled from the outdoor temperature, making the direct adaptive relationship less pronounced.
findings.quote: For heated and cooled buildings the relationship is more complex.

findings.antecedent: building type distinction (centrally air-conditioned vs. naturally ventilated) for predicting occupant thermal response
findings.mechanism: The distinction based on building services (AC vs. NV) is not supported by field evidence as a primary driver of adaptive response, suggesting more fundamental adaptive mechanisms.
findings.quote: Nor is this distinction supported by evidence from the field [6].

findings.antecedent: building type distinction (free-running vs. heated or cooled buildings)
findings.consequent: precision of the relationship between comfort temperature and outdoor temperature
findings.mechanism: This distinction better captures the degree of environmental control and adaptive opportunity, leading to more precise relationships.
findings.quote: Humphreys and Nicol [14] argue that using Humphreys' original distinction (between free-running and heated or cooled buildings) increases the precision of the relationship...

findings.mechanism: Control over one's environment provides affordances for adaptation, leading to higher satisfaction and tolerance for minor discomforts.
findings.quote: Leaman and Bordass [20] have demonstrated that there is more 'forgiveness' of buildings in which occupants have more access to building controls.

findings.antecedent: occupant control over conditions (e.g., opening windows, using fans)
findings.mechanism: When occupants can adjust their environment, variability can be a positive outcome of their adaptive actions to maintain comfort.
findings.quote: In buildings where the occupants are in control, variability may result from people adjusting conditions to suit themselves. A certain amount of variability then becomes a 'good thing'.

findings.antecedent: control left to building manager (through HVAC system)
findings.mechanism: Lack of personal control limits adaptive opportunities, making occupants less forgiving and reducing the range of acceptable conditions.
findings.quote: If the control is left to the building manager (through the HVAC system) there is a smaller envelope of acceptable conditions, comfort changes more quickly with temperature and the occupants appear less forgiving.

findings.antecedent: alpha value for exponentially-weighted running mean outdoor temperature (Trm)
findings.consequent: correlation of Trm with comfort temperature
findings.mechanism: The exponentially-weighted running mean with an alpha value of approximately 0.8 best reflects the temporal dynamics of human adaptation to past temperatures.
findings.quote: The correlation with Tod falls consistently with increasing a, the correlation with comfort temperature rises gradually until a reaches about 0.8 and then starts to decrease.

findings.antecedent: daily mean outdoor temperature (alpha=0) and monthly mean outdoor temperature (alpha≈0.95)
findings.mechanism: Neither instantaneous daily mean nor long-term monthly mean temperatures fully capture the temporal aspect of adaptation as effectively as an exponentially-weighted running mean.
findings.quote: The correlation with Tod (x = 0) and with the monthly mean of outdoor temperature (α≈ 0.95) are both less than the correlation with Trm where a = 0.8.

findings.antecedent: control regime with variable indoor set-point (changing with running mean outdoor temperature) compared to constant set-point
findings.mechanism: People's adaptive capacity allows them to remain comfortable even with a variable indoor temperature set-point, as long as it aligns with the running mean of outdoor temperature.
findings.quote: Recent work suggests that the use of a control regime which provides a set-point temperature changing with the running mean of the outdoor temperature does not increase discomfort among occupants as compared with a constant set-point...

findings.antecedent: control regime with variable indoor set-point (changing with running mean outdoor temperature) compared to constant set-point
findings.mechanism: Aligning indoor temperature set-points with outdoor conditions through adaptive algorithms reduces the energy demand for cooling.
findings.quote: ...but can result in substantial savings in energy use [13].

findings.antecedent: free-running buildings (data from 1970s [9] and 1998 ASHRAE database [15])
findings.consequent: relationship between comfort temperature (Tc) and outdoor temperature (To) (Tc = 13.5 + 0.54 To)
findings.mechanism: The fundamental adaptive mechanisms linking outdoor climate to indoor comfort in free-running buildings are remarkably stable across different datasets and time periods.
findings.quote: Humphreys and Nicol [14] showed that this relationship between comfort temperature Tc and outdoor temperature To for free-running buildings (Eq. (2)) is remarkably stable as between data presented by Humphreys in the 1970s [9] and in the 1998 ASHRAE database [15] (see Fig. 5).

findings.mechanism: This high correlation quantifies the strong adaptive relationship between outdoor temperature and comfort in free-running buildings.
findings.quote: The correlation coefficient r for the relationship was 0.97 for 1978 data and 0.95 for ASHRAE database.

findings.antecedent: heated and cooled buildings (comparison between 1970s [9] and 1990s [11] databases)
findings.mechanism: Changes in custom, expectations, or other factors over time may influence preferred comfort temperatures in controlled environments.
findings.quote: There is also a difference of some 2 °C in indoor comfort temperatures for heated and cooled buildings between two databases [9], one compiled in the late 1970s and the other [11] compiled in the 1990s (see Fig. 5).

findings.antecedent: no possibility of changing clothing, activity, or air movement
findings.mechanism: The absence of adaptive opportunities severely restricts the range of thermal conditions perceived as comfortable.
findings.quote: In a situation where there was no possibility of changing clothing or activity and where air movement cannot be used, the comfort zone may be as narrow as ± 2 °C.

findings.antecedent: adaptive opportunities available and appropriate (e.g., changing clothing, activity, using air movement)
findings.mechanism: The ability to perform adaptive actions allows individuals to maintain comfort over a significantly wider range of environmental conditions.
findings.quote: In situations where these adaptive opportunities are available and appropriate the comfort zone may be considerably wider.

findings.antecedent: use of a variable indoor temperature in air-conditioned buildings
findings.mechanism: Allowing indoor temperatures to vary adaptively with outdoor conditions reduces the energy required for cooling.
findings.quote: The extent of energy savings has been estimated in the region of 10% of the cooling load in UK conditions. In a recent European project [31] estimated energy savings were in the region of 18%.

findings.mechanism: Naturally ventilated buildings rely on adaptive comfort, which inherently requires less energy for conditioning compared to air-conditioned buildings.
findings.quote: Naturally ventilated buildings typically use about half the energy of ones which are air-conditioned [32].

tables.description: Descriptors for the ASHRAE and Bedford scales for thermal sensation votes

limitations: Environmental conditions in field studies are inherently variable and difficult to measure accurately, leading to potential errors in statistical relationships.
It is difficult to generalize results from one field survey to another due to contextual differences.
Rational indices require knowledge of clothing insulation and metabolic rate, which are difficult to estimate accurately in the field.
Quantifying 'adaptive opportunity' in terms of building controls is difficult, as the mere existence of a control does not guarantee its use or effectiveness.
Comfort surveys do not consistently produce data coherent enough for a precise statistical determination of the best time-series to use for adaptive algorithms.
It is unclear whether observed differences in comfort temperatures for heated/cooled buildings over time are due to changes in preference or other database differences.

findings.antecedent: Bike Cycle exhibit (complex machine work schema, immediately recognizable robot, four large, color-coded buttons)
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema reduces cognitive load, allowing focus on challenge.
findings.quote: 73% of visitors persisted until they had succeeded, and 70% said they thought the level of challenge was about right.

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit (competition/race schema, two lanes, six disks with varying features)
findings.consequent: visitor predictions, explanations, and new understandings
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema (race) provides context, freeing cognitive resources for scientific inquiry.
findings.quote: several studies have shown that this exhibit provokes predictions, explanations, and new understandings that can be articulated

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.consequent: complex inferences from visitors (theories about camouflage, froggy lifestyle)
findings.mechanism: Familiar schema (waiting/watching for reward) reduces frustration, allowing for deeper cognitive engagement and social interaction.
findings.quote: most likely of any in the exhibition to elicit complex inferences from visitors

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.consequent: stories, personal associations, declarations of previous knowledge
findings.mechanism: The exhibit's design, despite hidden frogs, allowed visitors to engage in social meaning-making and knowledge sharing.
findings.quote: second most likely element to evoke stories and personal associations, and the second most likely to elicit declarations of previous knowledge

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (watching and waiting schema, tank with hidden nocturnal frogs)
findings.mechanism: The 'watching and waiting' schema set appropriate expectations, preventing frustration.
findings.quote: None of the 30 pairs of visitors expressed frustration or annoyance at having to look for the frogs

findings.antecedent: Detective puzzle schema (framing the Whodunit exhibition)
findings.consequent: immediate apprehension of purpose and relationship of distinct elements

findings.quote: allowed visitors to immediately apprehend the purpose and relationship of distinct elements

findings.antecedent: Highly interactive (changeable lighting, focus, dish location) and live specimens OR Less interactive (changeable lighting, focus) and live specimens
findings.consequent: visitor holding time, exhibit enjoyability rating, reconstruction of relevant details
findings.mechanism: Live specimens and interactivity enhance engagement and memory.
findings.quote: visitors who saw one of the live, interactive versions of the exhibit stayed longer, rated the exhibit as more enjoyable, and were able to reconstruct more relevant details of their experience, than the noninteractive version

findings.antecedent: More interactive version (changeable lighting, focus, dish location, live specimens) vs. Less interactive version (changeable lighting, focus, live specimens)
findings.mechanism: Adding more interactivity beyond a certain point does not necessarily improve experience or learning.
findings.quote: we found no significant differences between the experiences of visitors who used the more interactive version and those who used the less interactive version.

findings.antecedent: Display of seven optical illusions (low physical interactivity)
findings.consequent: visitor stopping behavior (stopping at all seven illusions)
findings.mechanism: Intriguing visual phenomena can sustain attention even without physical interaction.
findings.quote: a display of seven optical illusions at which more visitors stopped at all seven than stopped at any one

findings.antecedent: Exhibits with live animals in glass terrariums (low physical interactivity) vs. Physically interactive exhibits
findings.mechanism: Live animals, even without direct interaction, can be highly engaging and promote social learning.
findings.quote: exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums were more attractive and evoked significantly more frequent and more diverse “learning-talk”... than the physically interactive exhibits.

findings.antecedent: Videotape of frogs catching and eating prey (non-interactive)
findings.consequent: diversity of learning-talk, longest holding times
findings.mechanism: Compelling visual content, even if non-interactive, can be highly engaging and stimulate discussion.
findings.quote: The single exhibit in the exhibition that evoked the greatest diversity of learning-talk (as well as the longest holding times) was a videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey.

findings.mechanism: APE design supports deeper cognitive and physical engagement.
findings.quote: APE exhibits engaged visitors for more than twice as long as traditional exhibits.

findings.mechanism: APE design encourages diverse forms of inquiry.
findings.quote: elicited a broader variety of “driving questions,” defined as the initial thought that visitors had as they approached the exhibit.

findings.consequent: variety in physical interaction patterns/sequences, later label reference, self-generated explorations
findings.mechanism: APE design supports more open-ended, self-directed inquiry.
findings.quote: visitors' physical interactions with APE exhibits varied in both pattern and sequence more than with the traditional exhibits, and labels were often referred to later in the sequence of exhibit use

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.mechanism: Making the key variable more salient helps visitors identify the correct principle.
findings.quote: When the exhibit was used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten the salience of the key variable of mass distribution, more visitors succeeded in figuring out the correct principle behind the disks' behavior.

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.mechanism: Making the principle too obvious might reduce the challenge and intrinsic motivation for deeper engagement.
findings.quote: the overall holding time decreased, and fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Wooden disks designed to heighten salience of mass distribution (in Downhill Race exhibit)
findings.mechanism: Making the principle too obvious might reduce the challenge and intrinsic motivation for deeper engagement.
findings.quote: the overall holding time decreased, and fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (containing invitation to interact and then explanation of underlying principle)
findings.mechanism: Providing direct explanations helps visitors articulate the scientific principle.
findings.quote: A more traditional exhibit label... resulted in more visitors articulating the correct principle

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (containing invitation to interact and then explanation of underlying principle)
findings.mechanism: Providing direct explanations might reduce the need for active inquiry and deep engagement.
findings.quote: but led them to be less deeply engaged with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Simple partitions around a group of related exhibits
findings.consequent: percentage of visitors correctly identifying common theme
findings.mechanism: Partitions reduce distraction and visually group related exhibits, aiding conceptual coherence.
findings.quote: increased the percentage of visitors who correctly identified their common theme from 30 to 51%

findings.antecedent: New Seeing collection (designed for eye/brain function, cultural effects on seeing) vs. Original Optics collection
findings.consequent: visitor talk about seeing as interpretation, mention of visual system parts, appreciation of attention, realization of different perceptions, connection to daily lives
findings.mechanism: The new design successfully communicated subtle and complex scientific ideas by focusing on interpretation and relevance.
findings.quote: significantly more visitors to Seeing talked about seeing as interpretation, mentioned specific parts of the visual system, said they had a new appreciation of the importance of attention in seeing, said they hadn't realized that people see things differently, and found that the exhibits related to their daily lives.

findings.antecedent: Traits of Life collection (displaying diverse living creatures to illustrate commonalities)
findings.consequent: communication of abstract theme (four common characteristics)
findings.mechanism: Visitors interpreted the display as diversity rather than commonality, possibly due to existing conceptual schemes.
findings.quote: our Traits of Life collection was less successful in communicating its abstract theme

findings.consequent: explicit connections made among exhibits by visitors
findings.mechanism: Visitors may not expect or have the cognitive resources to make explicit connections between exhibits in an open environment.
findings.quote: visitors made explicit connections among exhibits at only 5% of the exhibits at which they stopped.

findings.antecedent: Exhibit collections with diverse learning styles (quieter, carpeted, selective lighting, partitions, observation/reflection support)
findings.consequent: visitor noticing and valuing diversity of spaces
findings.mechanism: Providing varied environments caters to diverse learning preferences and reduces fatigue.
findings.quote: Evaluation studies have shown that our visitors notice and value the diversity of such spaces within the museum

findings.antecedent: Inquiry video clips (asking short questions for further exploration)
findings.consequent: visitor preference, integration of exhibit experience into prior knowledge
findings.mechanism: Inquiry-based prompts are more effective than personal narratives for integrating science content in this context.
findings.quote: inquiry videos were preferred by visitors, and helped them integrate the exhibit experience into their prior knowledge

findings.antecedent: Narrative video clips (personal story about connection to exhibit)
findings.mechanism: Personal narratives showed little or no impact compared to control for integrating science content.
findings.quote: while narratives showed little or no impact compared with the control condition.

findings.antecedent: Narrative video (unfolding drama with young children)
findings.consequent: evoking personal connections in visitors' lives
findings.mechanism: Specific narrative forms (drama with children) can be more effective at creating personal connections.
findings.quote: this showed some evidence of evoking personal connections in more visitors' lives than the control or inquiry conditions.

limitations: Need more research on the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and how the tension plays out at different scales, times, and audiences.
Designing exhibits to maximize visitor-directed inquiry may sometimes decrease the chances that visitors will understand a specific scientific principle.
The field badly needs more studies of nonverbal forms of learning, especially for children, as these may be dominant forms for three-dimensional physical interaction.
Large-scale design issues for conceptual coherence are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.
More research is needed to determine if narrative instantiations were flawed or if the chaotic, high-energy science museum environment makes storytelling an ineffective learning strategy.

Challenges for narrative include: noisy/chaotic environment not conducive to sitting/listening, upper limit of a few minutes on narrative length, visitor preference for concrete over metaphorical content, and attentional conflicts with group conversations.

limitations: Increasing the number of participants and including individuals from various age ranges and cultural backgrounds would enhance the diversity and generalizability of our findings.

Gathering qualitative feedback from participants through open-ended surveys or semi-structured interviews could enrich our insights and potentially reveal factors impacting the individual's perceived experience that sensors might not capture.
Measuring the peak wavelength of light during the experiment is helpful for understanding the non-visual effects of light, providing a more comprehensive analysis of its impact.
The use of the EEG cap can introduce some level of discomfort for participants which itself could influence the results.
EEG is highly sensitive to movement, we asked participants to minimize abrupt movements as much as possible.
The deployment of EEG in a real-world situation is currently time-consuming, costly, and requires expertise.
This work, however, should be considered as a primary study with a limited set of conditions.

stimuli.description: An open-plan office environment modified to laboratory-like conditions, including ceiling-high sound screens and acoustic panels, indirect lighting, and furniture.

Twelve different sound conditions: silence, unmasked speech, and ten masked speech conditions. Masked speech varied by SNR (-9 dB or -12 dB), masker location (same direction, 90° different direction, or conventional ceiling), and masker HPF (100 Hz or 200 Hz). Speech signals were German sentences from two studio monitors (T1, T2). Masking sounds were filtered pink noise from local emitters (M1, M2) or conventional ceiling emitters (M0).

tables.description: Measured A-weighted energy-equivalent SPL LAeq [dB(A)] for the five loudspeaker sets used to simulate different sound conditions.
Name, masking sound, target and masker location, and SNR [dB] of the tested sound conditions.
Overview of t-tests of mean error rates during the different sound conditions with adjusted p-values and Cohen's d effect sizes.
Overview of t-tests of mean annoyance ratings on a five-point scale during the different sound conditions with adjusted p-values and Cohen's d effect sizes.

limitations: The study was performed in an open-plan office with state-of-the-art acoustical design, but with room-high partitions, making it not comparable to a conventional open-plan office.
The direct and reverberant components reaching a worker, and thus sound fields, may differ notably between this office and conventional open offices.
The distances of the speech sources (3-4 m) were relatively small, which might be too short for effective sound masking or where communication is desired.

The study considered only sound conditions with one disturbing background speech signal with a single voice, whereas multi-talker environments are more realistic and may impair working memory performance differently.
The setup did not allow for a separation of the effects of speech and sound masking loudspeaker locations in multi-talker environments.

limitations: The effect of traffic stream in screening sound reflected from the farside barrier was not fully accounted for by prediction models.
The assumption of vehicle width and angle of incidence in calculations may slightly underestimate the degree of screening of reflected sound.
The effects of vehicle speed on source strength were not taken into account.
Simplified geometry assumed in the prediction model (e.g., presence of safety fences, reflective ground beams, limited barrier length and curvature) may have reduced recorded noise level increases.
The sides of many large vehicles may not provide conditions for specular reflections, affecting multiple reflections between vehicle and barrier.
Less than perfect absorption and reflective properties of barrier panel faces may have slightly reduced noise level increases.

Scattering by the vehicle stream and associated turbulence, and simplified geometries and acoustic performances of barrier panels assumed in models contribute to discrepancies between measured and predicted levels.
Further carefully controlled field studies with varying traffic flows are required to fully quantify these effects.

Six prints and two wind chimes placed on the walls of the experimental room (picture condition) vs. bare walls (no-picture condition).

limitations: Only male subjects were included in the study, limiting generalizability to females.

findings.mechanism: focus the learners' attention on problem states and associated operators (i.e. solution steps)

findings.mechanism: focus the learners' attention on problem states and associated operators (i.e. solution steps), enabling them to induce generalised solutions.

findings.antecedent: physically integrating spatially separated sources of complementary information

findings.quote: It was found that only presenting the diagram was superior to presenting both sources of information together.

findings.mechanism: increases the probability that similar features can be identified and that relevant features can be distinguished from irrelevant ones.

limitations: Current knowledge is incomplete, and future research is needed to continue development.
The assumption of fixed working memory capacity in CLT might be untenable, as working memory resource depletion occurs.
Current understanding of self-regulated learning and the interaction of primary and secondary knowledge needs rethinking for teaching.
CLT does not fully address how physical environments evoking stress, emotions, and uncertainty affect cognitive load.
The special role of human movement in working memory might require reconsideration of human cognitive architecture.
There is virtually no evidence that self-regulation is teachable as a domain-general procedure.
More research is needed into objective measurement techniques for cognitive load and their potential.

Muscle ergonomics analysis demonstrates that the use of passive exoskeleton systems significantly reduces lumbar vertical spine muscle activity and that the reduction is even greater when weight lifting loads (Antwi-Afari et al., 2021).

glare is a significant factor affecting the visual comfort of indoor personnel. PUI, BA, FR, and other indicators can indicate visual discomfort caused by glare, but increasing ambient luminance contrast can improve efficiency in a non-glare environment (Liu et al., 2021).

findings.quote: By studying the effect of ceiling height on aesthetic judgments in architectural design, researchers discovered that visuospatial processing activates the left anterior cuneiform and left middle frontal gyrus of the brain (Vartanian et al., 2015).

findings.antecedent: certain contemplative buildings (e.g., museums, churches, libraries, etc.)
findings.consequent: contemplative states (significant activation of specific brain regions)
findings.quote: Specific architectural styles can also induce contemplative states; for example, certain contemplative buildings (e.g., museums, churches, libraries, etc.) cause significant activation of the left posterior central gyrus and left inferior parietal phase, eliciting contemplative experiences (Bermudez et al., 2017).
