Meanwhile, fNIRs are being employed in indoor wayfinding research, where they are used to assist in the design of adaptive wayfinding systems by monitoring and classifying real-time cognitive load (Zhu et al., 2021).

extraction_result.title: Ageing- and dementia-friendly design: theory and evidence from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology and environmental psychology can contribute to design guidelines that minimise spatial disorientation

findings.consequent: Decline in spatial orientation and navigational skills, difficulty learning to navigate in new, unfamiliar environments
findings.quote: Spatial orientation and navigational skills start deteriorating relatively early in the ageing process, even when there are no apparent deficiencies in other cognitive abilities (Harris and Wolbers 2012; Moffat 2009).

findings.antecedent: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) or Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.quote: This gradual loss of navigational skills is even more evident in individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) (Fasano et al. 2018; Mitolo et al. 2013) or AD, of which disorientation is typically one of the first symptoms (Pai and Jacobs 2004; Serino et al. 2015), and in unfamiliar environments.

findings.antecedent: Retirement complexes and care homes designed to reduce wayfinding difficulties
findings.consequent: Easier transition to new accommodation, improved independence, quality of life, well-being, and reduced caregiver workload for people with AD
findings.quote: Designing retirement complexes and care homes with people whose navigational skills are declining in mind would make the transition to their new environment easier for people with AD (O'Malley et al. 2017).

findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance in complex navigation tasks
findings.quote: For instance, spatial anxiety has a detrimental effect on wayfinding performance, particularly in complex navigation tasks (Srinivas 2011).

findings.antecedent: Sense of spatial self-efficacy and pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments
findings.quote: whereas a sense of spatial self-efficacy and taking pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments positively correlate with wayfinding performance (Pazzaglia et al. 2018a, b).

findings.consequent: Reduction in dysfunctional behaviour, improved well-being (lessened depressive symptoms, improved mood, quality of life)
findings.quote: small-scale environments, an environmental aspect strictly related to spatial navigation (Marquardt and Schmieg 2009), are associated with the reduction in dysfunctional behaviour and improved well-being including lessened depressive symptoms and improved mood and quality of life.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks with properties: uniqueness, saliency, persistence, informativeness, nameability, relevant location
findings.quote: To be useful for the purposes of orientation and wayfinding, landmarks must have a number of properties (Nothegger et al. 2004; Raubal and Winter 2002; Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a).

findings.consequent: Decline in route learning ability (longer to learn novel routes, deficits in landmark-direction associations, impaired knowledge of landmark sequence)
findings.quote: Cognitive ageing is associated with a decline in route learning ability (Head and Isom 2010; Hilton et al. 2021) i.e., older adults take longer to learn novel routes (O'Malley et al. 2018).

findings.consequent: Deficits in using allocentric navigation strategies (longer to form cognitive maps, less efficient in planning new routes)
findings.quote: Healthy older adults also show deficits in using allocentric navigation strategies. Specifically, healthy older adults take longer to form cognitive maps and, in addition to their difficulty with encoding spatial information, their memory retrieval is also affected by cognitive ageing (Iaria et al. 2009).

findings.consequent: Preference for egocentric navigation strategies over allocentric, difficulty switching from egocentric to allocentric strategies
findings.quote: Specifically, older adults find allocentric navigation strategies more difficult to use than egocentric strategies (Wiener et al. 2013; Head and Isom 2010; Iaria et al. 2009) and, given the opportunity to choose, they prefer to use the latter (Rodgers et al. 2012).

findings.consequent: Spatial disorientation (early sign), severe navigation deficits (path integration, route learning, cognitive mapping)
findings.quote: Spatial disorientation is one of the earliest signs of AD (Pai and Jacobs 2004), and recent research even suggests that adults at a higher genetic risk of AD show signs of navigation deficits decades before they may develop AD (Kunz et al. 2015; Coughlan et al. 2019).

findings.consequent: More pronounced impairments in hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory tasks than egocentric parietal memory tasks
findings.quote: While AD affects both egocentric and allocentric navigation tasks, these effects seem more pronounced in spatial tasks that require a hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory, such as locating object or landmarks relative to the environment, rather than in tasks which can be solved with egocentric parietal memory in which object locations are remembered relative to the navigator (Kalova et al. 2005; Burgess et al. 2006).
In environmental psychology, navigability is related to good design for navigation, a key aspect of environmental quality (Zimring 1982, 1990).

findings.antecedent: Certain environmental features (large buildings, complex layouts, too many route options/choice points/corners, limited visual access, uniformity)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding difficulties, waste of time/money, increased cognitive/physical effort, impatience/hostility
findings.quote: Certain environmental features can generate wayfinding difficulties, particularly in large buildings or environments, that cause a waste of time and money (Zimring 1990), add to users' cognitive and physical effort (Carlson et al. 2010), and make users impatient with, or even hostile towards public buildings that are difficult to navigate (Berkeley 1973; Dixon 1968; McKean 1972).

findings.antecedent: Varying sizes, shapes, architectural styles, colours within a building (visual differentiation); low levels of spatial differentiation (repetition of similar elements, symmetrical structures)
findings.consequent: Positive effects on navigability (visual differentiation); problems with orientation (spatial uniformity)
findings.quote: Varying sizes, shapes, architectural styles and colours within a building can have positive effects on its navigability (Gärling et al. 1986).

findings.antecedent: Small-scale units with good visual access
findings.consequent: Reduced spatial disorientation, makes spatial memory/recall and wayfinding decisions redundant
findings.quote: The most effective layouts for care homes are small-scale units where everything a resident needs is always in view (visual access) from wherever they are within the facility (Caspi 2014).

findings.antecedent: Places (bedrooms, communal spaces) that are easily recognisable and meaningful (e.g., portraits, name signs, memory boxes, different furniture/color schemes/wallpaper, functional names)
findings.consequent: Improved recognition, easier navigation/orientation, support for decision points
findings.quote: The efficiency of their spatial navigation depends on people's ability to immediately recognise the place they are in or navigating to.

findings.antecedent: Corridors with clearly different design features (themes, colours, frames, entrances), visible from decision points
findings.consequent: Reduced disorientation, aid simple landmark-based navigation, compensate for impaired path integration
findings.quote: In large built environments, corridors often look very similar, and this is the most frequently mentioned factor causing disorientation in people with memory problems or dementia.

findings.antecedent: Brightly coloured, high-contrast objects used as landmarks
findings.consequent: Easier to remember and recognise for older adults/dementia patients, aid navigation
findings.quote: Objects that serve as landmarks need to be remembered and recognised. Older adults and people with dementia remember and recognise brightly coloured, high-contrast objects more easily than less-striking objects in pastel shades (Cernin et al. 2003).

findings.consequent: Support verbal encoding of landmarks, counter word-finding problems in dementia
findings.quote: To counter the increasing word-finding problems associated with dementia (Rohrer et al. 2008) and to support the verbal encoding of landmarks, it is crucial to choose landmarks or cues that are concrete, rather than abstract (such as an abstract painting), and therefore easy to name.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks unique in both visual appearance and verbal encoding
findings.consequent: Unambiguous identification of places, reduced confusion/disorientation
findings.quote: As discussed above, landmarks need to be unique in order to identify a place unambiguously (Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a). Since they can be encoded both visually and verbally, it is important to ensure that they are distinguishable in both domains.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks located at decision points (junctions, open areas) or visible from them (beacons)
findings.consequent: Better remembered, aid navigation (associative cues, beacons), less memory demanding (beacons)
findings.quote: Generally, people navigating along a route remember landmarks that are located at decision points better than those located elsewhere along the route (Aginsky et al. 1997).

findings.consequent: Overcome orientation/navigation problems, externalise spatial knowledge, compensate for declining cognitive abilities
findings.quote: Signage and maps can be used to overcome many orientation and navigation problems. Signage and maps essentially externalise spatial knowledge, decision-making and spatial planning, and can therefore compensate for declining cognitive abilities (Passini et al. 2000).

findings.antecedent: Signage with both icons and text, familiar icons, simple/uncluttered, clear contrast, placed at eye level or lower
findings.consequent: Improved recognition/understanding, aid navigation, reduced falls risk
findings.quote: Signage should therefore not rely on textual information alone, but also contain pictures or icons.

findings.antecedent: More personal environmental cues/features (pictures, memorable spaces) vs. institutional signage/YAH maps
findings.consequent: Preferred by care home residents (homely feel), but challenge to integrate effective signage without detracting from homely feel
findings.quote: most of the care home residents interviewed in a recent study said they preferred more personal environmental cues or features, such as relevant pictures and memorable spaces, over signage or maps (O'Malley et al. 2017).

findings.antecedent: You-are-here (YAH) maps oriented so 'up' on map aligns with straight ahead in real environment
findings.consequent: Minimised cognitive effort, reduced need for mental rotation
findings.quote: It is important for YAH maps to be oriented so that 'up' on the map is aligned with straight ahead in the real environment (McKenzie and Klippel 2016).

findings.consequent: Little use as navigation aids for people with dementia (often discarded, prefer landmarks)
findings.quote: There is currently only a handful of neuropsychological studies on map usage by older adults and people with dementia, but the available evidence suggests that maps in general, and even YAH maps, are of little use to them.

findings.consequent: Affects ability to discriminate between colours (blue/green range), less sensitive to contrast (needs stronger contrast)
findings.quote: It should be noted at this point that AD affects people's ability to discriminate between colours, particularly in the blue and green range, and less so in the red and yellow range (Wijk and Sivik 1995).

Colour naming and being able to make correct choices about colour becomes particularly problematic in patients with semantic dementia, which appears to be caused by the breakdown of conceptual knowledge (Rogers et al. 2007).

findings.antecedent: Brightness or darkness of a colour (lighter-coloured walls, less-contrasting furnishings)
findings.consequent: Affects space perception (sense of spaciousness or confinement)
findings.quote: Space perception (i.e. a sense of spaciousness or confinement) is affected by the brightness or darkness of a colour, rather than by a specific colour or shade. A sense of spaciousness can be enhanced by lighter-coloured walls and less-contrasting furnishings (Tofle et al. 2004).

findings.antecedent: Sufficient light levels and suitable colours (extra light, bright strong colours)
findings.consequent: Important for creating supportive environments, help residents find their way, improve object recall
findings.quote: The use of extra light and contrasting colours can help care home residents find their way more easily (Noell-Waggoner 2002; Netten 1989).

findings.antecedent: Personalising bedroom colours (given stable colour preferences in AD)
findings.consequent: Effective way to help care home residents recognise their own room
findings.quote: The fact that colour preferences seem to remain stable in people with AD (Wijk and Sivik 1995) suggests that personalising bedroom colours could be an effective way to help care home residents recognise their own room.

Task engagement on a first performance task may affect performance on a subsequent task, potentially confounding order effects.

stimuli.description: Two distinct light settings: 'warm, dim lighting' (CCT 2708 K, 97 lux on eye) and 'cool, bright lighting' (CCT 5854 K, 1021 lux on eye). These were used to create four experimental conditions: Warm Dim (no transition), Warm Dim to Cool Bright, Cool Bright (no transition), Cool Bright to Warm Dim.

tables.description: Participant descriptors including Body Mass Index, Midsleep (MSFsc), PSQI score, General Health (SF-36), Light Sensitivity (Eye Problems, Headache, Sunglasses), and Thermal Sensitivity.
a-opic irradiances of the warm, dim and cool, bright light settings for S-cone-opic, M-cone-opic, L-cone-opic, Rhodopic, and Melanopic.
Test statistics (Δ, T ratio, P value) of the main effect of light transition (WD to CB vs. Constant WD, and CB to WD vs. Constant CB) on various dependent variables.

limitations: CCT and illuminance were manipulated simultaneously, preventing attribution of effects to either alone.
Time of day effects on individual responsiveness to light could not be tested due to group sizes.
Abrupt transitions were used; results might differ with more gradual transitions.
Laboratory study (90 min duration); results need validation in longer field experiments and field settings.
Need for replication with participants from different cultural backgrounds.

stimuli.description: personal lighting system consisted of two Hue Aurelle Rectangular Lights (Signify) that measure 120 by 30 cm, of which one was mounted on the ceiling, and another was placed on the desk. The participants faced the desk light and used a laptop screen to mimic office activities. The illuminance of the laptop screen was fixed at a low level. When participants had personal control over CCT, they controlled the ceiling and the desk light simultaneously. CCT range between 2700 K and 5700 K in 20 perceptually equal steps. Illuminance was fixed at 498.9 ± 5.2 lux at the eye, air temperature at 17.2 °C±0.3 °C, the mean radiant temperature at 17.2 °C±0.2 °C, the relative humidity at 40-48%, and the air speed at 0.15-0.26 m/s.
stimuli.source: Fig. S1 and 2.2.2 Personal lighting system

tables.description: Parameter estimates for the effect of having and exercising control as well as the effect of actual CCT on all outcome measures.

limitations: The current study investigated only the causal route from visual comfort (induced by self-selected light condition) to thermal comfort. Similarly, one could in future work study the opposite direction.

The reference conditions in this study were not rated with a low visual comfort. In real-life situations where visual comfort is considerably compromised by CCT, the benefits of personal control of CCT may be more pronounced.
Participants were only allowed to control the CCT at the beginning of Period 2, potentially underestimating the positive effects of personal control of CCT.
The study was not able to distinguish the effects of merely perceiving control from the effects of personalization (i.e., exercising control) based on the regression models.

The test duration in this study was 70 min. The beneficial effects of personal control may accrue over a time span of days. Therefore, it is recommended to investigate the effects of personal control over CCT in the long term.
The sample size was too small to detect the effects.

limitations: Cannot exclude the possibility that hue-heat effects might exist in some populations or contexts, because null effects of CCT on thermal sensation might be caused by weak color-temperature associations among some participants.
Future studies are needed to investigate the color-temperature association in various populations and contexts, in terms of its magnitude, direction and variability.
Color-temperature association may be dynamic, therefore, an intervention itself using a specific pair of light color and temperature may change the strength of color-temperature association.
Only tested CCT in mildly cold conditions; non-visual effects of CCT on thermal perceptions in warm conditions are assumed to be different.
Cannot unequivocally recommend how to tune CCT to improve thermal comfort in practice.
Did not manipulate light level and hence cannot test interactions between CCT and illuminance.
The absence of CCT effects on visual comfort may be caused by large individual differences.

extraction_result.title: Adaptive and Sustainability for Visual and Perceptive Comfort: Neuroscience and Architecture
Lighting of space habitats: Influence of color temperature on a crew's physical and mental health

findings.quote: This demonstrates that health, well-being, and alertness are all influenced by light.

findings.consequent: People's health, biological processes, psychological processes
findings.quote: Inadequate artificial lighting directly affects people's health and alters biological and psychological processes.

findings.consequent: Circadian rhythms, physical and psychological disorders, health
findings.quote: The temperature of the light alters the circadian rhythms, causing physical and psychological disorders in the human body that affect health.
We can consider light as being the biggest indicator, powered by daily ocular stimulus, which allows us to reset the circadian rhythm.
Thus we can say that "static" artificial light¹¹ alters both our hormonal and our circadian rhythms.
One the one hand daytime light increases cortisol levels (a sunlight dependent hormone responsible for alertness) and makes us more active.
At night high melatonin levels in the blood help us to sleep.

findings.consequent: Timing of circadian rhythm, nocturnal melatonin production
findings.quote: Melanopsin is most sensitive to short-wavelength (blue portion of the spectrum) visible light (max 480 nm) ¹⁴ and studies on humans have concluded that it has a direct influence on resetting the timing of the circadian rhythm by suppressing nocturnal melatonin production¹⁵.

Light is also used effectively as a cure¹⁸ for people suffering from seasonal affective disorder¹⁹ (SAD), shift-work or jet-lag, caused by a lack of light during the winter or the desynchronicity of the light-dark cycle.
Furthermore, light has a strong influence on people's moods²⁰.
When performing a particular activity, such as reading, a non-appropriate light makes us feel uncomfortable.

findings.antecedent: Lighting systems not mimicking sunlight / stable prolonged artificial lighting
findings.quote: The implementation²¹ of lighting systems that do not mimic sunlight, as well as the use of stable prolonged artificial lighting that does not follow natural light patterns promotes feelings of sadness or irritability, feelings related to a biological and physiological human response to artificial lighting²².

findings.antecedent: Isolation and close relationships (in space habitats)
findings.quote: In these habitats, isolation and such close relationships with other human beings can create stress and interpersonal problems²⁴
and it is known that the interior design of space habitats improve the well-being of the crew.
“The warm white light (3,000 K) facilitates relaxation and improves wellbeing, while day-light (5,600 K) stimulates and activates the human body.”²⁷
“The warm white light (3,000 K) facilitates relaxation and improves wellbeing, while day-light (5,600 K) stimulates and activates the human body.”²⁷
A long-duration short-wavelength light exposure is a potentially effective countermeasure for fatigue and low performance³¹, particularly during biological night.

findings.antecedent: Dynamic lighting (reproducing chromatic diversity and intensity of natural light)
findings.consequent: Circadian system, pleasant atmosphere, crew alertness, performance
findings.quote: This type of lighting would reproduce chromatic diversity and the intensity of natural light. Being able to vary the intensity at a given time, depending on the activity to be performed and the time slot would help to prolong alertness and therefore performance.
It has been proven³⁹ that dynamic light benefits concentration and therefore work performance.

findings.antecedent: Crew control over their own space (according to needs, moods, activities)

extraction_result.title: The perception of cast shadows

findings.quote: Among all these roles, we found that cast shadows were perceptually most relevant for the recovery of spatial arrangement, especially when the shadow is in motion.

findings.consequent: Recovery of surface shape (casting object or background)
findings.quote: As we will show, the human visual system does not effectively use cast shadows as cues to surface shape, despite the potential reliability of the information they provide.

findings.consequent: Perception of an object moving in depth
findings.quote: Particularly striking is the observation that moving cast shadows can produce a very vivid impression of an object moving in depth.

findings.antecedent: Manipulation of an object's cast shadow motion
findings.quote: Moreover, simply manipulating the motion of an object's cast shadow can dramatically change the perceived trajectory of the object.

findings.antecedent: Cast shadow on a folded card (static image)
findings.quote: Even though the shape of the shadow in Fig. 2 is theoretically sufficient to disambiguate the shape of the card, the shape remains ambiguous perceptually.

findings.antecedent: Static cast shadow detaching from an object (Fig. 3)
findings.consequent: Perception of the object moving in depth
findings.quote: By moving only the cast shadow of a static object in a scene, we were able to induce a strong percept of object motion in depth (despite the fact that the object did not move or change size in the image).

findings.consequent: Perceived depth motion of object (from shadow translation)
findings.quote: The proportion of times the square is perceived moving in depth increases when a penumbra is surrounding the shadow boundary...

findings.antecedent: Shadow displacement consistent with light above scene
findings.consequent: Perceived depth motion of object (from shadow translation)
findings.quote: ...when the shadow displacement is consistent with a light located above the scene...

findings.consequent: Perceived depth motion of object (from shadow translation)
findings.quote: ...and when the shadow is dark rather than light.

findings.antecedent: Changing contrast, opacity, or shape of cast shadow (in ball-in-box animation)
findings.consequent: Perceived trajectory of the ball in space
findings.quote: Interestingly, the perceived trajectory of the ball in space was not affected by changing the contrast, the opacity or even the shape of the shadow.

findings.antecedent: Image sequence generated by moving the light source (instead of object)
findings.consequent: Perception of object moving in depth
findings.quote: Observers perceived a square moving in depth in Fig. 3 even when the image sequence was obtained by moving the light source rather than the square.

findings.antecedent: Adding more evidence that light was moving (e.g., more objects)
findings.quote: Adding more evidence that the light was actually moving, such as adding more objects in the scene, did not affect the perceived trajectory of the ball.

findings.antecedent: Changing shading to suggest alternative illumination directions
findings.quote: Changing the shading on the ball to suggest illumination from alternative directions only changed the perceived trajectory of the ball slightly – not nearly as much as was predicted by the new light source location.

findings.antecedent: Shadow motion (e.g., square moving in depth)
findings.quote: This ambiguity between observer and object motion was never experienced: none of the observers in our experiments ever reported a perception of self-motion.

findings.antecedent: Cast shadow cue for dynamic spatial layout
findings.consequent: Overriding of generic viewpoint constraint, constant size cue, and rigidity constraint
findings.quote: The fact that the cast shadow cue can override the generic viewpoint constraint, the constant size cue as well as the rigidity constraint is a qualitative index of the strength of the cast shadow cue for dynamic spatial layout perception.

findings.antecedent: Correlated motion between an object and its cast shadow (dynamic scenes)
findings.consequent: Reliable shadow labeling and linking of objects with shadows
findings.quote: In dynamic scenes, a feature appears which can very reliably determine proper shadow labeling: the relative motion of an object and its cast shadow is constrained to follow a line connecting the object to the light source.

findings.consequent: Robustness of phenomenal percept of motion to violations of shadow luminance constraints
findings.quote: In the ball-in-a-box movie, the object itself is moving, hence the object-shadow correlated motion which appears in the animation would be accidental if caused by anything other than an object casting a shadow. It therefore provides a strong cue to shadow labeling, and the phenomenal percept of motion is more robust to violations of shadow luminance constraints.

findings.antecedent: Object-shadow correlated motion (static object, trivial correlation)
findings.consequent: Efficacy of shadow cue when luminance constraints are violated
findings.quote: In this special case, object-shadow correlated motion does not provide a reliable cue to shadow labeling, and violations of shadow luminance constraints (such as making the shadow lighter than the background) do reduce the efficacy of the shadow cue.

findings.consequent: Global rather than local information about spatial layout
findings.quote: Cast shadows are non-commensurate with other depth cues because they provide global rather than local information about spatial layout.

findings.consequent: Interaction with other depth cues (size change, binocular disparity, motion parallax)
findings.quote: Nevertheless, an interaction between cast shadows and other depth cues has been found experimentally, in particular the cues of size change, binocular disparity and motion parallax.

limitations: The study is limited to the Turkish context.

The emergent categories provide an open-ended framework where themes and sub-themes may vary in different cultural and geographical contexts due to changing criteria, such as material intangible properties, cost, market availability, etc.
The restricted number of architects and interior designers with sufficient relevant experience as participants.

Future studies could yield different results by sampling newly graduated designers (who have been exposed to changing pedagogical programs that have introduced sustainability or new materials) across those with extensive experience (where the preference of certain materials based on experience has a major role).

Comparative studies carried out with architects and interior designers, and with professionals in larger firms with different responsibilities and ranging professional expertise (i.e. commercial, residential, or healthcare facility) may yield different results.
This study did not focus on end-user preferences. Participants composed of users investigating their health and well-being affected by material selections are suggested.
The singular space typology where we only cover material preferences and criteria for residential design. Therefore, they need verification for other building types and scales.

stimuli.source: Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 7, Figure 8, Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11, Figure 12, Figure 13

limitations: The influence or bias that an interviewee can have due to explanations provided by the tour guide is to be taken into account.

The predetermined path and sequence of spaces in a guided tour and the possible influence of other people's movements and reactions when visiting the house in groups of six also creates the possibility that an individual's consciousness is shaped by their personal and shared experiences.

The visit duration is of relevance, where the approximately 1-hour visit and the reasonably constant weather conditions make no room for the appreciation of daylight dynamics and the experience of the house for extended periods.

findings.consequent: Immune, cardiovascular, endocrine, sleep, emotional, cognitive responses
findings.mechanism: Noise acts as an environmental stressor disturbing various physiological and cognitive functions.
findings.quote: unwanted noise, at intensity levels below those known to cause noise-induced hearing loss, may disturb immune, cardiovascular, endocrine, sleep, emotional, and cognitive responses [6].

findings.antecedent: Low, unwanted, competing, or disturbing sound levels
findings.mechanism: Competing sounds interfere with cognitive processing and ability to rest.
findings.quote: Even low sound levels, if unwanted, competing or disturbing, may be associated with diminished speech intelligibility, lowered cognition, and lack of rest, along with increased stress responses [7].

findings.antecedent: Low, unwanted, competing, or disturbing sound levels
findings.mechanism: Unwanted sounds contribute to increased physiological and psychological stress.
findings.quote: along with increased stress responses [7].

findings.mechanism: High noise levels act as a chronic stressor, impacting cardiovascular health.
findings.quote: The Environmental Expert Council found a consistent trend toward an increased cardiovascular risk if the daytime noise levels exceed 65 dB(A) [8].

findings.antecedent: Long-term low-frequency traffic noise exposure (avg < 55 dB(A))
findings.mechanism: Chronic noise exposure, even at low levels, can disrupt the endocrine system and lead to stress.
findings.quote: Chronic stress reactions, such as cortisol disturbances, have been observed in children with long-term low-frequency traffic noise exposure averaged at less than 55 dB(A) [9].
Edelstein et al. (2008) logged continuous sound levels in emergency and intensive care units and found average levels ranging from 75 to 85 Leq dB(A)
Averaged sound pressure levels in intensive care units were up to 10 times greater than conversational speech.
healthcare environments have been steadily increasing over the past 50 years, with no single facility operating within the sound levels recommended by the World Health Organization [11].

findings.mechanism: Competing auditory stimuli interfere with the detection and interpretation of target sounds.
findings.quote: ambient noises mask the perception of body sounds [12].

findings.antecedent: Competing sounds or noise (wanted or unwanted)
findings.consequent: Perception and attention to speech and sound signals
findings.mechanism: Distracting auditory stimuli reduce the ability to perceive and attend to relevant speech and sound signals.
findings.quote: competing sounds or noise, wanted or unwanted, mask perception and attention to speech and sound signals [13].

findings.mechanism: Environmental noise interferes with the auditory information required for accurate diagnosis.
findings.quote: diagnostic accuracy by means of stethoscope auscultation is diminished in flight or ambulances [14].

findings.antecedent: Elevated sound levels (competing alarms, equipment, conversations, mechanical systems)

findings.quote: elevated sound levels from competing alarms, equipment, conversations, and mechanical systems may interfere with speech intelligibility

findings.antecedent: Elevated sound levels (competing alarms, equipment, conversations, mechanical systems)
findings.mechanism: Auditory confusion caused by noise contributes to errors in identifying similar-sounding medications.
findings.quote: and be a factor in “look-alike-sound-alike” medication errors [15].

findings.antecedent: Knowing location (vs. being lost) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: The cognitive state of knowing one's location versus being lost is reflected in distinct patterns of brain activity.
findings.quote: reveal differences in brain dynamics when subjects know their location compared with EEG components when they are lost.

findings.antecedent: Spaces rich with visual cues (vs. ambiguous spaces devoid of cues) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: The presence and absence of visual information in an environment differentially activate brain regions involved in spatial processing.
findings.quote: Differences in EEG responses associated with spaces rich with visual cues versus ambiguous spaces devoid of cues were found in parietal and occipitotemporal cortex.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with less visuospatial information (disorientation) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased cognitive load and attentional demands in disorienting environments lead to stronger theta synchronization.
findings.quote: A significantly stronger synchronization in theta waves and stronger desynchronization in the lower alpha band of EEG frequencies was observed.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with less visuospatial information (disorientation) in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased cognitive load and attentional demands in disorienting environments lead to stronger alpha desynchronization.

findings.antecedent: Disorientation in spaces with less visuospatial information in VR environment
findings.mechanism: Increased attentional demands to navigate in ambiguous spaces are reflected in alpha wave desynchronization.

findings.antecedent: Absence of obvious visual cues (in ambiguous VR space)
findings.consequent: Search for distinguishing features (shadows, patterned finishes)

findings.quote: In the case where obvious cue were not presented, subjects looked for any distinguishing features that might indicate location, including shadows around doors, or patterned finishes.

findings.consequent: Staff time spent giving directions to lost patients
findings.mechanism: Poor spatial design leads to increased operational burden and costs.
findings.quote: McCarthy (2004) reported that in one hospital, 4,500 h each year were spent by staff giving directions to lost patients, with an associated cost equivalent of $220,000 per annum [21].

findings.antecedent: Ineffective wayfinding design (compromising clean/contaminated space separation)
findings.consequent: Severe consequences, potentially fatal (during infectious epidemics)

findings.quote: the consequence of ineffective wayfinding design may have more severe consequences, and may even prove fatal during infectious epidemics, should the separation between clean and contaminated spaces be compromised.

SoniCAVEM virtual sound simulation environment merging ultrahigh definition recordings and sound simulations of real environments with visualizations.

limitations: An approach that gives credit to the proportion of space with daylight, rather than crediting adjustable lighting systems that provide for individual needs, is unlikely to address the range of human conditions, and the dynamically changing nature of functions that take place in architectural settings.

limitations: results on emotional response remain fragmented and inconsistent.
PCM cannot sufficiently distinguish between some of the mood/emotional categories.
facial expressions... insufficient at distinguishing emotions beyond the obvious types.
physiological response... hard to correlate these changes to specific emotions.
forcing participants to evaluate sound clips or sound environments through audio replay... ignores peoples' implicit emotional reactions.
behaviour observation method... could introduce the Hawthorne effect.
sampling biases... affect the generalisation of the study results.
POMS was originally developed in a medical context.
absence of an actual performer, leading to a reduction in eventfulness in a laboratory context.
sound clips were designed with a combination of sound types. Therefore, the design limited the investigation of individual sound types.
many different sound sources within each sound type category. This study only recorded a single source for each studied sound type.
sound appropriateness... beyond the scope of this study.
more dimensions in the soundscape study of mood states exists than simply pleasantness and eventfulness.
Whether the conclusions of this research can be extended to other music types will require further study.
The effect of music on listeners both depends on the music type and age difference of the listeners.
assumptions of the influence of differing contexts appears to be false.
Results obtained from laboratory tests may reveal the underlying nature of different types of sound on emotional responses, but should be always tested if applied to any in-situ environments.
validity of implementing the appraisal theory may require further exploration (such as cross examination with standardised soundscape research methods).
more emotional categories and soundscape factors should be examined for a more complete understanding of human-environment relationships.
positive emotions that were absent in this study.
need for new questionnaires suitable to observe the respective emotional changes.
uncertainty when it comes to when cognitive resource are being viewed as a psychophysiological function.
unclear how much this limit differs between individuals, how individual differences influence their cognitive resource repository and whether this repository fluctuates under different situations.
uncertain how much each dimension would dominate the cognitive resource required to appraise an environmental factor.
Can one of the dimensions explain more percentage of the requirement more fully than the other two?
unclear how the distraction effect is going to function under more complex acoustic environments.

extraction_result.title: Speech Privacy in Buildings

findings.antecedent: Average Transmission Loss (TL) rating of isolating wall
findings.consequent: Observed reaction to privacy (Extreme Dissatisfaction to Apparent Satisfaction)
findings.mechanism: The categorization scheme based on average TL is inadequate because other acoustical factors are important for speech privacy.
findings.quote: But it is clear from Fig. 1 that an average transmission loss of 35 db is not the demarcation between satisfaction and dissatisfaction.

findings.mechanism: Speech peaks are submerged by steady background noise (masking effect).
findings.quote: The intelligibility of intruding speech is destroyed when the speech peaks are submerged in steady background noise

findings.mechanism: Reduction of the speech signal relative to noise, similar to increasing background noise.
findings.quote: an increase in the background level has the same effect on intelligibility as an increase in the transmission loss.

findings.consequent: Background noise levels in speech-frequency bands
findings.mechanism: Varying sources of background noise (e.g., traffic, air-conditioning terminal devices).
findings.quote: Figure 2 shows that background levels in the speech-frequency bands vary from building to building by 30 db or more.

findings.antecedent: Published (laboratory) vs. field measurements of Transmission Loss (TL)
findings.mechanism: Incomplete test samples, panel size and boundary damping, special test conditions, and obsolete data in published values.
findings.quote: it is not uncommon to find differences in the order of 10 db or more between the advertised transmission-loss values of a partition, and the data obtained from a valid field measurement

findings.antecedent: Room size (small 6x8 ft office vs. large 40x40 ft classroom)
findings.consequent: Reverberant speech levels (for constant speech power)
findings.mechanism: Sound-absorbing area (Sā) is approximately equal to the floor area, which varies with room size.
findings.quote: Assuming a constant speech power, the corresponding range in reverberant speech levels is 15 db.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of wall area to listener-room floor area (1:2 to 2:1)
findings.mechanism: Geometric factors affecting sound transmission.
findings.quote: Figure 4 shows a range of ratios of wall area to listener-room floor area from 1 to 2; the corresponding variation in transmitted levels is 6 db.

findings.antecedent: Speech effort (conversational vs. raised vs. loud voice)
findings.mechanism: Increased vocal effort directly increases sound power level.
findings.quote: The sound levels for a 'raised voice' are about 6 db higher than those for conversational speech; a 'loud voice' is about 12 db higher.

findings.consequent: Tolerated intelligibility of intruding speech (or required speech signal to background noise ratio)
findings.mechanism: Different cognitive demands and social implications of privacy levels lead to different tolerance thresholds for intelligibility.
findings.quote: Generally, this amounted to a 6-db difference in the ratio of speech signal to background noise.

findings.antecedent: Varying background noise levels (within NC-20 to NC-35 range)
findings.mechanism: Privacy judgment is based on the relative signal-to-noise ratio, not the absolute level of background noise.
findings.quote: The data of Fig. 9 show that on the average our test subjects responded with a constant signal-to-noise ratio as the background levels varied.

findings.mechanism: Subjects generally give consistent responses after a short learning period.
findings.quote: during one day of testing, 13 subjects made 356 judgments of privacy. The rms variation from their average responses was 1.3 db.

findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: When asked to define 'normal' or everyday privacy, the least critical subject allowed 20-db higher speech levels than the most critical.

findings.mechanism: Individual differences in perception and tolerance for intruding speech, even for confidential tasks.
findings.quote: When defining 'confidential' privacy, the maximum variation among subjects was about 10 db.

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (normal vs. confidential) for most critical subjects
findings.mechanism: The perceived importance of privacy for confidential tasks leads to a lower tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: There was a shift of about 6 db between the definitions of 'normal' and 'confidential' privacy as given by the most critical subjects.

findings.antecedent: Wall type ('flat' wall with weak low-frequency speech components vs. other walls)
findings.mechanism: The spectral characteristics of the intruding speech (e.g., weak low-frequency components) influence its perceived intelligibility and annoyance, even at a given AI.
findings.quote: It appears that both the most critical 10% of the subjects and the average subject tolerated a higher articulation index for the 'flat' wall

findings.mechanism: Even if speech is unintelligible, its presence, especially in certain frequency bands, can still be perceived as annoying.
findings.quote: Thus, we do find annoyance caused by unintelligible, narrow-band speech, especially at the low frequencies.

findings.antecedent: Bandwidth of intruding speech (1/3-octave 250 cps vs. wider bands)
findings.mechanism: Narrower bands contribute less to overall speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: The AI for the 250 cps, 1/3-octave was only 2% when the subject responded. This compares with 5-10% for the wider bandwidths.

findings.mechanism: The effect of a narrow TL dip is small and accounted for by the articulation-index rating scheme.
findings.quote: As may be seen, a 10-db dip only one-third octave wide was judged to be relatively unimportant.

findings.antecedent: 15-dB dip in TL at lower frequencies
findings.mechanism: Low-frequency narrow bands of speech have a larger function relating annoyance to signal-to-noise ratio than to intelligibility.
findings.quote: As may be seen, there is a response which at the lower frequencies is not predicted by the change in the articulation index caused by the dip.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of intruding speech to ambient noise vs. level of speech itself
findings.mechanism: Privacy perception is driven by the masking effect of background noise on intruding speech, not the absolute loudness of the speech.
findings.quote: The typical test subject's feeling of privacy appears to be related to the ratio of the intruding speech to the ambient or background noise rather than to the level of the speech itself.

findings.mechanism: AI quantifies speech intelligibility, which is a primary determinant of perceived speech privacy.
findings.quote: More particularly, the subject reaction seems to be correlated with the articulation index which is a 'weighted' signal-to-noise ratio.

findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 represents a threshold of intelligibility beyond which privacy is compromised for critical subjects.
findings.quote: the most critical 10% of the subjects began to feel a lack of privacy when the articulation index reached 0.05.

findings.antecedent: Total rating computed from proposed scheme (integrating source room size, speech use, background noise, noise reduction, privacy requirement)
findings.mechanism: The scheme integrates multiple acoustical and social factors that collectively determine speech intelligibility and privacy perception in real-world settings.
findings.quote: The most significant fact about Fig. 20 is the fairly tight grouping of the data.

findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 represents a critical threshold for perceived privacy, marking the transition from satisfaction to dissatisfaction.
findings.quote: situations with an articulation index of 0.05 are more or less on the borderline between apparent satisfaction and some degree of dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Small change in noise reduction or background noise
findings.consequent: Significant variation in occupant's reaction to privacy
findings.mechanism: The relationship between physical acoustic parameters and subjective privacy perception is steep near the privacy threshold, indicating high sensitivity to small changes.
findings.quote: the slope of the curve in Fig. 20 is quite steep. This means that a small change in the noise reduction or background noise can make a significant variation in the occupant's reaction.

findings.antecedent: Increase in signal-to-noise ratio by 10 dB
findings.mechanism: A direct relationship exists between the signal-to-noise ratio and the ability to understand speech.
findings.quote: on the average, an increase in the signal-to-noise ratio of only 10 or so db would be expected to result in fairly complete sentence intelligibility.

findings.antecedent: Occasional loud talker / self talking loudly
findings.mechanism: Social norms and personal control over sound production influence privacy expectations and allowances.
findings.quote: most occupants desire privacy on the average but may be willing to make allowances for the occasional loud talker and do not expect privacy when they themselves talk loudly.

limitations: Studies were strictly limited to speech as the intruding signal.
Laboratory studies were performed in the context of a typical office situation.
Field study and case histories were mostly office situations, with limited data from hospitals, dormitories, and motels.
Applicability to other kinds of spaces (e.g., apartments) needs further verification.
Studies were restricted to buildings in the United States, and the average response curve may shift laterally in other countries.
The probable total uncertainty in estimating the five items of the proposed rating scheme is ±4 or 5 dB, requiring an accuracy of ±2 dB for each component for overall accuracy.

extraction_result.title: The Benefits of Daylight through Windows

findings.quote: Physically, daylight is just another source of electromagnetic radiation in the visible range. Electric light sources can be constructed to closely match a spectrum of daylight, but none have been made that mimic the variation in light spectrum that occurs with daylight at different times, in different seasons, and under different weather conditions.

findings.consequent: Human visual system and circadian system stimulation
findings.quote: Physiologically, daylight is an effective stimulant to the human visual system and the human circadian system.
Psychologically, daylight and a view are much desired.

findings.antecedent: Daylight (delivered in large amounts with good spectrum)
findings.quote: Daylight does have a greater probability of maximizing visual performance than most forms of electric lighting because it tends to be delivered in large amounts with a spectrum that ensures excellent color rendering.

findings.antecedent: Daylight (poorly delivered, causing glare, distraction, veiling reflections, shadows)
findings.consequent: Visual discomfort, task difficulty, visual performance
findings.quote: Daylight can cause visual discomfort through glare and distraction, and it can diminish the stimuli the task presents to the visual system by producing veiling reflections or by shadows. The effectiveness of daylight for visual performance will depend on how it is delivered. The same conclusion applies to electric lighting. People will take action to reduce or eliminate daylight if it causes discomfort or increases task difficulty.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light during the day and little or no light at night (daylighting)
findings.consequent: Entrainment of circadian system, performance of visual/non-visual tasks, long-term health problems
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light during the day and little or no light at night will accurately entrain the circadian system. Daylighting is an attractive way to deliver bright light during the day.

Windows are strongly favored in work places for the daylight they deliver and the view out they provide, as long as they do not cause visual or thermal discomfort or a loss of privacy. Whether windows will produce an improvement in mood seems to depend on what the individual's preferences and expectations are.

The understanding of how mood influences productivity is weak. Different studies have emphasized worker happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction as predictors of productivity while others have suggested that productivity is itself a generator of feelings of happiness, well-being, and job satisfaction.
Exposure to daylight can have both positive and negative effects on health.
The strongest effects occur outdoors. Exposure to daylight outdoors can cause tissue damage, which is bad, and generate vitamin D, which is good.

findings.antecedent: Daylight and sunlight delivered through glass (reduced UV-B, view out)
findings.consequent: UV-B radiation, stress, incidence of health problems (from electric lighting fluctuations)
findings.quote: Daylight and sunlight delivered through glass will have much less short wavelength ultra-violet (UV-B) radiation than the same radiation outdoors, but can still have adverse effects on people who are sensitive to ultra-violet radiation. ... Windows that provide a view out as well as daylight, can reduce stress and hence reduce the demand for health services. Daylight reduces the incidence of health problems caused by the rapid fluctuations in light output typical of electric lighting.

findings.consequent: Construction/maintenance costs, building operating costs, rental value
findings.quote: A wall containing windows costs more to construct and maintain than one without. These costs may be offset by reductions in building operating costs. However, the presence of windows is believed to have a positive effect on the rental value of a space.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting of a conventionally windowless retail space
findings.quote: Daylighting of a conventionally windowless retail space can have a positive effect on sales.

findings.antecedent: Windows with view of natural landscape (for prisoners/patients)
findings.consequent: Sick calls, hospital stay duration, negative comments from nurses
findings.quote: Moore (1981) studied the healthcare demands of prisoners, and found that those whose windows looked out over hills and farmland made significantly fewer sick calls to the prison infirmary than those whose windows overlooked the prison yard. View through a window has also been found to influence recovery from surgery. Ulrich (1984) found that patients whose rooms afforded a view of the natural landscape rather than of other buildings spent fewer days in hospital (7.96 compared with 8.70), and that nurses recorded fewer negative comments regarding their progress.
Similarly, Keep and Inman (1980) found that patients in a windowless intensive care units showed more confusion.

findings.antecedent: Daylight vs. electric lighting as primary source
findings.quote: There is no doubt that people prefer daylight over electric lighting as their primary source of illumination.

findings.antecedent: Windows (view out vs. admission of daylight)
findings.quote: The results of surveys of office workers suggest that of this list, the two most important attributes of windows are the view out and the admission of daylight (Collins, 1975; Brill, 1985). The importance of a view out is demonstrated by the work of Young and Berry (1979). They examined people's preference for an office with either a real window, providing both a view out and daylight in the office, or an artificial window showing a dynamic view of nature but providing very little light into the office. There was very little difference in the preferences for the two window types, implying that it is the view that is dominating the preference.

findings.antecedent: Small windowless offices (little opportunity to leave, lack of stimulation)
findings.consequent: Job satisfaction, satisfaction with physical environment, use of visual decor
findings.quote: Surveys of the occupants of windowless offices have shown that when the space is small and the occupant has little opportunity to leave the space, the occupants are less satisfied with their jobs and with the physical environment (Finnegan and Solomon (1981); and the lack of variety is noticeable and the lack of windows is disliked (Ruys, 1970). ... Some support for this view comes from the work of Heerwagen and Orians (1986). They observed that people occupying small private offices without windows used twice the number of visual materials to decorate their offices as did people whose offices had windows.

findings.antecedent: Direct sunlight, solar glare, radiant heating, passers-by (ground floors)
findings.quote: Measurements of the use of window blinds in multi-story office buildings have shown two trends. The first is that window blinds are most likely to be closed on ground floors where there are many passers-by, and, on all floors, as the sun begins to shine on the window and so cause solar glare and radiant heating (Maniccia et al., 1999). This might be expected. Less expected is the second trend, that many of these blinds are kept closed even after the sun has ceased to shine directly on the window; and that, in some cases, the blinds are left closed for days, months, or years (Rea, 1984).

prolonged measurements in a set of deep, private offices with large windows have shown that, given the opportunity, people tend to increase the amount of electric light as the amount of daylight in the office increases (Begemann et al., 1994, 1995).

findings.antecedent: Carefully designed daylight delivered through windows
findings.consequent: Good lighting, environmental stimulation (variation, view out)
findings.quote: one reason why daylight is so popular as a means of lighting is that, if carefully designed, daylight delivered through windows provides a comprehensive package which can meet the requirements of good lighting by revealing both the task and the space clearly and the requirement of environmental stimulation by variation of lighting conditions in the space and a view out through the window.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to daylight (high illuminance at eye, matched spectrum)
findings.quote: exposure to daylight is a very potent means of providing enough light to entrain the circadian system. This is evident in a study by Eastman et al. (1994)... Further, the spectrum of daylight is better matched to the spectral sensitivity of the human circadian system, which shows a peak sensitivity at about 465 nm (Brainard et al., 2001; Thapan et al., 2001), than commonly used electric light sources...

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (daylight) at appropriate times
findings.consequent: Advanced/delayed sleep phase disorder, sleep onset/maintenance insomnia
findings.quote: Exposure to light has been shown to be an effective treatment for these sleep disorders... What is clear is that daylight, assuming it is available at the required time, is a convenient means to provide the high light levels apparently required to sustain the operation of the circadian system.

What is clear is that exposure to bright light is often an effective treatment (Rosenthal et al., 1985; Terman et al., 1989; Tam et al., 1995)... there is no doubt that daylight could also be used as a source of 'bright light.'

findings.antecedent: Daylighting provided without glare (high light levels, good color rendering)
findings.consequent: Vision of Alzheimer's patients (reduced contrast sensitivity)
findings.quote: This finding, suggesting as it does that Alzheimer's patients are struggling to make sense of the world with diminished visual and cognitive capabilities, raises the intriguing possibility that daylighting, with its high light levels and good color rendering properties, would be of advantage for the visual capabilities of Alzheimer's patients, provided it is delivered without glare.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to bright light (daylight) during the day and little light at night
findings.consequent: Regularity of circadian rhythm, nighttime wandering, agitation in Alzheimer's patients
findings.quote: Exposure to bright light during the day has been shown to improve the regularity of their circadian rhythm, which will reduce the prevalence of such undesirable behavior as nighttime wandering... The result was reduced agitation and wandering at night and more stable rest / activity rhythms... Further, it may be that daylighting is the most convenient means of providing high light levels for people with Alzheimer's disease.

findings.antecedent: View of a natural scene through a window (real or simulated)
findings.quote: a view of a natural scene through a window (real or simulated) has been suggested as a means of relieving stress (Clearwater and Coss, 1991; Kaplan, 1992; Ulrich, 1993).
What is proven is that prolonged exposure to the sun results in skin aging.

findings.antecedent: Poor lighting (inadequate illuminance, excessive luminance ratios, lamp flicker) or poorly delivered daylight (excessive luminance ratios)
findings.quote: The symptoms of eyestrain, such as sore eyes, blurred vision, and headaches, can be produced by both electric lighting and daylighting.

findings.antecedent: High illuminances from daylighting, large-area/repetitive/high-contrast patterns
findings.consequent: Migraine attacks, visual discomfort in migraineurs
findings.quote: However, high illuminances such as are produced by daylighting will also tend to exacerbate the disturbing effects of any large-area, repetitive, high-contrast patterns.

findings.antecedent: High light levels and variation from daylighting (environmental stimulation)
findings.consequent: Arousal level, repetitive behavior in autistic children
findings.quote: The high light levels often provided by daylight are inherently arousing. Further, the variation in lighting of an interior that is associated with daylighting, especially when there are scattered clouds in the sky, can be regarded as a form of environmental stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Level of individual control of environment (lighting, heating, cooling, ventilation, noise)
findings.quote: For personal control, Leaman and Bordass (2000) report that there was a small but statistically significant correlation (r = 0.16 to 0.49) between level of individual control of the environment and self-reported productivity in seven of eleven office buildings evaluated in 1996-97. However, they also make the point that of the five different aspects of the physical environment examined; heating, cooling, lighting, ventilation, and noise, lighting control is the only one that is not statistically significantly linked to self-rated productivity.

As for building depth, Leaman and Bordass (2000) report that as buildings get deeper, the levels of satisfaction with the building and self-reported productivity decrease. The critical threshold depth appears to be about 15 m, from wall to wall.

findings.consequent: Improvement in standardized test scores (reading, mathematics)
findings.quote: children in the classrooms with the best daylighting achieved a 20 to 26 percent greater improvement over the year than average.

findings.antecedent: Skylight design allowing patches of sunlight (visual/thermal discomfort)
findings.quote: Although most of their analyses show an improvement in test scores with more daylight, there is one analysis for skylights that shows a reduced improvement in test scores with greater daylight. This deterioration is explained by saying that the skylight design allowed patches of sunlight to strike the walls and students desks, with consequent potential for visual and thermal discomfort.

findings.antecedent: Daylight provided through windows or skylight (higher illuminance, matched spectrum)
findings.consequent: Production and timing of hormones (cortisol), ability to concentrate, sociability in children
findings.quote: What was found was a statistically significant interaction between the concentration of cortisol and classrooms... Further, the cortisol concentration was related to observations of the children's ability to concentrate and sociability, ability to concentrate being greater at low cortisol concentrations and sociability being greater under higher cortisol concentrations.

findings.antecedent: Animal spatial circumstances (disrupting personal/social spatial domains)
findings.quote: The experiments influenced by these ideas sought evidence of psychological stress or aggression as automatic responses to very close individual distances, territorial invasions, or overcrowded conditions.

findings.antecedent: Unusual spatial circumstances (humans, e.g., close individual distances, territorial invasions, overcrowded conditions)

extraction_result.title: Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.antecedent: Affective bond with places (home, neighborhood, city, country, continent)
findings.consequent: Positive effect on identity, meaning, values, goals, and significance
findings.quote: The feeling we experience towards certain places and to the communities that the places help to define and that are themselves defined by the places – home (family, relations, friends), workplace (colleagues), neighbourhood (neighbours), city, country, continent - certainly has a strong positive effect in defining our identity, in filling our life with meaning, in enriching it with values, goals and significance.

findings.antecedent: Equal attachment to the same place (by different groups)
findings.quote: These conflicts stem from an equal attachment to the same place, which puts them in competition.

findings.consequent: Spiritual unity for a scattered people
findings.quote: the importance in Jewish culture of the idea, or rather the feeling, of a 'Promised Land', of the greeting 'next year in Jerusalem' that kept a people, physically scattered to the four corners of the Earth, spiritually united for centuries.
it is perceived as one of those important factors that sometimes help and sometimes hinder our equilibrium, our material and spiritual well-being.

findings.antecedent: Early onset and stability of attachment cognitive structures
findings.consequent: Prototype of relational behavior, organizing principle of affective personality
findings.quote: the relationship of attachment thus comes to represent a prototype of relational behaviour, an organising principle (Stroufe and Waters, 1977) of the affective personality.

findings.antecedent: Richness of social interaction (intensity and quality)
findings.quote: The formation of an affective bond seems mainly to be a function of the richness of the social interaction (intensity and quality of the interaction) with the person(s) towards whom the attachment behaviour is directed

findings.antecedent: Stronger and healthier attachment to main figure
findings.quote: It seems even that the stronger and healthier the attachment to the main figure, the more likely there are to be secondary attachments (Bowlby, 1969, p. 308).

findings.consequent: Capacity to adapt internal working models to environment
findings.quote: The capacity to adapt the models to fit the environmental situation is greater in the case of healthy development, that is of secure attachment, whereas adaptation becomes more difficult in the case of insecure attachments, as defence mechanisms come into play (Bowlby, 1980).

findings.antecedent: Forced transfer from place of residence
findings.consequent: Sorrow, interruption of sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial identity and group identity
findings.quote: the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: Feeling of belongingness, sorrow at moving out (age-linked)
findings.quote: length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked
interest in what goes on in the community decreases with age
Attachment to place is considered a fundamental human need (Relph, 1976)

findings.antecedent: Spatial uniformity, increased mobility, functionalistic relationship with places (contemporary society)
findings.consequent: Ability to satisfy attachment to place
findings.quote: contemporary society is increasingly unable to satisfy owing to its tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility and hence a purely functionalistic relationship with places.

findings.consequent: Universal and necessary for authentic relationship with environment
findings.quote: the geographers advance the hypothesis that the affective bonds in question are universal and necessary for an 'authentic' relationship with the environment.

findings.antecedent: Strong affective ties with place (for particular groups)
findings.quote: strong affective ties with the place of residence may be characteristic of particular groups of population under certain circumstances. Among other things, his work shows how such ties may to some extent prove dysfunctional, precluding adaptation to new opportunities (Fried 2000).

findings.antecedent: Congruity between needs and physical/social environmental resources
findings.quote: in positive cases attachment is developed, whereas in the case of incongruity, the individuals will either not form attachments or be repulsed.

findings.consequent: Individual hardship, conformist attitudes, social refutation
findings.quote: attachment does not necessarily have a positive outcome, but may represent a source of individual hardship, conformist attitudes or social refutation.

findings.antecedent: Positively-valenced knowledge of environment largely exceeds negatively-valenced knowledge
findings.consequent: Feeling of affection for a place
findings.quote: The feeling of affection for a place would develop in individuals whose positively-valenced knowledge of the environment in question largely exceeds the negatively-valenced knowledge.

findings.consequent: Feelings of affection or aversion for the place
findings.quote: places normally associated with a positive affect can also preclude the emergence of any feelings of affection or even cause aversion when they threaten the individual's identity.
a positive correlation between length of residence and the intensity of attachment to the place of residence is a widely reported finding

findings.consequent: Lack of affective bonds with places
findings.quote: the causal relationship postulated between high residential mobility and lack of affective bonds with places is far from having been proved.
attachment, that is the affective investment made in the neighbourhood of residence, is comparatively unaffected by the length of residence.

findings.antecedent: Modality of arrival in neighborhood (free vs. compulsory choice)
findings.quote: the modality of arrival in the neighbourhood, or the perception of whether it was a free or a compulsory choice, carries greater weight.

findings.antecedent: High degree of mobility during childhood
findings.quote: a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood

findings.antecedent: Neighborhood quality, previous experiences, compatibility with residential identity
findings.quote: Affective investment seems to be closely linked to neighbourhood quality, but also to previous experiences and compatibility with residential identity.

findings.antecedent: Environments experienced in childhood or adolescence
findings.quote: Strong positive affective bonds seem to develop towards the environments experienced in childhood or adolescence, and more occasionally towards environments experienced only in adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Unsatisfactory residential experiences during infancy and adolescence
findings.consequent: Capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood, even towards the more satisfactory environments.

findings.consequent: Expression of individual/social identity, strength of attachment
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment, while secondary territories tend to express a social or group identity.
the street layout can facilitate attachment to the neighbourhood and thus the development of a secondary territoriality.
the 'tendency to equate attachment with more permanent residences may have more to do with our cultural bias toward home ownership than with reality' (p. 297).

findings.antecedent: Prolonged association between individual and place
findings.quote: prolonged association between an individual and a place is widely recognised as one of the distinctive features of attachment to place.
individuals may not be conscious of their attachment to a place... and only become aware of it under particular circumstances, such as when the bond is threatened.

findings.consequent: Place of greatest affection for majority (but few want to return)
findings.quote: for the vast majority the place of greatest affection is one's birthplace, but there is also a great variability related to mobility experiences and life stages.

findings.antecedent: Age of moving away from birthplace (after 12 vs. earlier)
findings.consequent: Strength and nature of birthplace bond (strong nostalgic bond for later movers vs. only warm memories for earlier movers)
findings.quote: among people who had moved away after the age of 12, there were strong bonds to the birthplace in a 'nostalgic' sense, as there was no intention to move back. Among those who had moved away at an earlier age, 'only some warm memories for the former place remained'.
bonds with sacred places discussed by Mazumdar and Mazumdar (1993) are very intense.

findings.antecedent: Involuntary separation from place or loss of place
findings.consequent: Distress, grief (similar to loss of loved one)
findings.quote: The fact that reactions similar to those for the loss of a loved one can be felt in relation to places was the starting point for the considerations on attachment to places

findings.consequent: Symptoms of malaise (mixed relationship with health)
findings.quote: a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise, but also that the relationship between mobility and health is not always negative.

findings.antecedent: Less opportunity for choice (obliged to live in unsatisfactory environment)
findings.quote: Persons with less opportunity for choice who are obliged to live in an environment that does not come up to their expectations are more likely to have health problems than those with a high residential mobility.

findings.consequent: Future mobility (as a strategy to correct undesirable aspects)
findings.quote: mobility may be a strategy to correct undesirable aspects of one's life and one such undesirable aspect could be lack of attachment, since such a lack is a significant indicator of future mobility.

findings.consequent: Feeling of security for young children (not physical protection)
findings.quote: the feeling of security is perceived as particularly important by the younger children (less than 13 years old) and is not a function of the physical protection offered by the home but of permanence (in Bowlbian terms we could say of accessibility).
the feeling of comfort appears more and more frequently in women's description of homes.

findings.antecedent: Life stage (childhood, old age vs. adolescence, adulthood)
findings.quote: the need for security and protection preponderates during certain stages of life (e.g. childhood and old age), while other needs emerge more forcefully in adolescence and at various stages of adult life (e.g. exploration, affiliation, self-expression, etc.).

findings.consequent: Strong attachment to home (interpreted as re-emergence of security/protection need)
findings.quote: The strong attachment the elderly display towards the home might thus be seen as the re-emergence of the dominant need for security and protection.

findings.antecedent: Impaired physical resources, diminished capacity to adapt spatial behavior (elderly)
findings.quote: Impaired physical resources and the diminished capacity to adapt spatial behaviour patterns to changes in the immediate environment contribute to making the elderly retreat from the novel and seek security.

the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources (Fried 2000).

stimuli.description: Two strongly contrasting light settings: Warm, dim light (CCT 2708 K, 97 lux) and Cool, bright light (CCT 5854 K, 1021 lux) in a climate chamber. Four conditions: constant warm dim, constant cool bright, transition warm dim to cool bright, transition cool bright to warm dim.

tables.description: Participant descriptors including Body Mass Index, Midsleep (MSFsc), PSQI score, General Health (SF-36), and Light Sensitivity scores.
a-opic irradiances of the light settings (S-cone-opic, M-cone-opic, L-cone-opic, Rhodopic, Melanopic) for Warm Dim and Cool Bright light.
Test statistics (Δ, T ratio, P value) for the main effect of light transition (WD to CB vs. Constant WD, and CB to WD vs. Constant CB) on various dependent variables.

limitations: CCT and illuminance were manipulated simultaneously, preventing attribution of effects to either illuminance or CCT alone.
Time of day moderation of light effects on dependent variables could not be tested due to group sizes.
Abrupt transitions were used, and it is unknown if gradual transitions would yield similar positive or negative results.
Study was conducted with participants from a single cultural background, limiting generalizability.
Laboratory study lasted only 90 min, requiring validation in longer experiments and field settings.

stimuli.description: Optic flow stimuli simulating linear or curvilinear 2D trajectories over a horizontal ground plane, with or without a single landmark (red dot attached to ground via blue dots). Landmarks could be shifting or fixated. Stimuli were 8s duration, preceded and followed by 2s stationary periods.

tables.description: List of simulated manoeuvre conditions, including trajectory type, observer orientation (yaw), size, and landmark presence/type.
Performance metrics (globally correct, trajectory correct, rotation in place) for each stimulus condition, including landmark types and number of responses.

limitations: The recorded reproductions did not always exactly match verbal descriptions, making it difficult to ascertain if the reproduction reflected actual perception or a categorization/sloppy response.
The good perception of yaw might partly be due to an observational/response strategy, as subjects tended to categorize rotations in steps of 90° or 180°.
The VR head-mounted display (VR4) had cushion distortion in the corners of its view, and the Datavisor LCD had a slightly different type of distortion.
Linear observer speed cannot be determined from optic flow alone without additional scaling information (e.g., knowledge of dot size).
