findings.antecedent: Larger ships, greater mechanization, and reduced manning levels
findings.consequent: Fewer outlets for affiliation, reduced sense of collective identity, individual worth, and support for seafarers
findings.quote: With larger ships, greater mechanization and reduced manning levels, more is required from seafarers and there are fewer outlets for the sort of affiliation that sustains both a sense of collective identity and individual worth and support.

findings.antecedent: Fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment (e.g., 'sweat ships', flag-of-convenience)
findings.consequent: Counterproductive individual psychological interventions, maintenance of unjust workplaces, negative impact on psychological well-being and rights of individuals, negative impact on sense of organizational justice and expectations for decency
findings.quote: So no matter what sort of clever individual psychological interventions maritime psychologists can develop, implementing these in a fundamentally unfair and exploitive working environment can be counterproductive, individualizing a systems problem (McVeigh et al. 2016).

findings.antecedent: Resolutions adopted by the International Labour Conference (94th maritime session, 2006) concerning 'human element' and 'recruitment and retention of seafarers'
findings.consequent: Increased recognition of psychosocial factors and impetus for further development of maritime psychology
findings.quote: Resolutions adopted by the International Labour Conference at its 94th (maritime) Session in 2006 include a “Resolution concerning addressing the human element through international cooperation between United Nations specialised agencies” (p. X).

findings.antecedent: Many psychologists employed in aviation and space sectors
findings.consequent: Few psychologists employed in the maritime sector
findings.quote: Bengt Schager—who describes himself as a “maritime psychologist”—arguing for the role of psychologists in the maritime transport sector, notes that while many psychologists are employed in the aviation and space sectors, few are employed in the maritime sector (www.profilschager.com).

findings.antecedent: Taking thousands of passengers on a cruise for weeks with a much larger crew
findings.consequent: Requires important leadership and participation skills (more than crewing a Boeing 747 for a few hours)
findings.quote: He points out that while crewing a Boeing 747 across the Atlantic requires many important leadership and participation skills for a few hours, taking thousands of passengers on a cruise for weeks, with a much larger crew, undoubtedly requires these and additional skills.

findings.antecedent: Alert! series ('The International Maritime Human Element Bulletin')
findings.consequent: Helped bring psychological thinking to a wider audience of seafarers
findings.quote: The very useful and accessible Alert! series, subtitled “The International Maritime Human Element Bulletin”, and published by the Nautical Institute, has certainly helped to bring psychological thinking to a wider audience of seafarers.

findings.consequent: Clear importance in a range of issues covered by 'Textbook of Maritime Medicine' (e.g., work roles, manning, piracy, crisis interventions, environmental health, motion sickness, shipwreck, fatigue)
findings.quote: The scope of maritime psychology also overlaps with some complementary fields, so for instance, the “Textbook of Maritime Medicine”, now in its second edition (Carter and Schreiner 2013), is freely available to download. It covers a range of issues where psychological factors are of clear importance.

findings.antecedent: Unfair working conditions (e.g., long hours, lack of leisure/privacy, low-income crew)
findings.quote: However, maritime psychology should also be about setting fair working conditions that recognize the needs of seafarers to have leisure time, privacy, opportunities to socialize and indeed sufficient time off work—just as the quote from Sampson illustrates.

findings.antecedent: Diminishing communal living space on board merchant ships
findings.consequent: Reflects legislative environment and company attitude towards social spaces; impacts teamwork and congeniality
findings.quote: For instance, the space allocated to communal living on board merchant ships has been diminishing in recent times (Sampson 2015): the design of living space on board will reflect the legislative environment and the attitude of the company towards social spaces; the use of such space will reflect the sense of teamwork and congeniality on board—and the existence of such an atmosphere will in turn reflect the demand for such space to be built into ships at the design stage.

findings.antecedent: 'Under-considered' welfare of seafarers by many companies
findings.consequent: Low standards for living conditions (despite MLC stipulations)
findings.quote: Sampson and Ellis (2015) argue that the welfare of seafarers is “under-considered” by many companies. While the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) makes important stipulations regarding seafarer living conditions, these are in reality quite low standards and the aim should be to improve on these rather than simply adhere to them.

findings.antecedent: Modelling human behaviour under extreme stress during ship evacuation
findings.consequent: Very complex and difficult to predict behaviour
findings.quote: Modelling human behaviour under situations of extreme stress is very complex, and such behaviour may be difficult to predict...

findings.antecedent: Minimizing bottlenecks in ship layout (e.g., door sizes, number of doors, heel/trim angles)
findings.consequent: Can guide naval architects to reduce evacuation time
findings.quote: Yuan et al. (2014) illustrate, using a neighbourhood particle swarm optimization model, how door sizes, the number of doors, the number of passengers, along with the ship’s heel and trim angles, all affect the evacuation time of a given ship design.

findings.antecedent: Frailty or mobility of passengers, cognitive or sensory impairments (especially elderly on cruise ships)

findings.quote: What these models may not adequately consider is the frailty or mobility of passengers, the range of cognitive or sensory impairments they may have, and so on. With the majority of passengers on some cruise ships being elderly, it seems likely that the evacuation scenarios and times for these passengers are going to be more complex and take longer than for younger or less impaired passengers.

findings.antecedent: Seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates
findings.consequent: Concerns about returning to work, sleep disturbances, diminished energy, increased alcohol use, loss of pleasure, irritability, thoughts of suicide
findings.quote: A study of 25 seafarers attacked or held hostage by pirates (Stevenson 2012), which found that most had concerns about returning to work (20), sleep disturbances (12) and diminished energy (10). Some of them also reported increased use of alcohol (7), loss of pleasure from what had been formerly pleasurable activities (6), with fewer reporting a deterioration of significant relationships (5), irritability (5) and sometimes thoughts of suicide (3).

findings.antecedent: Longer time seafarers were held captive
findings.quote: Within this small sample there was no relationship between subjective descriptions of stress, and age, rank or length of service at sea, but there was a relationship with the length of time seafarers were held captive—the longer they were held, the more severe the symptoms.

findings.antecedent: Fear of losing jobs or not being rehired (due to stigma of mental health problems)
findings.consequent: Discourages seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy
findings.quote: Stigma discourages many seafarers from seeking consultation or effective therapy … because they fear losing their jobs or not being rehired” (p. 993).

findings.consequent: Psychologically equivalent to other serious life-threatening events (terrorist incidents, natural disasters), feelings of detachment/alienation, startled by noises, nightmares, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depressive reactions

Participants reported feelings of detachment and alienation from those close to them, being startled by noises, having nightmares and sleep disturbance. Anxiety manifest through apprehension, tension and fear in particular situations, and depressive reactions manifest through low mood, lack of interest and engagement in activities were also noted.
O’Shea (2005) has demonstrated that certain styles of command—generally more democratic styles—are associated with better seafarer well-being.

findings.antecedent: Work Improvement on Board (WIB) programmes (participatory action-oriented training)

findings.antecedent: Modern merchant ships crewed by seafarers from a range of nationalities

findings.consequent: Can help solve problems, does not need to be a challenge to a narrow ethos
findings.quote: Organizational culture should also cultivate pluralism (MacLachlan and O’Connell 2000) as a diversity of views in the workplace can in fact help solve problems and does not need to be a challenge to one narrow prevailing ethos (Cox and Blake 1991).

findings.consequent: Positively associated with perceptions of safety climate

findings.consequent: Perception of safer ship, mediated by job satisfaction

findings.consequent: Associated with benefits for some groups (European crew), but not all (Filipino crew)

findings.antecedent: Cultivating pluralism (recognizing human differences, finding value in diversity)

findings.consequent: Maritime health focus on occupational health services and international health problems

findings.consequent: seeking pleasure (pursuing exciting experiences/possessions) as a coping strategy
findings.mechanism: Diversion strategy to provide psychic relief from anxiety related to environmental problems.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found that ‘seeking pleasure' was the strategy most highly endorsed across three samples of adults.

findings.antecedent: extent of using 'seeking pleasure' coping strategy
findings.consequent: lower level of reported stress from awareness of environmental problems
findings.mechanism: Seeking pleasure provides psychic relief, reducing reported stress.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found a negative association between the extent to which people reported using this strategy and the level of stress they reported as arising from an awareness of environmental problems.

findings.mechanism: Diversion strategies do not translate into pro-environmental action.
findings.quote: seeking pleasure did not motivate positive environmental behaviours, and in some samples this strategy was actually associated with less engagement in such beneficial behaviours.

findings.antecedent: using 'relativisation' coping strategy (claiming environmental problems are not so great)
findings.consequent: lower levels of stress from environmental damage
findings.mechanism: Reinterpreting threats reduces their perceived severity and associated stress.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found that this strategy was consistently associated with lower levels of stress from environmental damage

findings.mechanism: Reinterpretive coping strategies do not translate into pro-environmental action.
findings.quote: endorsing relativisation did not promote greater pro-environmental behaviour.

findings.antecedent: deploying 'denial of guilt' coping strategy (claiming environmental damage is not one's fault)
findings.consequent: lower levels of stress from environmental problems
findings.mechanism: Denial reduces personal responsibility and associated stress.
findings.source: text, p.27 (Homburg et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann et al., 2001; Norgaard, 2006)
findings.quote: denial of guilt helps lower levels of stress from environmental problems but did not propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.consequent: propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Denial of guilt does not motivate pro-environmental action.
findings.source: text, p.27 (Homburg et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann et al., 2001; Norgaard, 2006)
findings.quote: denial of guilt helps lower levels of stress from environmental problems but did not propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.consequent: projection (blaming other individuals or groups, e.g., 'Amerika')
findings.mechanism: Projection is a defense mechanism to manage guilt by externalizing blame.
findings.quote: Norgaard found substantial evidence for this form of emotion management, as many of her Norwegian respondents repeatedly identified “Amerika” as the real source of ecological problems.

findings.antecedent: using 'resignation' coping strategy (accepting environmental problems as inevitable)
findings.consequent: significantly less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Apathy and resignation lead to inaction regarding environmental problems.
findings.quote: people were significantly less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours to the extent that they used the strategy of resignation

findings.antecedent: briefly reminded of one's own death (writing essays)
findings.consequent: attached greater importance to money, image and status (materialistic values)
findings.mechanism: Terror management theory: mortality salience leads to self-esteem enhancement through cultural values like materialism.
findings.quote: subjects randomly as-signed to write short essays about their own death attached greater importance to money, image and status

findings.consequent: reported being more excited at the prospect of finding $20
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases the appeal of material rewards as a means of self-esteem enhancement.
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death reported being more excited at the prospect of finding $20

findings.consequent: more attracted to high-status goods (e.g., Lexus car, Rolex watch), but not low-status goods (e.g., Geo-Metro car, Pringles)
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases the appeal of status-enhancing material possessions.
findings.quote: after having mortality made salient, subjects were more attracted to goods such as a Lexus car or a Rolex watch

findings.consequent: increased expectations about future financial worth and expected spending on clothing, entertainment, leisure activities
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience drives a compensatory striving for material success and consumption.
findings.quote: Writing about their own death has also been found to increase undergraduates' expectations about their future financial worth, as well as how much they expect to spend on clothing, entertainment and leisure activities

findings.consequent: leads judges to assign harsher punishments to prostitutes, Americans to provide greater monetary rewards to those who uphold common cultural values, and college students to be more antagonistic towards out-group members
findings.mechanism: Terror management theory: mortality salience increases in-group favoritism and out-group derogation to bolster cultural worldviews.
findings.quote: thinking about death leads judges to assign harsher punishments to prostitutes, Americans to provide greater monetary rewards to those who uphold common cultural values, and college students to be more antagonistic towards out-group members

findings.consequent: became especially disgusted by animals (e.g., maggots, cockroaches) and body products
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases disgust towards aspects of existence that remind humans of their animal nature.
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death became especially disgusted by animals (seeing maggots or cockroaches) and body products

findings.antecedent: written about their own death AND read essay proclaiming similarities between animals and humans
findings.consequent: rated the author of the essay as less likable, intelligent, and knowledgeable
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience leads to derogation of those who challenge human uniqueness from animals.
findings.quote: the subjects who had written about their own death rated the author of the essay proclaiming the similarities between animals and humans as less likable, intelligent, and knowledgeable

findings.consequent: express more negative attitudes towards aspects of human behaviour shared with animals (e.g., breastfeeding, sex) and towards animals in general
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases efforts to distance humans from their animal nature.
findings.source: text, p.30 (Goldenberg et al., 2006; Beatson & Halloran, 2007)
findings.quote: thoughts of death can cause people to express more negative attitudes towards those as-pects of human behaviour that are shared with animals... and towards animals in general

findings.consequent: significantly more likely to report thinking about death than when in cultivated nature or the city
findings.mechanism: Wild nature, being untamed, can evoke existential fears and reminders of mortality.
findings.quote: subjects were significantly more likely to report that they thought about death when they were in wild nature

findings.consequent: view cultivated, humanised nature as more beautiful and rate wild, untamed nature as less beautiful
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience leads to preference for tamed, controlled environments over wild, untamed ones.
findings.quote: Reminders of death... were also found by these researchers to cause subjects to view cultivated, humanised nature as more beautiful and to rate wild, untamed nature as less beautiful.

findings.antecedent: writing brief essays about their own death
findings.consequent: made bids to cut down significantly more acres of forest in a simulated forest-management game
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience stimulates a tendency to transform or destroy wilderness.
findings.quote: Subjects who had written about death made bids to cut down significantly more acres of forest.

findings.antecedent: exposing people to messages promoting materialistic values (social modelling, media, competitive context)
findings.consequent: tend to adopt such values themselves / express materialistic values more strongly
findings.mechanism: Social learning and cultural context shape individual values.
findings.quote: exposing people to messages promoting materialistic values tends to lead them to adopt such values themselves.

findings.antecedent: psychological insecurity (death reminders, cold/controlling parents, divorce, economic deprivation, temporary hunger)
findings.mechanism: Insecurity drives compensatory striving for material possessions and status.
findings.quote: Psychological insecurity is the second factor known to cause an orientation towards materialistic values.

findings.antecedent: greater priority on intrinsic/self-transcendent values (self-acceptance/self-direction, affiliation/benevolence, community feeling/universalism)
findings.consequent: oppose environmentally damaging self-enhancing/materialistic values and promote more positive environmental attitudes and sustainable lifestyles
findings.mechanism: Intrinsic and self-transcendent values are psychologically antagonistic to materialistic values and align with pro-environmental outcomes.
findings.quote: such values both oppose environmentally damaging self-enhancing and materialistic values and promote more positive environmental attitudes and sustainable lifestyles

findings.antecedent: reading task framed as relevant to intrinsic goal of benefiting the community
findings.consequent: learned the material in the text more deeply and were more likely to voluntarily visit the library and a recycling plant to learn more about recycling
findings.mechanism: Intrinsic motivation enhances engagement and learning, leading to pro-environmental actions.
findings.quote: those who had the goal framed in intrinsic terms not only learned the material in the text more deeply, but were also more likely to voluntarily visit the library and a recycling plant to learn more about recycling.

findings.antecedent: chosen to ‘downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle
findings.consequent: live in more ecologically sustainable ways than mainstream Americans
findings.mechanism: Lifestyle choices driven by intrinsic values lead to reduced ecological footprint.
findings.quote: those who have chosen to ‘downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle also live in more ecologically sustainable ways

findings.consequent: effective in increasing compliance with speed limits, decreasing amount people drive, increasing use of public transportation and stores selling sustainable products
findings.mechanism: Implementation intentions automatize behavior, reducing cognitive effort for goal-consistent actions.
findings.source: text, p.45 (Elliott & Armitage, 2006; Eriksson et al., 2008; Bamberg, 2002)
findings.quote: implementation intentions have been effective in in-creasing compliance with speed limits... in decreasing the amount people drive... and in increasing people's use of both public transportation and stores that sell sustainable products.

findings.antecedent: higher levels of Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) (college students)
findings.consequent: significantly more likely to endorse and personally use “products made by injuring or killing animals”
findings.mechanism: SDO reflects a desire for group dominance, extending to exploitation of non-human nature.
findings.quote: college students displaying higher levels of SDO are sig-nificantly more likely to endorse and personally use “products made by injuring or killing animals”

findings.consequent: most frequent justification given by participants was 'necessity'
findings.mechanism: Legitimizing myths are used to justify behaviors that exploit animals.
findings.quote: The most frequent justification that participants in her study gave for using animals was "necessity”.

findings.consequent: low in materialistic values and high in intrinsic values
findings.mechanism: Empathy fosters other-oriented values, conflicting with self-enhancing materialism.
findings.quote: People high in empathy tend to be low in materialistic values and high in intrinsic values

findings.consequent: lower levels of prejudice across a number of different types of out-groups
findings.mechanism: Empathy promotes understanding and reduces negative attitudes towards out-groups.
findings.quote: They also tend to display lower levels of prejudice across a number of different types of out-groups

findings.antecedent: value confrontation (feedback on discrepancies between egalitarian values and behavior/peers)
findings.consequent: effective for individuals who endorse egalitarian values but still hold prejudicial attitudes towards out-groups (reduction in prejudice)
findings.mechanism: Creating cognitive dissonance motivates individuals to align their values and behaviors, reducing prejudice.
findings.quote: recent re-search suggests it can be quite effective for individuals who endorse egalitarian values but nonetheless still hold some prejudicial attitudes towards out-groups

findings.antecedent: perspective-taking intervention ('try to feel the full impact' of someone's experience)
findings.consequent: increases empathy for groups and declines in prejudice towards these individuals
findings.mechanism: Perspective-taking fosters empathy, which reduces prejudice.
findings.source: text, p.52 (Batson et al., 2002; Whitley & Kite, 2006)
findings.quote: this relatively simple intervention increases empathy for groups as diverse as drug dealers, older people, African Americans, AIDS patients and the homeless, with consequent declines in prejudice towards these individuals

findings.antecedent: asked to take animals' perspective (viewing pictures of harmed animals)
findings.consequent: express significantly higher levels of biospheric environmental concern (concern for all living things)
findings.mechanism: Perspective-taking generates empathy, leading to greater concern for non-human nature.
findings.quote: Subjects who were asked to take the animals' perspective were found to express significantly higher levels of biospheric environmental concern

findings.antecedent: reporting unpleasant emotions such as anger and sadness in response to environmental stresses
findings.consequent: more likely to engage in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Unpleasant emotions can motivate action when processed constructively.
findings.quote: those subjects who report unpleasant emotions such as anger and sadness in response to environmental stresses are more likely to engage in posi-tive environmental behaviours.

findings.antecedent: sustained, reflective meditation on the feelings aroused by thoughts of death
findings.mechanism: Sustained reflection on mortality can lead to a shift towards self-transcendent and intrinsic values, reducing materialism.
findings.source: text, p.58 (Cozzolino et al., 2004; Lykins et al., 2007)
findings.quote: a more sustained, reflective meditation on the feelings aroused by thoughts of death can actually decrease materialistic strivings

findings.antecedent: mortality salience (fear of death) AND thinking about the possibility of an afterlife (alternative coping)
findings.consequent: disappearance of the effect of mortality salience on unsustainable resource use
findings.mechanism: Alternative coping mechanisms can buffer the negative effects of mortality salience.
findings.quote: this effect disappeared when people were provided with an alternative means of coping with the fear of their own death: in this case, thinking about the possibility of an afterlife.

findings.antecedent: endorsing problem-solving coping strategy (seeking information, educating oneself, social support)
findings.consequent: one of the best predictors of engaging in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Active engagement with problems and seeking solutions directly leads to positive behaviors.
findings.quote: one of the best predictors of engaging in positive environmental behaviours was endorsing this problem-solving coping strategy.

findings.consequent: increased levels of reported stress from an awareness of environmental challenges
findings.mechanism: Directly confronting environmental problems can increase stress, even if leading to action.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found problem-solving strategies to be associated with increased levels of reported stress from an awareness of environmental challenges.

findings.consequent: reduced desire for materialistic attainments, less likely to endorse materialistic values, and more likely to endorse intrinsic values
findings.mechanism: Mindfulness promotes acceptance of present experience, reducing compensatory materialistic strivings.
findings.source: text, p.60 (Brown et al., 2009; Brown & Kasser, 2005)
findings.quote: mindfulness was associated with reduced desire for materialistic attainments, and Brown and Kasser (2005) found that more mindful people were less likely to endorse materialistic values and more likely to endorse intrinsic values.

findings.consequent: engaged in more positive environmental behaviours and had lower ecological footprints
findings.mechanism: Mindfulness fosters greater awareness and acceptance, leading to more sustainable behaviors.
findings.quote: adults who were more mindful engaged in more positive environmental behaviours and had lower ecological footprints

findings.consequent: extent to which people endorse materialistic values
findings.mechanism: Materialistic values are primarily shaped by social experiences, not genetics.
findings.source: text, p.67 (Giddens et al., 2009; Kasser et al., 2004)
findings.quote: the extent to which people endorse materialistic values seems to have little to do with genetics

findings.mechanism: While categorization may be innate, the evaluative content of prejudice is learned.
findings.quote: the evaluations they attach to those categorisations are largely learned

findings.consequent: means by which people cope with threat
findings.mechanism: Cultural norms and messages shape acceptable and common coping strategies.
findings.quote: the means by which people cope with threat is largely shaped by messages received from their culture

findings.consequent: less concern for social justice, equality, and a world at peace, less pro-social behaviour, and more manipulative, competitive behaviour
findings.mechanism: Materialistic values prioritize self-interest, conflicting with broader social and environmental concerns.
findings.quote: self-enhancing, materialistic values are not only associated with more negative environmental attitudes and behaviours, but also with less concern for social justice, equality, and a world at peace, less pro-social behaviour, and more manipulative, competitive behaviour

findings.antecedent: tendencies that promote prejudice towards non-human nature
findings.mechanism: Underlying mechanisms of prejudice are generalizable across different out-groups.
findings.quote: the tendencies that promote prejudice towards non-human nature probably span numerous other out-groups

findings.antecedent: maladaptive responses to fear and threats
findings.consequent: problematic social behaviours, such as aggression or victimisation of out-groups
findings.mechanism: Maladaptive coping mechanisms can lead to externalized aggression and social conflict.
findings.source: text, p.73 (Greenberg et al., 2004; Stephan & Stephan, 2000)
findings.quote: maladaptive responses to fear and threats not only create a tendency towards problematic environmental behaviour, but also towards a number of other problematic social behaviours, such as aggression or victimisation of out-groups

findings.consequent: cognitively and psychologically susceptible to advertising (do not understand intent to sell, accept claims at face value)
findings.mechanism: Children's undeveloped cognitive skills make them vulnerable to persuasive advertising techniques.
findings.quote: young children are cognitively and psychologically susceptible to advertising – they typically do not understand the notion of intent to sell, and frequently accept advertising claims at face value

findings.consequent: increases children's scores on assessments of materialistic values
findings.mechanism: Media exposure acts as social modeling, promoting materialistic values.
findings.quote: exposure to commercial television increases children's scores on assessments of materialistic values

findings.consequent: contributes to alcohol and cigarette use, eating disorders, violence and sexual promiscuity
findings.mechanism: Marketing messages promote values and behaviors that can lead to various social problems.
findings.quote: exposure to marketing messages is also known to contribute to a host of other problems for young people, including alcohol and cigarette use, eating disorders, violence and sexual promiscuity

stimuli.description: short essays about their own death or about a neutral topic
pictures of wild animals being harmed (e.g., a seal caught in a fishing net)
text about recycling framed as relevant to materialistic goal of saving money or intrinsic goal of benefiting the community
lists of words typically associated with humans (e.g. wife, civilian) or with animals (e.g. wildlife, creature) presented with British or foreign names

Summary of identity-based campaign strategies for environmental challenges

limitations: Mainstream environmentalism's focus on economic benefits and 'simple and painless' changes may inadvertently reinforce materialistic values and problematic coping strategies.

Environmental organizations sometimes inadvertently exacerbate in-group/out-group distinctions between humans and nature, for example, by dismissing animal welfare concerns or framing nature instrumentally.

The paper notes that 'little research has been conducted' on experiential factors that promote environmental identity, particularly regarding human-nature interactions beyond human social interactions.

limitations: The sample includes employees from three cities of different scales, Amsterdam, Almere, and Eindhoven, each with distinct dwelling types, which may further contribute to these variations in preferences.
This study focused on civil servants working in municipal office buildings, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other types of office workers.
The findings are based on hypothetical scenarios presented in the discrete choice experiment, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world office environments.
Participants may have evaluated familiar office attributes more reliably than unfamiliar ones.

Although this study explicitly asked participants to assume no home obligations (e.g., childcare, package delivery, shopping), such responsibilities may nonetheless influence real-world workplace choices.
Although this study revealed heterogeneity in workplace preferences, it did not examine personal characteristics such as gender, age, or education level.

This study examined three environmental zones with a total of only eleven home and office attributes. Future studies should build on the findings of this study and explore additional attributes to provide further understanding of workplace preferences within these three environment zones.

Aesthetics were assessed by combining three elements (colour, presence of art and greenery). However, each of these elements may impact office attractiveness in different ways. Future hybrid studies should therefore investigate them separately to understand how either combinations or separate effects influence the office's appeal.

extraction_result.title: The cognitive neuroscience of auditory distraction

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task (visual presentation of 6 digits, report in order) compared to control task (1-6 in numerical order)
findings.consequent: activation of brain regions (left inferior frontal cortex, left anterior cingulate cortex, left inferior parietal cortex, right precuneus, bilateral anterior insular cortex, left lentiform nucleus, left thalamus, bilateral cerebellum)
findings.mechanism: involvement of this region in working-memory function
findings.quote: This comparison revealed a working-memory effect characterised by an activation of a large-scale network of brain regions.

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task with changing-state speech sounds compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.consequent: deactivation of brain regions involved in working memory (left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, bilateral secondary auditory cortex, left inferior parietal cortex)
findings.mechanism: Changing-state material resulted in a suppression of several brain areas, crucially involving left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and brain regions implicated in the temporary storage of speech-based material
findings.quote: relative to steady-state material, change-of-state caused a deactivation of several of the regions involved in working memory.

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task with changing-state speech sounds compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.mechanism: these effects of changing-state sound on the brain were not shown to adversely influence working-memory performance on this task.
findings.quote: these effects of changing-state sound on the brain were not shown to adversely influence working-memory performance on this task.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task (8 digits per list) compared to easy working-memory task (6 digits per list)
findings.consequent: involvement of the right dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex
findings.mechanism: The additional demands of the task recruited the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex on this difficult working-memory task [4].
findings.quote: The additional demands of the task recruited the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex on this difficult working-memory task [4].

findings.antecedent: ignored speech sounds during a difficult working-memory task (8 digits)
findings.quote: ignored speech sounds disrupted working-memory performance [4].

findings.antecedent: changing-state speech sounds during a difficult working-memory task compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.mechanism: this changing-state effect also activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.
findings.quote: this changing-state effect also activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.

findings.antecedent: higher memory demands of a difficult task AND changing-state sound
findings.mechanism: this distracting sound thus crucially influences the processes of executive functioning within the brain [12,16] that support the active selection, monitoring and manipulation of information in working memory.
findings.quote: similarities between the brain regions activated by working-memory and changing-state effects were confined to the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task (8 digits) compared to easy working-memory task (6 digits)
findings.mechanism: The 10% decrease in baseline performance (6 digits: 93% correct, compared with 8 digits: 83% correct) on this more difficult task might be one of the reasons why this task was more susceptible to disruption.
findings.quote: The 10% decrease in baseline performance (6 digits: 93% correct, compared with 8 digits: 83% correct) on this more difficult task might be one of the reasons why this task was more susceptible to disruption.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task with ignored speech disrupting performance
findings.quote: Indeed, on the difficult task, when ignored speech disrupted working-memory performance [4], this physiological suppression was not apparent.

stimuli.description: steady-state (e.g., AAA...) and changing-state (e.g., ABAB...) speech sounds
lists of 6 or 8 digits presented visually

limitations: It remains an open question whether disruption of working memory by auditory distraction on tasks with low memory demands is related to the absence of suppression or the activation of some additional brain mechanism.

It remains an open question whether the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is crucial to the disruption of working-memory performance when the content of the to-be-remembered material is visual-spatial.

limitations: The study focused on primary schools in the UK, which may limit generalizability to other building types, countries, or educational dimensions (e.g., behavioral development).
The specific climatic conditions and cultural differences of the UK may affect the realization of optimum environmental conditions and pedagogical approaches.
The study's measures for some factors, like visual complexity, are currently judgmental, indicating a need for more objective measures.
Data limitations led to the exclusion of pupils from reception classes, those with incomplete performance measures, and some EAL pupils without sufficient English skills.
The whole-building level of analysis showed a muted impact on learning, with only 3% of variance at the school level, potentially influenced by all schools being state-funded and locally controlled.

Some factors (Sound, Links to Nature, Connection) that showed bivariate correlations with learning progress were 'competed out' in the multi-level model, suggesting their individual importance might be weaker when other factors are controlled.

findings.antecedent: Stronger sensorial experiences (through research and design)
findings.consequent: Increased awareness, perceptibility, and new design conversations

stimuli.description: A wall surface (6.5 meters long, 1.8 meters high) laser-cut into 32 sheets of flat paper material, mixed with different densities of salt, covered with crystallization coatings, and combined with layers of different colors to create varied textures and light interactions.

Augmented reality overlays via Microsoft HoloLens headset and iPhone app, displaying a full-scale hologram in a physical art space. The AR expanded on the physical installation by growing, changing densities, colors, and increasing the size and scale of patterns.
Crystallizing sound effects, edited through www.sodaphonic.com, creating rigid, striking soundtracks.
Olfactory stimulation (smell of salt) combined with sound, texture, white color, and AR.

limitations: The data collection devices (wearables) were not as sensitive as desired.

extraction_result.title: STRESS RECOVERY DURING EXPOSURE TO NATURAL AND URBAN ENVIRONMENTS¹
The Benefits of Daylight through Windows
MODERN TRENDS IN THE DIGITAL AGE OF ARCHITECTURAL LEARNING
Human Spatial Behavior

findings.antecedent: Animal social life (species-specific interaction distances, territoriality)
findings.quote: Observations conducted on a wide variety of animals indicated species-specific interaction distances (Hediger 1964, 1968), which seemed to be 'preprogrammed.' Additionally, animal social life seemed to be regulated by territoriality, an instinctive attachment to place (Wynne-Edwards 1964; Eibl-Eibesfeldt 1970).

findings.antecedent: Situations disrupting personal and social spatial domains (crowding, territorial invasions) in animals
findings.quote: it was thought to be obvious that placing animals in situations that disrupt personal and social spatial domains would create abnormal behavior and psychological stress.

findings.antecedent: Very close individual distances, territorial invasions, or overcrowded conditions in humans
findings.consequent: Heightened arousal (measured by self-reports and machines)
findings.quote: Several studies in fact found a relationship between spatial circumstances and heightened arousal as measured by self-reports and machines (Aiello et al 1975; Baxter & Deanovitch 1970; McBride et al 1965; Smith & Haythorn 1972; Evans 1978).

findings.antecedent: Abnormal spatial situations (infringement of spatial domain) in humans
findings.quote: There is no consistent evidence, however, that abnormal spatial situations elicit specific kinds of responses among humans.

findings.consequent: Variation in appropriate interpersonal distances and densities
findings.quote: Hall... noted that persons from different cultures vary in the interpersonal distances and densities that they consider to be appropriate.

findings.consequent: Spatial behavior (interaction distance, density preference, touching)
findings.quote: 'Contact cultures' are considered to be highly involved in their interactions and thus use small interaction distances, like high densities, and engage in frequent touching... 'Noncontact cultures,' on the other hand, shun touching, dislike high densities, and avoid close interpersonal distances.
Further, Hall (1966:172–73) argued that even subcultures within the United States (e.g. blacks, Puerto Ricans, Northern Europeans) exhibit different spatial preferences.
The data on interpersonal distances support the notion that cultural differences do exist, although the methods used in these experiments have been less than ideal.

findings.antecedent: Teachers' actions (rewarding proper distance, punishing close approaches, prompting distant individuals)
findings.quote: A more powerful factor seemed to be the teachers in these settings, who rewarded what they saw as proper interpersonal distance, punished children who approached others too closely, and physically prompted individuals who maintained distances too far from others (see also Bailey et al 1973).

The results of this study and others indicate that spatial behavior is no more a cultural trait than it is a biological instinct, since individuals adjust their personal distances on the basis of new contingencies.

findings.antecedent: Physical characteristics of a setting (buildings, microenvironment, design)
findings.quote: this view assumes that the physical characteristics of a setting per se have a large influence on our attitudes and actions, rather than our environments 'triggering' a biological or cultural trait.
The belief was that 'good' design can lead to healthy and happy tenants, while 'bad' design can have disastrous effects on residents.

findings.antecedent: Design factors (e.g., lack of territoriality, lack of community surveillance)
findings.consequent: Differential crime rates in urban public housing
findings.quote: One of the most widely publicized examples of the environmental perspective is the book Defensible Space (Newman 1973), which claimed that differential rates of crime in urban public housing could be explained by design factors.

findings.antecedent: Design forcing spatial proximity (low-rise, high-density, shared facilities)
findings.consequent: Social interaction, community spirit, cooperation, communality
findings.quote: Similar research indicates that design can force spatial proximity, and this inevitably leads to social interaction and community spirit.

findings.consequent: Social and psychological difficulties (rather than density per se)
findings.quote: There has also been a view expressed that it is environmental design that causes social and psychological difficulties and not density per se (Mitchell 1974).

findings.antecedent: Well-planned interior design (e.g., even distribution of objects/resources)
findings.consequent: Alleviation of crowding difficulties (e.g., clustering of people)
findings.quote: A well-planned interior design is thus seen as the solution to difficulties associated with crowding.
Osmond (1957, 1959) coined the terms 'sociopetal' and 'sociofu-gal' to suggest that interior design can encourage or discourage group formation.

findings.consequent: Pathology among the general population (rather than spatial factors)
findings.quote: An examination of the literature on the impact of crowding, for example, suggests that it is social structural factors and not spatial factors that cause pathology among the general population (see Cassel 1971; Fischer & Baldassare 1975).

findings.antecedent: Physical distances and high density per se
findings.quote: Physical distances among individuals and high density per se were poor predictors of specific individual responses, and this led to a closer examination of social and psychological factors operating within settings.
Stokols et al (1977) found that perceived crowding was related to poorer academic performance and health among university students.

First, when examining survey items on perceived crowding, only a moderate amount of the vari-ance seems to be explained by objective household space (i.e. persons per room), which indicates that objective density is only part of the spatial problem in these homes.

Second, perceived household crowding has an independent effect on measures of housing satisfaction (i.e. when account-ing for persons per room), including an impact on preferred mobility (see also Rossi 1955).

findings.consequent: Increased room density without adverse psychological effects (due to decreased visible social stimuli)
findings.quote: For example, in Desor's (1972) previously cited simulation, she found that subjects placed more figures within a space as the number of partitions increased. This indicated to her that room density may be increased (with no adverse psychological effects) when the number of visible social stimuli decrease.

findings.consequent: Faster pedestrian walking speed (suggesting minimization of social stimulation)
findings.quote: A study conducted by Bornstein & Bornstein (1976) found that pedestrians walked through the streets faster as city size increased, which suggested to the authors that the more crowded individuals were trying to minimize the level of social stimulation they experienced.
Yet another field experiment in a department store in New York City suggested that people had task and performance deficits due to overstimulation in dense shopping environments (Saegert et al 1975).

findings.consequent: Involvement in primary relationships (no withdrawal) and involvement in secondary social encounters (decrease)
findings.quote: The results of social survey analyses suggest that individuals experiencing residential crowding do not withdraw from primary relationships (friends, social networks, family, organizations), though they seem to decrease involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature (reactions to strangers, neighboring, meeting new people), which indicates a cost-effective method of limiting social overload.
A field study found that chronic household crowding created task deficits among children (Rodin 1976).
Therefore, if people's perceptions of control are increased, the negative aspects of spatial shortages can be alleviated (Sherrod & Cohen 1977).

findings.antecedent: Low social status and high demand for space
findings.quote: This readily brings to mind the fact that people of low status (e.g. the urban poor, the child in the crowded household) may have less of a claim to space when it is in high demand than do people of high status (the urban affluent, adults in the home).

findings.antecedent: Actual power over spatial use (more vs. less)
findings.consequent: Overload and interference (decrease with more power), interruptions and inability to conduct preferred activities (increase with less power)
findings.quote: Actual power over spatial use should minimize overload and allow one to conduct desired activities with less interference, while less power would lead to more interruptions and the inability to conduct preferred activities.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between low social power, attitude of powerlessness, and crowding
findings.consequent: Generalized learned helplessness among low-income crowded children
findings.quote: In fact, it is this subgroup (i.e. low in real and felt power) that may actually be the basis of Rodin's (1976) findings of a generalized learned helplessness among low-income crowded children.

findings.antecedent: Stable, status-differentiated group experiencing a shortage of space
findings.consequent: Greater control over space use and activities (e.g., scheduling, regulating utilization)
findings.quote: A common response of a stable, status-differentiated group experi-encing a shortage of space is greater control over space use and activities in its territory.

findings.antecedent: People's imagery of spaces (fantasy vs. reality)
findings.consequent: Coping with existing circumstances and imagining better positions
findings.quote: Sometimes the images people have of their spaces are more fantasy than reality, and Lym (1978a,b) argues that people develop these images in order to cope with the existing circumstances and imagine themselves in better positions.

findings.consequent: Spatial differentiation and mechanisms for controlling movement across boundaries (privacy)
findings.quote: In other words, role differentiation demands some degree of spatial differentiation within territories (Lym 1978b) and a mechanism for controlling movement across boundaries.

findings.antecedent: Disagreement on space allocation for role enactments
findings.quote: Problems arise when those sharing a common space do not have the same views about how this resource should be allocated, since this could hinder the enactment of individually preferred roles.

findings.antecedent: Short supply of household space (lack of room/privacy)
findings.consequent: Role conflict, competition for space, incomplete role performances, intrusions, blocking of desired role enactments, loss of control over boundary mechanisms
findings.quote: If there is not enough room or privacy to conduct desired roles alone and with others, competition for space use may occur. Undoubtedly, the possibilities of incomplete role performances, intrusions, and the blocking of desired role enactments are heightened.

findings.antecedent: Alteration of one nonverbal factor (e.g., distance)
findings.consequent: Shifts in another nonverbal factor (e.g., eye contact) to maintain optimal interaction
findings.quote: Importantly, the alteration of one factor seemed to create shifts along another dimension (e.g. closer distances led to less eye contact, or vice versa). Thus, they argued for an 'optimal' distance when, not attained, led to compensatory reactions to decrease the stress felt from the inappropriateness of the situation.

findings.consequent: Optimal distances for interaction; comfort and distance relationship is not always monotonic
findings.quote: Another reexamination of the research literature by Sundstrom & Altman (1976) supports the basic premise that there are optimal distances for interactions varying in level of involvement (interacting friends and strangers; non-interacting strangers), suggests that the relationship between comfort and distance need not be monotonic in every case (e.g. close and far distances are not desired for most interactions), and argues that other compensations are available when spatial variables are unadjustable.

findings.consequent: Objective value (resource) and communicative roles in social life
findings.quote: Space obviously has value for individuals and should be consid-ered as a resource, as is time or money. It is cherished by some, denied to others, and competed for by all.

findings.antecedent: Spatial behavior and uses, environmental cues, and positions others take in space
findings.quote: Beyond its objective value, spatial behavior and uses have communicative roles in social life. Reactions to our use of space, environmental cues, and the positions others take in space all inform us of what is expected of us and how others relate to our presence.

extraction_result.title: Biophilia, Health, and Well-being

findings.antecedent: Contact with nature (based on biophilia hypothesis)
findings.quote: If there is an evolutionary basis for biophilia, as asserted by E.O. Wilson in the opening quote, then contact with nature is a basic human need: not a cultural amenity, not an individual preference, but a universal primary need.

findings.antecedent: Ongoing connections with the natural world
findings.quote: Just as we need healthy food and regular exercise to flourish, we need ongoing connections with the natural world.

findings.antecedent: Experience of nature across evolutionary time periods
findings.consequent: Marks on human minds, behavioral patterns, and physiological functioning
findings.quote: The experience of nature across evolutionary time periods has left its mark on our minds, our behavioral patterns, and our physiological functioning.
The biophilia hypothesis and supporting research tells us that, as a species, we are still powerfully responsive to nature's forms, processes, and patterns

findings.antecedent: Knowledge of human affinity for nature (biophilia)
findings.consequent: Generation of health and wellness experiences through created environments
findings.quote: Using knowledge of our affinity for nature, adapted and refined over millions of years, we can generate experiences of health and wellness through the environments we create.

findings.consequent: Provision of resources necessary for human survival (water, sunlight, food, building materials, shelter, vistas, fire)
findings.quote: For the vast majority of human existence, the natural landscape provided the resources necessary for human survival, chief among them water, sunlight, animal and vegetable food, building materials, shelter, vistas, and fire.

findings.consequent: Reinforcement of values of respect and care for the environment
findings.quote: Connection to nature on a daily basis reinforces the values of respect and care for the environment that are necessities for sustainable communities.

findings.antecedent: Spaces with dead and dying plants and trees
findings.quote: However, not all nature is equally attractive or beneficial. Spaces with dead and dying plants and trees signal habitat depletion and are largely avoided.

findings.antecedent: Places with rich vegetation, flowers, large trees, water, and meandering pathways
findings.consequent: Sought out for relaxation and enjoyment
findings.quote: In contrast, places with rich vegetation, flowers, large trees, water, and meandering pathways that open suddenly to views are sought out by many as places of relaxation and enjoyment.
Improved moods and reduced stress are the most consistent benefits of nature contact across research studies

findings.antecedent: Nature contact (visual, multi-sensory, active, passive; across settings, cultures, ages)
findings.quote: Furthermore, contact with nature can be purely visual or multi-sensory, active engagement (walking, running, gardening) or passive (viewing only). Benefits are found in multiple settings, multiple cultures, and across the age span, from early childhood to late adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Hospital patients with window views of outdoor landscapes (trees)
findings.consequent: Less narcotic and milder analgesic use, shorter hospital stays, more positive post-surgical recovery
findings.quote: Ulrich found that patients with the tree view used less narcotic and milder analgesics, indicating lower pain experience. They also stayed in the hospital for a shorter time period and had a more positive post-surgical recovery overall than did patients who had the view of the brick wall.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature scenes (real or simulated) after a stressor
findings.consequent: Faster and more positive recovery (physiological stress reduction, mood enhancement)
key_citations: Ulrich and colleagues, Texas A&M University
findings.quote: Subjects exposed to a stressor recover faster and more positively if they are shown nature scenes or urban scenes with nature, rather than urban scenes devoid of natural elements. Subjects viewing the completely natural scenes do the best overall, with the greatest and most rapid reduction in physiological stress and more rapid mood enhancement.

findings.consequent: Increased use of nature elements (posters, photos) for decoration
findings.quote: They found that people in windowless spaces used twice as many nature elements (posters and photos especially) to decorate their office walls than those who had window views to natural areas outdoors.

findings.consequent: Preference and belief in better health and psychological functioning
findings.quote: We have known for a long time that people prefer daylight environments and that they believe daylight is better for health and psychological functioning than is electric light.

findings.consequent: Medicinal properties: entrains circadian rhythms, enhances mood, promotes neurological health, affects alertness
findings.quote: We know now that bright daylight has medicinal properties. It entrains circadian rhythms, enhances mood, promotes neurological health, and affects alertness.

findings.consequent: More rapid recovery, reduced pain levels, fewer strong analgesics, shorter hospital stays
findings.quote: Research in hospital settings shows that patients in bright rooms recover more rapidly from illness, show reduced pain levels, take fewer strong analgesics, and stay in the hospital fewer days than patients who are in more dimly lit rooms located on the north side or in locations where nearby buildings block sun penetration

findings.antecedent: Large trees close at hand (in public housing)
findings.consequent: Attraction of people outdoors, increased neighbor interaction, stronger social bonds
findings.quote: the researchers found that housing developments with large trees attracted people to be outdoors and, once there, they talked to their neighbors and developed stronger social bonds than people in similar housing projects without green space and trees.

findings.antecedent: Children performing activities in green settings ('green time')
findings.consequent: Reduced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
findings.quote: children performing activities in green settings have shown reduced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder

findings.antecedent: Proximity to green spaces (household gardens, neighborhood parks, large green spaces)
findings.consequent: Better health profiles (physical, mental health, social safety)
findings.quote: the researchers have found preliminary evidence that residents who are closer to green spaces, including household gardens and neighborhood parks as well as large green spaces, have better health profiles than residents who are farther away.

findings.antecedent: Active and passive contact with gardens
findings.consequent: Psychological, emotional, and social benefits (stress recovery, escape, improved moods)
findings.quote: benefits of gardens include recovery from stress, having a place to escape to, and improved moods.

findings.antecedent: Horticulture therapy (in clinical settings and nursing homes)
findings.consequent: Improved mobility, dexterity, confidence, and social skills (in dementia and stroke patients)
findings.quote: Other studies provide evidence that dementia and stroke patients show improved mobility and dexterity, more confidence, and improved social skills as a result of gardening activities.

findings.antecedent: Gardens containing rich foliage, flowers, a water feature, congruent nature sounds (bird songs, moving water), and visible wildlife (birds)
findings.quote: According to Ulrich, gardens will be more likely to be calming and to ameliorate stress if they contain rich foliage, flowers, a water feature, congruent nature sounds (bird songs, moving water), and visible wildlife, particularly birds.

findings.antecedent: Viewing pleasant nature scenes (rural and urban)

findings.antecedent: Walking in an urban environment with nature
findings.consequent: Stress reduction (compared to similar walk without natural elements)
findings.quote: Similar results have been found in field studies by Hartig and colleagues (1991) who looked at the stress reducing effects of walking in an urban environment with nature as compared to a similar walk without natural elements.

findings.antecedent: Playing in natural environments (home, school, camp)
findings.consequent: Sustained benefits for social, emotional, and cognitive development in children
findings.quote: Playing in outdoor environments, whether at home, school, or camp, has sustained benefits for social, emotional, and cognitive development in children.

findings.antecedent: Nature providing platform and objects for play
findings.consequent: Encouragement of exploration, building, aid in orientation, wayfinding, group decision-making, knowledge of changing contexts, improved problem-solving (in older children)

It encourages exploration and building among older children which aids orientation and wayfinding, group decision-making, knowledge of how to respond to changing contexts, and improved problem-solving.

findings.antecedent: Small-scale natural environments with props (flowers, stones, sticks, water)
findings.consequent: Stimulation of imaginative play (cornerstone of social and cognitive development in younger children)
findings.quote: Among younger children, small-scale natural environments with props (flowers, stones, sticks, water) stimulate imaginative play which is considered a cornerstone of social and cognitive development.

findings.consequent: Unequal distribution of nature amenities in urban environments (access to parks, street trees, landscaping)
findings.quote: We know from everyday experience that nature is not equitably distributed in urban environments. Those who can afford to do so live near parks, have large street trees and rich landscaping around their homes, and work in places that have design amenities.

limitations: Old methods are often limited by their focus on specific environmental stimuli and evaluation systems.
New methods integrate virtual reality and neuroscience, but art and architecture are not interchangeable, requiring caution when applying findings from other fields.

Limitations arise at ontological (breadth of perceptual experiences, focus on unimodal stimuli, subjective nature of beauty/pleasure), epistemological (explaining experiences solely through physiological terms, accounting for influencing factors), and methodological (diversity of stimuli/presentation, conflicts in procedures, technical restrictions) levels.
These limitations hinder the development of a universally accepted methodology and translation of research findings into practical architectural guidelines.
Architecture cannot be equated with artistic-aesthetic experiences as it serves broader human needs.
Architecture entails a continuous experience, influenced by transitions between spaces and architectural narrative.
Peripheral vision plays a crucial role, and architecture engages all sensory modalities, extending beyond mere visual perception.
These limitations hinder the fragmentation of the cognitive-emotional dimension of architecture, often leading to reliance on case studies.
Achieving universal solutions for architecture may be difficult due to individual differences and environmental factors.
There hasn't been a comprehensive study on the emotional and cognitive aspects of architecture.
Challenges remain in designing for diverse groups and addressing specific needs like dementia care.
Humans are more than just neurological beings, and architecture is also guided by intuitive design principles.
The information gathered from different studies was inconsistent.
Emotional experience is subjective and differs person to person.
Individual responses to specific design elements vary greatly due to differences in personality, culture, past experiences, and genetics.
The wide scope of the study involves many different fields, making it hard to cover everything thoroughly.
Valuable sources, such as 'gray literature' not widely published, might have been missed.

limitations: The installation of the automatic light variation was more complicated and took longer than expected.
The study did not intend to make extensive observations and measurements beyond the primary focus.
The spatial distribution of light was hardly assessed in this thesis.
No daylight-related control of the lighting level was included in the design or installation for practical and economic reasons.
This thesis does not aim to contribute to the basic scientific knowledge on how non-visual effects influence circadian cycles.
The study did not include new furniture, plants, etc., which could enhance the effect of lighting.

The study does not intend to prove how this particular light affects pupils' health, well-being, and performance, acknowledging other influencing factors like visual connections to the yard, noise, air quality, and social relations.
The installation of luminaires and initial controls was subject to continuous improvements, indicating ongoing technical challenges.
A large rapid (400 Hz) and irregular variation was noticed on the oscilloscope screen during flicker measurements, which is an important area for further research.
There was a significant dip in illuminance during the first minute of light character start-up, which is assumed to be a technical problem.

limitations: Early research was exploratory and atheoretical.
Spatial studies are often discredited as outside the framework of social science.
Substantive findings sometimes discount the importance of spatial factors, suggesting social structural factors are more influential than spatial ones.
Causal explanations of spatial phenomena often lack sociological relevance, being too biological, cultural, or environmental.
Methodological developments are needed for subjective-crowding models, such as measuring different kinds of perceived spatial inadequacies and accounting for reciprocal effects.
Past models of stimulus overload underestimate human learning and response capabilities and ignore social differences among potential contacts.
The idea that manipulating perceived control without actual power in long-term crowded residential environments will make crowding 'better' is untested and naive from a sociological perspective.
Most 'control' studies concentrate on attitudes, short-term crowding experiences, or special groups, shifting attention from larger social structural issues.
The study of roles and symbolic spatial meanings has little empirical confirmation of a dependable nature.
Equilibrium theories can be misleading if improperly used, assuming all spatial problems result in balanced solutions or that individuals always achieve optimal circumstances.
Equilibrium models often lack notions of social position and examination of antecedent conditions.
Lack of sociological input in spatial differentiation, ordering activities, and control of space through social mechanisms.
Studies of socialization of space use and development of spatial meanings are lacking.
Little work on 'antecedent variables' of spatial factors and behaviors has occurred.
Sociological methods like systematic large-scale surveys and observations over time are in short supply.

limitations: Limited Scope: This experiment exclusively investigates the restorative effects of different autumn landscapes in a virtual environment, while the effects of real-world landscapes may be influenced by seasonal and regional variations. Future research could broaden the scope, considering landscape effects under various conditions.

Further Exploration of Other Sensory Dimensions: While this study primarily focuses on visual and auditory perception, future investigations could delve into other sensory aspects such as olfaction and tactile sensation. Expanding research in these areas would offer a more comprehensive understanding of how landscapes impact individuals.

Despite stringent control over visual and auditory experimental conditions in this study, subtle differences might exist between the visual and auditory groups in terms of material collection for experiments, laboratory setups, and testing methods. Hence, future research might consider segregating the visual and auditory groups into separate laboratory environments or conducting experiments at different time intervals to minimize potential mutual influences between the two groups.

Regional and Seasonal Variations: The materials for this experiment were gathered on a campus setting, and variations in landscapes and plant species may differ significantly in various regions and seasons. Future research should take regional and seasonal factors into comprehensive consideration by studying a wider range of landscapes and plant species.

Experiment Duration Limitation: The stimulation duration in the virtual environment was only three minutes, which may affect the accuracy of the results concerning restorative effects. Future research could contemplate extending the duration of virtual environment stimulation for a more in-depth understanding of these effects.

Comparison between Real and Virtual Environments: This study did not extensively explore the differential sensory effects in real and virtual environments. Future research can delve deeper into comparing these two, aiming for a more profound understanding of their similarities and differences. Additionally, prior to the experiment, this study involved stress tests, such as typing and other laborious tasks, to enhance performance. However, we did not conduct control tests without stress to evaluate performance differences. This is a direction for further in-depth investigation. These improvements will contribute to a more comprehensive comprehension of disparities between real and virtual environments and enhance the scientific rigor and credibility of the study.

tables.description: Qualitative summary of positive repercussions and risks of collaborative/participatory design projects on education/students, community groups, and the environment.

limitations: The potential effects of these proposals are currently under investigation, but the immediate impact they have had is considerable.
The interpretation of clients' needs/wants is complex and requires preparation to prevent gross assumptions.

When only confronted with students' ideas, residents' demands often ended up being treated as strict design requirements, compromising the overall quality of the design outcomes: students' responses to such demands were not critical enough to elaborate from them.

Although the experience of joining communities and universities is still at its initial stages, it is possible to list a number of challenges, risks and limitations that need to be addressed and resolved in similar experiences. Further developments will be presented in the new year.
Risk to raise expectations in participants: goals and realistic scenarios of what can be achieved must be clearly stated immediately.
Students project very rarely can deliver concrete and finite outcomes.

Academic priorities must be clear; clients must be aware that what they can obtain from this experience is - for the moment - simply a repertoire of ideas. Further developments are expected to be produced, but this will require time and experience.
Not everyone will be willing - or capable - to contribute to the process with equal skills.

The community group identified should have an organisation structure. During the process, new relationships and groups can - and almost surely will - be formed, but an initial central core helps and prevents from spending vast amount of time in identifying potential community leaders, locating target groups etc. On the other side, starting from scratch can also have benefits; leaders must in this case do a lot of networking and research in advance.
Often users' requirements and goals won't coincide with academic requirements and goals.
When working with large communities do not assume that those willing to be directly involved will accept to overcome social, racial, cultural, political barriers and get along well together.
Students tend to be defensive and patronising.
Both professions will manifest resistance to such a collaboration.

limitations: The present research did not conduct Phase IV of the SCED design.
The study was subjected to limitations of the applied settings, including the school’s strictures and its term semester timeline, which were affected due to political unrest in the country.
The generalizability of the results was delimited by a small sample size and a specific ASD population group.

Some one-to-one learning sessions were conducted outside the designated blue and green cubicle sections but within the classroom bounds due to the ASD student participant’s temporary resistance to a specific setting, which may have affected the results with some variance.
The complete intervention refurbishment involved only the fixed single mode of the acoustic modification aspect, which impacted experiment flexibility.

As the research was experimental and subject to the school calendar time duration, the study was not able to gauge the graduated modification instalment and the flexibility of phase shifting effect correlated to individual participant progress.

The unforeseen consequentiality of the acute heterogeneity of the children participants in the research, including absenteeism and non-attending behaviour, limited the consistency of the number of sessions, sequenced-session and duration for some students.
Data were only collated regarding student-specific sensory disruptive and on-task behaviours.
The important prevalent heterogeneity factor depicted the spill-over impact of tantrums and meltdowns on other children present in the classroom, shifting the normalcy of observations.
The heterogeneity factor was starkly demonstrated due to staff sickness or short leave absenteeism, which impacted the participant’s behaviour and class-peer rapport with the substitute teacher.

limitations: Interdisciplinary Nature: The intersection of sound and architectural design draws upon insights from a wide range of disciplines, including architecture, acoustics, psychology, engineering, and environmental science. Bridging the gap between these disparate fields requires a nuanced understanding of their respective methodologies, languages, and frameworks.

Technical Complexity: The field of architectural acoustics encompasses a vast array of technical concepts and calculations. Navigating this complexity requires a strong foundation in scientific principles, as well as access to specialized tools and software for modeling and simulation. Moreover, interpreting and applying the results of acoustic analyses to real-world design scenarios requires a high level of expertise and experience.

Subjectivity and Perception: Sound is inherently subjective, shaped by individual preferences, cultural norms, and personal experiences. Understanding and accommodating these differences in perception and preference presents a significant challenge for architects and designers seeking to create universally appealing spaces.

Resource Constraints: The study has been constrained by limitations in resources, including time, funding, and access to data and expertise. Conducting research in the field of architectural acoustics often requires specialized equipment and facilities for measurements and experiments, as well as funding to support data collection, analysis, and dissemination. Moreover, accessing relevant literature and expertise can be challenging, particularly for researchers working in interdisciplinary or niche areas where information may be scattered across multiple disciplines and sources.

Evolution of Technology and Design Practices: The research has been challenged by the rapid pace of technological innovation and evolution in design practices. As new technologies emerge and design paradigms shift, the landscape of architectural acoustics is constantly evolving, presenting both opportunities and challenges for researchers and practitioners.
