extraction_result.title: The Effects of Lighting Design on Mood, Attention, and Stress

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) change score (post-session - pre-session) on POMS-SF
findings.mechanism: SAD and blue light conditions were expected to positively affect mood, creating a negative Total Mood Disturbance Score, while control was hypothesized to have no effect.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Total Mood Disturbance was not significantly different across light condition, F(2, 10) = 0.55, p = .58.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Depression-Dejection POMS subscale change score (post-session - pre-session)
findings.mechanism: Control condition was numerically slightly less effective at reducing depressive mood than SAD or blue light conditions, as expected if SAD and blue light were effective.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Depression-Dejection was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.089, p =.92.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Fatigue POMS subscale change score (post-session - pre-session)
findings.mechanism: Blue light condition was numerically the least effective at reducing fatigue, contrary to the expectation that it would reduce melatonin production and fatigue.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Fatigue was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.14, p= .34.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to show a larger change in heart rate, indicating more physiological stress.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,9) = 1.49, p= .25.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Change in heart rate from pre-session to post-session
findings.mechanism: Numeric pattern implies a link between a slightly elevated heart rate and the control condition compared to SAD and blue light conditions.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heat rate pre-session to post-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.044, p= .96.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Average reaction time in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to result in slower reaction times than blue light and control conditions due to potential distraction and irritation.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that average reaction time during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.34, p = .28.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Standard deviation of reaction times in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Numerically, response times varied less in the blue light condition, potentially indicating more consistent attention, but results were inconclusive.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that the standard deviation of reaction times during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.18, p= .33.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Percentage of omission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to result in increased error rates due to potential distraction and irritation.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that omission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.5, p=.62.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Percentage of commission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Color discrimination might have been more difficult in the blue light condition due to after-images, potentially explaining the numeric pattern.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that commission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.9, p=.42.

stimuli.description: A light therapy condition with a 10,000 lux, 6500°K white light; a blue light condition with a 50 lux 450 nm light; and a control condition with a 50 lux 3500°K standard office light.

Visual stimuli for the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT) including four distinct shapes (square, circle, triangle, star) and four distinct colors (red, blue, green, yellow). Target was a red square.

limitations: Small sample size (N=11) leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Experimental procedures might not have been sensitive enough or were flawed.
Extraneous variables such as weather patterns (non-uniform cloudy/sunny days) influenced participants' mood or stress levels.
Variations in time of day for sessions, with stronger effects potentially missed due to few evening sessions.
Variations in time of semester (normal week, midterms, spring break) affected participant workload, stress, and sleep patterns.

Measures might have been unfit: CCPT might not target the specific type of attention affected by lighting; POMS-SF might not be sensitive enough or included irrelevant subscales, and participants found adjectives synonymous or unfamiliar.
Participants might have remembered and intentionally maintained consistency in POMS-SF responses across repeated administrations within a session.
Heart rate might not fully capture physiological arousal as precisely as skin conductance or cortisol, and was easily influenced by researcher presence.
Possibility of a genuine null effect, suggesting previous literature might have erroneously reported or exaggerated lighting effects due to methodological issues.
Subjective opinions and personal preferences for lighting conditions might have influenced participant psychological states.

extraction_result.title: Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.consequent: distinction from other affective systems (objects, persons, ideas) and influence on individual equilibrium/well-being
findings.quote: affect related to places therefore exists, and is of a nature that, albeit not fully explicit and defined, nevertheless seems to distinguish it from other affective "systems” (towards objects, persons, ideas, etc.); furthermore it is perceived as one of those important factors that sometimes help and sometimes hinder our equilibrium, our material and spiritual well-being.

findings.antecedent: richness of social interaction (intensity and quality)
findings.quote: The formation of an affective bond seems mainly to be a function of the richness of the social interaction (intensity and quality of the interaction) with the person(s) towards whom the attachment behaviour is directed

findings.antecedent: forced transfer from place of residence
findings.consequent: interruption in individuals' sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial and group identity, sorrow resembling loss of a loved one
findings.quote: the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: feeling of belongingness to place and sorrow at moving out of community
findings.quote: length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked – while interest in what goes on in the community decreases with age and is linked mainly to socioeconomic class.

findings.antecedent: contemporary society's tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility, and functionalistic relationship with places
findings.consequent: inability to satisfy the fundamental human need for attachment to place
findings.quote: Attachment to place is considered a fundamental human need (Relph, 1976), a need that contemporary society is increasingly unable to satisfy owing to its tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility and hence a purely functionalistic relationship with places.

findings.antecedent: strong affective ties with place of residence
findings.consequent: dysfunctional outcomes, precluding adaptation to new opportunities
findings.quote: strong affective ties with the place of residence may be characteristic of particular groups of population under certain circumstances. Among other things, his work shows how such ties may to some extent prove dysfunctional, precluding adaptation to new opportunities (Fried 2000).

findings.consequent: social involvement, mobility, well-being, mental health, individual hardship, conformist attitudes, social refutation
findings.quote: Also other outcomes of attachment may be postulated at a level of both social involvement and mobility, and at that of well-being and mental health. Moreover, like residential stability, attachment does not necessarily have a positive outcome, but may represent a source of individual hardship, conformist attitudes or social refutation.

findings.consequent: relationship between them (separate concepts vs. components)
findings.quote: the relationship between satisfaction and attachment – that is, whether they are to be considered two separate concepts or whether satisfaction represents a component of or actually coincides with attachment – remains a controversial issue.

findings.consequent: lack of affective bonds with places
findings.quote: although a positive correlation between length of residence and the intensity of attachment to the place of residence is a widely reported finding, the small number of studies in which longitudinal aspects of residential life have been taken into consideration have shown that the causal relationship postulated between high residential mobility and lack of affective bonds with places is far from having been proved.

relational rootedness (quality and intensity of social bonds), attachment, that is the affective investment made in the neighbourhood of residence, is comparatively unaffected by the length of residence. On the other hand, the modality of arrival in the neighbourhood, or the perception of whether it was a free or a compulsory choice, carries greater weight.

findings.antecedent: high degree of mobility during childhood
findings.consequent: greater desire for stability in adulthood
findings.quote: One further interesting fact is that a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood, while global residential mobility does not seem to play any significant role.

findings.antecedent: neighborhood quality, previous experiences, compatibility with residential identity
findings.quote: Affective investment seems to be closely linked to neighbourhood quality, but also to previous experiences and compatibility with residential identity.

findings.antecedent: environments experienced in childhood or adolescence
findings.quote: Strong positive affective bonds seem to develop towards the environments experienced in childhood or adolescence, and more occasionally towards environments experienced only in adulthood.

findings.antecedent: unsatisfactory residential experiences during infancy and adolescence
findings.consequent: negative long-term consequences on capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood, even towards the more satisfactory environments.

findings.consequent: formation or intensification of affective bonds between occupant and territory
findings.quote: The identifying function is expressed not so much in the form of occupancy and control behaviours but in the personalisation of space, which results in the formation or intensification of affective bonds between occupant and the territory.

findings.consequent: expression of individual identity and stronger feelings of attachment
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment, while secondary territories tend to express a social or group identity.

findings.consequent: attachment to the neighbourhood and development of secondary territoriality
findings.quote: The results of research show that the street layout can facilitate attachment to the neighbourhood and thus the development of a secondary territoriality.

findings.antecedent: attachment associated with expression of identity
findings.consequent: demand for long-term experience with place
findings.quote: not all forms of attachment – in particular that associated with the expression of identity – demand a long term experience with place and that the 'tendency to equate attachment with more permanent residences may have more to do with our cultural bias toward home ownership than with reality' (p. 297).

findings.antecedent: prolonged association between individual and place
findings.consequent: persistency of attachment bond over time
findings.quote: The persistency over time of the bond is a characteristic that also seems to apply perfectly to bonds with places; indeed, prolonged association between an individual and a place is widely recognised as one of the distinctive features of attachment to place.

findings.antecedent: threat to attachment bond with a place
findings.quote: individuals may not be conscious of their attachment to a place (Stokols and Shumaker, 1981; Giuliani, 1991), and only become aware of it under particular circumstances, such as when the bond is threatened.

findings.consequent: particular status in the affective hierarchy
findings.quote: As concerns places, those of childhood often seem to maintain a particular status in the affective hierarchy, but because of the lack of longitudinal studies, there is too little data to be able to formulate precise hypotheses.

findings.consequent: variability in the place of greatest affection (birthplace)
findings.quote: for the vast majority the place of greatest affection is one's birthplace, but there is also a great variability related to mobility experiences and life stages. In addition, only a minority wants to go back and live there.

findings.consequent: strong nostalgic bonds to birthplace without intention to move back
findings.quote: among people who had moved away after the age of 12, there were strong bonds to the birthplace in a "nostalgic” sense, as there was no intention to move back. Among those who had moved away at an earlier age, 'only some warm memories for the former place remained'.

findings.antecedent: desire to remain in contact with attachment figure
findings.quote: The third criterion, that is the desire to remain in contact with the attachment figure, seems to correspond to a desire for residence stability, widely used as one of the indicators of attachment to place.

findings.antecedent: involuntary separation or loss of a loved one
findings.quote: The criterion complementary to the joy of reunion is the distress provoked by involuntary separation or the grief of loss. The fact that reactions similar to those for the loss of a loved one can be felt in relation to places was the starting point for the considerations on attachment to places and is amply described in all research on displacement (for a review, see Brown and Perkins, 1992).
literature on homesickness (for a review, see Van Tilburg et al., 1996) shows that it occurs frequently among both children and adults (Fisher, 1989; Eurelings-Bontekoe et al. 2000).

findings.consequent: increased presence of symptoms of malaise
findings.quote: a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise, but also that the relationship between mobility and health is not always negative.
mobility may be a strategy to correct undesirable aspects of one's life and one such undesirable aspect could be lack of attachment, since such a lack is a significant indicator of future mobility.

The final, and most important criterion, is the seeking of security and comfort. In environmental literature, the association between place and security has been investigated in particular with reference to the concept of home.

Feelings of security and comfort are included among the constituent elements of the experience of home in several empirical research studies (Sixsmith, 1986; Dupuis and Thorns, 1996; Case, 1996; Wiesenfeld, 1997).

Sebba and Churchman (1986) observed that the feeling of security is perceived as particularly important by the younger children (less than 13 years old) and is not a function of the physical protection offered by the home but of permanence (in Bowlbian terms we could say of accessibility).

findings.consequent: feeling of affection associated with security and family love
findings.quote: The most common form of attachment that emerges is that of a feeling of affection associated with security and family love.
the feeling of comfort appears more and more frequently in women's description of homes.

findings.antecedent: age (childhood, old age vs. adolescence, adult life) and social class (lower classes)
findings.consequent: preponderance of need for security/protection vs. exploration/affiliation/self-expression, and stronger attachment to home/neighborhood
findings.quote: the need for security and protection preponderates during certain stages of life (e.g. childhood and old age), while other needs emerge more forcefully in adolescence and at various stages of adult life (e.g. exploration, affiliation, self-expression, etc.). The strong attachment the elderly display towards the home might thus be seen as the re-emergence of the dominant need for security and protection. Impaired physical resources and the diminished capacity to adapt spatial behaviour patterns to changes in the immediate environment contribute to making the elderly retreat from the novel and seek security. Similarly, the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources (Fried 2000).

findings.consequent: similarities in psychological functions (well-being, stage-dependent importance, persistence, sorrow from loss)
findings.quote: Many similarities emerge in the identification of aspects typical of affective relationships between human beings and between persons and places: the importance of the psychological functions performed by these relationships in enhancing the well-being of individuals, the varying importance of particular functions at different stages of one's life, the persistence of the bonds over time, the reactions of sorrow in the case of loss, etc.
On balance, however, the differences seem to outweigh the similarities.

limitations: Some villagers believe the new Hougou New Village environment lacks space to raise large livestock because their previous way of life was related to farming labor.
Most villagers over 55 years old retain nostalgia for the old village life, affecting their emotional evaluation of the new village.

The interior part of the Chinese folk Cultural Heritage Rescue Project memorial Hall was still under construction and not fully open to the public, leading to a 'General' rating for post-use evaluation.
Tourists' evaluation of the visual design of scenic spots in the Tourist Reception Center declined, indicating a need to strengthen aesthetics and identification (e.g., road signs).
The planning of supporting facilities for new energy vehicles (charging system, exclusive area) was not fully considered in the Tourist Reception Center project.
Some tourists preferred to experience local traditional cave buildings for accommodation, suggesting possibilities for reusing vernacular buildings in Hougou Ancient Village.
The multimedia information device of the kindergarten entrance building facade could not be permitted in the later period, limiting the full reflection of the building's sociality.
The shared landscape designed in the periphery of the kindergarten park occupied part of the urban road system, preventing its full realization and affecting the functional evaluation.
Poor sealing performance of the perforated aluminum plate of the kindergarten entrance building curtain wall led to rain leakage, affecting aesthetics and increasing maintenance workload.
Children often used their hands to dig the carved aluminum plate of the kindergarten entrance building, posing security risks.

limitations: Small sample size (N=11) potentially leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Experimental procedures may not have been sensitive enough or were flawed.
Presence of extraneous variables (e.g., weather patterns, time of day, time of semester/academic workload) may have affected data quality and increased variability.

The specific type of attention measured by the CCPT (sustained attention) might not be the type most affected by lighting conditions; other forms like multitasking or suppression of distraction might be more relevant.
The POMS-SF measure might not have been sensitive enough to detect minor mood changes, or its subscales (e.g., 'Confusion', 'Anger') were irrelevant to lighting effects.
Participants might have remembered and tried to maintain consistency with their previous responses on the POMS-SF.
Some adjectives in the POMS-SF were closely related or unfamiliar to participants (e.g., 'Bushed'), potentially reducing the measure's specificity and accuracy.
Heart rate might not have fully captured physiological arousal as effectively as other measures (e.g., skin conductance, cortisol), and was easily influenced by the researcher's presence.

The possibility of a genuine null effect, suggesting that lighting conditions may not affect the measured constructs, and previous literature might have erroneously reported effects due to methodological flaws.
Subjective preferences for certain lighting conditions might have influenced participants' emotional states more than the direct physiological effects of light.
The sample did not predominantly include participants with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), which might have reduced the likelihood of observing changes in mood, attention, and stress.

extraction_result.title: Place Matters: The Significance of Place Attachments for Children's Well-Being

findings.quote: strong bonds with particular places endure (Hay, 1998).

findings.antecedent: Sense of belonging to a particular place
findings.consequent: Fundamental component of identity, security, and belonging
findings.quote: The sense of belonging to a particular place that this extract from a newspaper article conveys is a fundamental component of the way that most people understand who they are.

findings.consequent: Place identity, local social ties, personal meanings, linking life events to place
findings.quote: Long-term residence therefore strengthens place identity, facilitating local social ties, providing the time to invest places with personal meanings, and linking significant life events to place, although the quality and intensity of experiences are usually more important than simple duration (Tuan, 1977; Rowles, 1983).
although the quality and intensity of experiences are usually more important than simple duration (Tuan, 1977; Rowles, 1983).

findings.consequent: Place attachment (as part of identity, memories, feelings, beliefs, meanings)
findings.quote: Place attachment is normally understood to be part of a person's overall identity, consisting of the memories, feelings, beliefs and meanings associated with their physical surroundings (Proshansky et al., 1983; Corbishley, 1995; Lalli, 1992).

findings.antecedent: Places imbued with personal, social, and cultural meaning
findings.quote: Places imbued with personal, social and cultural meaning therefore provide a framework within which personal identity is constructed (Cuba and Hummon, 1993; Hay, 1998).

findings.consequent: Significance of place attachment, belonging, security
findings.quote: In these circumstances, where the processes of modernization create risks and uncertainties for individuals, attachment to place, and the sense of belonging and security that it engenders can take on a particularly significant role in people's lives.
Children gain their personal identity through their place attachment (Spencer and Wooley, 2000, p. 182).

findings.consequent: Positive and negative feelings in children
findings.quote: From a very young age, children develop (initially unconscious) positive and negative feelings about their everyday surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Unhappy social interactions/life events in ideal settings OR positive experiences/memories in poor environments
findings.quote: As a consequence, ideal settings may not result in positive place attachment if they were the site of unhappy social interactions or life events, just as poor environments can do so if they are associated with positive experiences and memories.

Even when neither the physical environment nor the social context is ideal, resilient individuals are capable of transforming their experiences into positive cognitions (Proshansky et al., 1983; Newman, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Direct/repeated childhood experiences of places + social meaning
findings.quote: Direct and repeated experiences of places in childhood, together with the social meaning attached to them by children and others (e.g. parents, teachers and peers), tend to have the biggest influence on the subsequent development of place attachments.

findings.consequent: Home as main source of place attachment
findings.quote: Up to the age of four or five years, the home is likely to be the main source of place attachment.

findings.consequent: Understanding of geographical place, exploration of local neighbourhood
findings.quote: However, by the time they leave primary school, children will normally have developed some understanding of their geographical place in the wider world, and will also have experience of exploring parts of their local neighbourhood, either independently or in the company of adults, siblings and peers (Siegel and White, 1975; Matthews, 1992).

findings.consequent: Conscious attachment to places, identification with area, desire to live there
findings.quote: Typically, this is followed in the teenage years by a more conscious attachment to the places in which young people have grown up, evident in growing identification with the area and a desire to continue to live there into adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Perceived inclusion/acceptance in local community OR close connections through local ancestry
findings.quote: Feelings of belonging tend to be strongest amongst young people who perceive that they have been fully included and accepted within their local community, or who have close connections through local ancestry (Gould and White, 1968; Lynch, 1977; Hay, 1998; McCreanor et al., 2006).

findings.consequent: Identity and well-being in children and young people
findings.quote: Research with children and young people has repeatedly shown that place, identity and well-being are often closely connected (Rowles, 1980, 1983; Chawla, 1992; Twigger-Ross and Uzzell, 1996; Day, 2007; Green and White, 2007; Irwin et al., 2007).

findings.antecedent: Children's daily experience of living and learning in the environment
findings.quote: children's daily experience of living and learning in the environment around them is a critical factor in their overall well-being (Sustainable Development Commission, 2007, p. 6).

One of the main influences on children's use of space is their age, with many researchers noting the way that children typically progress from exploration and play close to home in the pre-school years, through widening exploration of their local environment in middle childhood, to town- or city-wide exploration during adolescence (Moore, 1986; Matthews, 1992; Chawla, 1992).
This study, like many others (e.g. Jones et al., 2000), also noted that, with increasing age, boys tend to be given greater freedom to roam than girls.

findings.consequent: Favourite places (homes, gardens, streets, open spaces, parks, playgrounds, sports fields)
findings.quote: However, studies that have examined children's use of space indicate that favourite places for the majority of children include homes and gardens, nearby streets and associated open spaces, parks, playgrounds and sports fields (Moore, 1986; Gill and Sharps, 2004; Burke, 2005).
Several studies also emphasize the particular significance of unsupervised 'secret places' that facilitate imaginative play (Lynch, 1977; Moore, 1986; Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Parental fears (safety, risk, sectarian violence, traffic, crime)
findings.consequent: Children's mobility, independent use of space
findings.quote: The levels of safety and risk posed by the local environment, as assessed by both parents and children, also have major influences on children's use of space (Garbarino et al., 1992; Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

Assessments of the dangers posed by traffic and crime in different locations also mean that children living in inner-city or other urban locations, where these issues are more prominent, tend to enjoy less independent mobility than their peers living in suburban or rural areas (Deakin, 2006; Morrissey and Smyth, 2002).

findings.consequent: Young people's perceptions of local area (safety, friendliness, helpfulness)
findings.quote: Other studies have revealed the way that fear of crime, or the presence of busy traffic, have negative impacts on young people's perceptions of their local area, affecting not only their views about its safety, but also about the level of friendliness and helpfulness of local people (Morrow, 2002; Mullan, 2003).

findings.antecedent: Unaccompanied journeys to school, unstructured use of local areas, independent visits to places/people
findings.consequent: Social/environmental interactions, personal/community identities, place attachments, feelings of belonging/security
findings.quote: For the majority of children in this study, unaccompanied journeys to school, together with the freedom to use local areas in a relatively unstructured way and to visit favourite places and people independently, facilitated a wide range of social and environmental interactions with people and places, contributing to their personal and community identities.
There is also a strong relationship between children's use of space and the rules and meanings that exist within particular cultures (Rappaport, 1978).

findings.antecedent: Rapid growth of home entertainment (TV, video games, computers) + fears (traffic, crime, stranger danger)
findings.quote: In combination with fears about traffic, crime and 'stranger danger', the increasing availability of such cultural artefacts has resulted in children spending more and more of their time indoors (Sustainable Development Commission, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Surveillance and regulation by public/private authorities (patrolling, prohibiting activities)
findings.quote: For example, public and private authorities often take steps to manage children's use of space through a combination of surveillance and regulation, which includes the employment of staff to patrol neighbourhoods and shopping centres, and the erection of signs prohibiting a range of activities such as cycling and playing ball games (Holland et al., 2007).

findings.consequent: Perception of injustice by children and young people
findings.quote: Restrictions like these are often perceived by children and young people to be unjust, especially as they typically lack effective means of challenging them (Morrow, 2002).

findings.antecedent: Being told off by neighbours for playing outside
findings.quote: The great majority of children also report having been told off by neighbours for playing outside, with a third of seven to eleven-year-olds saying that this stopped them playing outdoors (Stockdale et al., 2003).

findings.antecedent: Protective discourse + growing anxieties about children's safety
findings.consequent: Children's freedom to use local environment ('shrinking world of childhood')
findings.quote: Several researchers and commentators have argued that a 'protective discourse' has developed over this period, with growing anxieties about children's safety greatly reducing their freedom to use the local environment (e.g. Scott et al., 1998; Morrow, 2002; Gill, 2008).

findings.consequent: Desire to spend more time outdoors
findings.quote: surveys also reveal that the overwhelming majority of children want to spend more time outdoors (e.g. Thomas and Thompson, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Limited availability of public open space
findings.consequent: Children's freedom to walk, cycle, or play safely
findings.quote: Restrictions on children's freedom of use of the local environment are also dependent on factors in the environment itself, including the increasingly limited availability of public open space in which children can walk, cycle or play safely in their local areas (Thomas and Thompson, 2004; Westbury, 2007).

Although restrictions on children's freedom, which are not unique to the UK, are generally imposed in the name of protecting children from harm, there is growing evidence about the damaging effects that they may actually be having on children's health, evident, for example, in rising levels of childhood obesity and mental health problems (Gaster, 1991; Armstrong, 1993; Mental Health Foundation, 1999; Collishaw et al., 2004; Irwin et al., 2007).

findings.consequent: Mood, anger/anxiety, concentration/self-discipline (in children with conduct disorders)
findings.quote: Some of the evidence for this conclusion comes from studies examining the effects of increased access to the outdoors, which has been shown to have positive effects on mood, reducing feelings of anger and anxiety (Pretty et al., 2005), and improving the concentration and self-discipline of children with conduct disorders (Taylor et al., 2001).

findings.antecedent: Restricted use of local environment ('shrinking world of childhood')
findings.consequent: Development of children's place attachments, identity, security, and belonging
findings.quote: Less obvious, but arguably just as harmful, is the effect that the increasingly restricted use of the local environment is having on the development of children's place attachments.

findings.antecedent: Children in care (insecure attachments, major dislocations)
findings.consequent: Rootlessness, fragmented identity, diminished sense of self, increased anxiety/vulnerability to depression
findings.quote: Not only are children in care disproportionately likely to have developed insecure attachments to their primary care-givers, with negative consequences for the confidence with which they explore their surroundings and the degree to which they are able to successfully integrate experiences into their self-identity (Howe et al., 1999), but they have also experienced at least one major dislocation in their lives.
The real significance of place attachment is often only revealed in its absence (Brown and Perkins, 1992; Cuba and Hummon, 1993).

findings.antecedent: Government policies (Healthy Schools, Travelling to School)
findings.consequent: Children's independent use of local environment, strength of place attachments
findings.quote: However, it should be noted that neither of these programmes necessarily increases children's independent use of their local environment, which is the key ingredient in developing the strength of their place attachments and their feelings of belonging in their local communities (Engwright, 2008).

findings.antecedent: Increasing car ownership, school choice agenda, media reporting of crime
findings.quote: Meanwhile, other aspects of social change and government policy, like increasing car ownership and use, and the school choice agenda (which has increased the length of home-to-school journeys in many areas, thereby reducing the likelihood that children will walk or cycle to school), coupled with the distorting effects of wall-to-wall media reporting of crimes involving children, serve to further undermine children's independent use of their surroundings.

findings.consequent: Children's independent use of local environments, place attachments
findings.quote: only the space-oriented approach specifically aims to increase children's independent use of their local environments, through the creation of what are often referred to as 'child-friendly communities' (e.g. Arnold and Cloke, 1998; Gill, 2008).

Areas where successful traffic calming or pedestrian-oriented measures like home zones have been introduced demonstrate an increase in informal social activities and children's play (British Medical Association, 1997; Pharaoh and Russell, 1989).

findings.antecedent: Regular experience of local surroundings (for children in care)
findings.consequent: 'Visible presence', sense of belonging, secure emotional attachments, resilience
findings.quote: For children of all ages looked after in care for prolonged periods of time, regular experience of being out and about in their local surroundings will also help to give them the sort of ‘visible presence' that is key to the development of a sense of belonging (Ross, 2007). They also provide the basis for potentially rich and rewarding inter-personal interactions, which help to build secure emotional attachments in the home and a sense of belonging in the community, thereby promoting children's resilience (Newman, 2004).

limitations: Data collected was not modeled for other areas of nature-driven design such as sustainable design and/or environmental design.
Data analysis was fixed solely to gain the perception of specified biophilic elements in a restorative healing environment and excluded those elements not present in the developed framework.
Participants were shown only three digital renderings that depicted each biophilic attribute being studied; the digital renderings represented only one view of a larger, three-dimensional space.
Data collected was based on the perception of that particular digital rendering of the space, as participants were not able to physically experience and/or occupy each space that was being presented.
The building selected to model design ideas is located in a dense urban environment.
The conceptual and final design excluded biophilic attributes deemed unachievable based on the building’s size, geographic location, or physical adjacencies limited by its urban context.

The design focused on mimicking realistic limitations and opportunities that the interiors of a space in a highly dense urban environment would face when introducing selected attributes of biophilic design.
Generalization to other urban built environments was not warranted.
The study did not investigate the perception of biophilic design in any aspects other than those in the alternative healthcare and restorative settings.
Generalization to other types of healthcare environments was not warranted.
The framework only included nine of the 70+ biophilic design attributes defined by Stephen Kellert, allowing only those listed to be surveyed and emphasized.
Some may argue that based on personal perception, the chosen nine biophilic attributes may not be the most vital design attributes to emphasize.

limitations: Paper I: Large sampling errors made correlations unreliable, requiring replications.
Paper I: Sound context difference between presentation and recall in noise condition might have contributed to the effect.
Paper I: Sentence recognition task might have been too easy, leading to no significant effect on error rate.
Paper II: Wide confidence intervals of correlations in a group of 32 persons require further studies for definite conclusions.
Paper II: Need to test effects on more realistic learning tasks (longer spoken texts) for better acoustical norms.
Paper III: Previous studies (e.g., Rabbitt) had methodological issues like group testing and lack of control for individual differences in memory capacity or speech perception abilities.
Paper IV: All results of memory performance could be an effect of incorrect word identification.
Paper IV: Repeating stimuli during experiments might lead to better recall performance than in real-world scenarios, potentially underestimating the true effects of degraded conditions.

limitations: Logistical constraints prevented recruiting a sufficiently large sample for a sufficient amount of time to convincingly answer questions about adaptation.
The estimates are necessarily specific to the noise and task combination at hand, limiting generalizability.
Noise levels were kept below typical factory levels for ethical reasons, which might have influenced workers' perceived need to reduce noise further.
The experiment's duration might be too short for workers to form correct beliefs about the effects of noise on their productivity.
The true underlying variation in past-noise exposure in the sample may be relatively small, limiting heterogeneity analysis.
Learning in the experimental setting might not fully reflect learning in the real world.
The study does not assess whether firms are aware of the effects of noise, screen workers, or optimally abate.

limitations: Small sample sizes and limited to single groups in several studies (Cupkova et al. [4], Kim et al. [12], Kazemi et al. [11], Sun et al. [20]).
Difficulty generalizing results beyond specific populations (e.g., postgraduate students, young college students) [11, 12, 20].
Privacy concerns with data collection methods (e.g., Digital ID in Deng et al. [5]).
Limitations in experimental techniques and model approaches in some studies [14, 10].
Failure to account for temporal variables (e.g., morning vs. afternoon) affecting working memory [14].
Lack of clear distinction between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements [10].
Insufficient deep research on the impact of lighting glare and Colour Rendering Index (CRI) on human behaviour, visual performance, and comfort.

findings.antecedent: Biological imitation strategies (biomimicry) in building design
findings.consequent: Wellness (human comfort, physical, mental, social well-being)
findings.quote: This research is about applying biological imitation strategies in building design to see wellness fostered in the light of nature's adaptive and efficient capabilities

findings.consequent: Improved daylighting, ventilation, indoor air quality
findings.quote: or spatial designs like those receiving light and air openings from rainforest canopies' tiered structure
buildings developed through this approach not only stand as sustainable structures but additionally support user comfortability.

findings.antecedent: Good physical environment (indoor air quality, thermal comfort, acoustics)
findings.quote: Research has demonstrated that the physical environment, including indoor air quality (IAQ), thermal comfort, and acoustics, plays a significant role in the physical health of individuals residing or working within these spaces.

findings.antecedent: Good lighting, color schemes, and views
findings.quote: the psychological well-being of occupants is also a priority, with factors such as lighting, color schemes, and views significantly impacting mental health (Liu et al., 2023).

findings.antecedent: Accessibility to green spaces (core principle of biomimetic architecture)
findings.consequent: Physical activity, overall health and well-being among building occupants
findings.quote: The accessibility to green spaces, a core principle of biomimetic architecture, encourages physical activity among building occupants, thereby contributing to their overall health and well-being.

findings.consequent: Physical health, quality of sleep, general health
findings.quote: Furthermore, the emphasis on creating environments that regulate circadian rhythms underscores the commitment of biomimetic design to the physical health of individuals, enhancing the quality of sleep and, by extension, their general health (Hower et al., 2018).

findings.antecedent: Biomimetic strategies (passive cooling, natural ventilation, water harvesting)
findings.quote: Biomimetic strategies such as passive cooling, natural ventilation, and water harvesting can significantly reduce a building's environmental impact.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry (studying natural forms for strength, flexibility, load-bearing)
findings.quote: Biomimicry offers architects insights into optimizing building structures by studying the strength, flexibility, and load-bearing capabilities of natural forms.

findings.antecedent: Proper ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC with filters, UV lights, bipolar ionization)
findings.consequent: Indoor air quality, reduced biological/chemical pollutants
findings.quote: Proper ventilation and air conditioning is crucial for maintaining indoor air quality. According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air. HVAC systems should include air filters (MERV 13 or higher as recommended by ASHRAE) to remove particulate matter, and may use technologies like UV lights or bipolar ionization to reduce biological and chemical pollutants (Ottney, 1993).

findings.consequent: Occupant comfort, prevention of mold growth
findings.quote: Controlling temperature (68-75°F) and humidity (30-60% RH) is also important for occupant comfort and preventing mold growth (Wu & Wong, 2022).
Building materials can off-gas volatile organic compounds (VOCs) like formaldehyde which are linked to respiratory issues and cancer risks.

findings.antecedent: Access to daylight and views to the outdoors
findings.quote: Access to daylight and views to the outdoors can improve mood, focus and sleep quality according to studies.
Excessive noise can increase stress and negatively impact sleep and cognitive performance.

Experiments in controlled environments reveal green walls' considerable promise as an acoustic insulator for architectural structures and that Rw15 dB and a 0.40 can be delivered with ease (Azkorra et al., 2015).

findings.consequent: Lower operating costs, enhanced efficiency, sustainability
findings.quote: Biomimetic designs contribute to lower operating costs in buildings through several mechanisms that enhance efficiency and sustainability.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry (termite mound inspired ventilation and temperature regulation)
findings.consequent: Use of air conditioning and heating systems, energy consumption, utility bills
findings.quote: For example, buildings that mimic termite mounds for natural ventilation and temperature regulation can significantly cut down on the use of air conditioning and heating systems, leading to lower energy consumption and reduced utility bills.

findings.consequent: Need for frequent cleaning and maintenance
findings.quote: For instance, self-cleaning surfaces inspired by the lotus leaf can reduce the need for frequent cleaning and maintenance (Finsterwalde, 2011).

Biomimicry encourages the use of materials in a way that mimics the efficiency of natural systems, often leading to less waste during construction (Al-Ketan et al., 2022). This efficient use of materials can reduce the overall material costs and waste management expenses.

findings.antecedent: Reduced HVAC use (due to biomimetic designs)
findings.quote: The energy savings from reduced HVAC use can be substantial, often reducing energy consumption by 30-50% compared to conventional buildings.
By mimicking the resilience of natural systems, biomimetic buildings can be more durable and require fewer repairs over time (Gruber, 2011).

findings.antecedent: Enhanced indoor air quality and natural light
findings.consequent: Occupant health, productivity, healthcare costs, overall productivity in commercial settings
findings.quote: Enhanced indoor air quality and natural light can improve occupant health and productivity, potentially reducing costs associated with healthcare and increasing the overall productivity in commercial settings (Al Horr et al., 2016).
Healthier environments also tend to have lower turnover rates and absenteeism.

findings.antecedent: Innovative biomimetic designs and improved indoor air quality
findings.consequent: Attractiveness to tenants/buyers, occupancy rates, rental incomes
findings.quote: Buildings with innovative biomimetic designs and improved indoor air quality are often more attractive to tenants and buyers, leading to higher occupancy rates and potentially higher rental incomes.

findings.antecedent: Hard-edged glass and concrete-dominated built environments
findings.consequent: Human inflammatory conditions and degraded public health/well-being

findings.antecedent: Mismatch between ancient genes and modern building habits
findings.quote: must we not also extend our care and efforts to protect the public from buildings that are physiologically and neurologically degrading because they represent “a mismatch between our ancient genes and our modern building habits.”

findings.antecedent: Removal from physiologically nourishing place ingredients (nature)

findings.antecedent: Cognitive dualism in built environments (disconnect from embodied animal nature)
findings.consequent: Neurobiologically mismatched places and cognitive dissonance

findings.consequent: Chronic stress with public health consequences (anxiety, depression, dementia, hypertension, heart attacks, death)
key_citations: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health (OASH), 2023

findings.consequent: Decreased microbial gut diversity and increased inflammatory diseases (especially in children)

findings.antecedent: Extreme urban heat (due to mechanical systems, heat-absorbing materials, lack of natural cooling)
findings.consequent: Increased deaths, blackouts, and health risks for humans and birds

Urban Form and Wayfinding: Review of Cognitive and Spatial Knowledge for Individuals' Navigation
limitations: How visitors make sense of an urban environment, create mental imagery and then use that image to navigate through the city is not fully known.

There is little research on how ubiquitous smart phone technology and global positioning systems (GPS) are complementing or disrupting processes of spatial knowledge acquisition and mental image creation.
The space syntax approach is not yet tested whether the elements it measures match well with actual image creation in human wayfinders.
The space syntax approach struggles to encapsulate issues of the conceptual, as criticized by semiologists of Lynch's work.
The flâneur approach has limitations in exploring internal processes of image creation, as social geographers tend to use it for higher-brow investigations of urban social relations.
Cullen's way of city interpretation is no longer fully applicable in modern urban environments due to changes in urban fabric and homogeneous planning.

Lynch's theory on urban form and cognitive mapping has limitations, as urban structures may act as symbols rather than directly facilitating movement, suggesting a conceptual rather than perceptual image of the city.
Lynch's cognitive mapping methodology is based on perception rather than conception, reducing the urban environment to only perceptual knowledge.
Lynch's five elements focus mostly on movement activity in urban environments, to the exclusion of other aspects of urban use.

The perception of cast shadows

findings.consequent: Information about object shape, background surface shape, and spatial arrangement
findings.quote: When an object casts its shadow on a background surface, the shadow can be informative about the shape of the object, the shape of the background surface and the spatial arrangement of the object relative to the background.
Among all these roles, we found that cast shadows were perceptually most relevant for the recovery of spatial arrangement, especially when the shadow is in motion.
the human visual system does not effectively use cast shadows as cues to surface shape, despite the potential reliability of the information they provide.

findings.consequent: Perception of object motion in depth
findings.quote: moving cast shadows can produce a very vivid impression of an object moving in depth.

findings.antecedent: Manipulation of an object's cast shadow motion
findings.quote: simply manipulating the motion of an object's cast shadow can dramatically change the perceived trajectory of the object.

The effects of static cast shadows on perceived depth relations between surfaces is phenomenologically clear, as shown in Fig. 3. Their perceptual salience has also been demonstrated experimentally, particularly in their ability to anchor surfaces in depth when they are placed in a perspective rendering.

cast shadows are non-commensurate with other depth cues because they provide global rather than local information about spatial layout.

findings.quote: In dynamic scenes, a feature appears which can very reliably determine proper shadow labeling: the relative motion of an object and its cast shadow is constrained to follow a line connecting the object to the light source.

The importance of correlated motion as a cue to shadow labeling may explain the divergent phenomenal effects of violating luminance constraints in the square-above-the-checkerboard movie and the ball-in-a-box movie.

findings.consequent: Reliable source of information for linking cast shadows and objects
findings.quote: In dynamic scenes, in which both objects and their cast shadows are moving, the correlated motion between an object and its shadow provides a reliable and simple source of information for linking cast shadows and objects.
